instances.label: Cement, lime or mineral kiln operator: at scheduled intervals takes grab samples of kiln feed, hot clinker and finished product from process points (chute, belt, sample port), splits/cools them, and sends them to the plant QC lab for XRF/free-lime analysis, adjusting kiln operation on the result.

Lumber dry kiln operator: places/retrieves sample boards in a kiln charge and takes moisture-content readings with a handheld or probe meter on boards from the dried charge, deciding whether the charge meets the moisture spec or needs more drying/reprocessing.

Chemical, soap or resin kettle/reactor tender: draws a hot batch sample through a sample valve or by dipping into the kettle, cools/quenches it into a labeled container, runs a quick bench check (viscosity, pH, titration, solids) and/or sends the vial to the on-site lab before the batch is released.

Rubber/composite curing oven or press tender: cuts a specimen from cured stock or a test slab and runs cure/hardness checks (rheometer, durometer) to verify the cure meets specification before the batch is released.

Drier operator (grain, minerals, sludge, wood chips): grabs samples of dried product off the discharge stream or conveyor, runs an on-site moisture/quality test or bags the sample for the lab, and adjusts drier settings to hold spec.

tasks.label: Stop equipment and clear blockages or jams, using fingers, wire, or hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Simple discrete-piece jam at a continuous oven/dryer/kiln conveyor: one rigid workpiece (part, board, veneer sheet, ware piece) has tipped or shifted at the infeed/outfeed and tripped the line. Operator hits e-stop, reaches in from outside the machine, frees or lifts the piece out by hand, restarts.

Complex jam inside a continuous dryer/oven/kiln: several pieces wedged, crossed or entangled under guide rails, rollers, chains or inside the hot chamber. Operator locks out, waits for partial cooldown, works in an awkward/hot space with pry bar, hook or hammer to free the material, checks for damage, restarts.

Bulk material bridging or plugging a feed chute, hopper, screw conveyor, air-lock or discharge on a dryer, kiln or kettle (damp sand or aggregate, sawdust, powder, clinker, lime). Operator stops the feeder, rods/hammers the chute, breaks the plug with a bar and shovels out spillage.

Clogged small orifice: burner tip or pilot port, spray/atomizing nozzle, lubricant or additive injection line, small feed tube, sight-glass port or kettle drain valve. Operator shuts down the burner/pump and clears the bore with wire, a drill bit, or a small hand tool, then verifies flow.

Hardened residue clogging removable components: screens, grates, strainers, filter elements, duct or pipe sections, kettle fittings. Operator removes the component with hand tools and clears the plugged passages at a bench or wash station before reinstalling.

Hardened buildup inside a fixed vessel or chamber: soap/asphalt residue on kettle walls and outlet, clinker or refractory rings inside a kiln, coating buildup in dryer ducts and cyclones. Requires shutdown, cooldown, sometimes confined-space entry, and chipping/scraping with hand tools.

instances.label: Commercial heat-treating shop or foundry: operator opens a batch furnace/quench/temper line, lifts hot baskets, trays or fixtured steel parts out with a hoist or charge car, lets them cool, then unloads parts into bins/racks and stages them for shipment or downstream machining.

Brick, structural clay, refractory or ceramic-tile plant: fired ware comes out of a tunnel or roller kiln on kiln cars; the tender dehacks/unloads ware from the car deck, culls broken pieces, and forms banded, wrapped dispatch packs for the yard.

Sawmill/lumber dry kiln: dried lumber packages are pulled from the kiln (track carts or forklift), stickers removed and destacked at the planer infeed, or packages trimmed, strapped and wrapped and staged in the shipping yard.

Rubber/composite curing: tender removes cured tires or molded rubber/composite parts from curing presses, vulcanizers or autoclaves, trims flash, places them on racks/conveyors for inspection, then stacks or palletizes them for shipment.

Chemical/soap kettle or industrial drier: after the batch is cooked or dried, the operator discharges product into drums, totes or bags, caps/seals and labels the containers, palletizes and stretch-wraps them, and moves them to warehouse storage.

Low-volume job shop batch oven or shuttle kiln (custom coatings, refractory shapes, composite tooling, lab driers): a small number of mixed, odd-shaped, sometimes fragile items are removed by hand or with a jib hoist, inspected, and hand-packed for the next operation.

tasks.label: Melt or refine metal before casting, calculating required temperatures, and observe metal color, adjusting controls as necessary to maintain required temperatures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Melt deck of a jobbing iron/steel foundry: tender charges a coreless induction furnace with scrap/returns and alloy, runs the melt to a target superheat computed for the casting job, dips a thermocouple lance and pulls a chemistry sample, adds trim alloys, rakes slag, and holds temperature until tap to the pouring ladle.

Aluminum/zinc melting-and-holding station in a die casting or permanent-mold plant: charge ingots and returns into a shaft/reverb melter, hold the bath at the casting temperature (e.g., 660-700 C), rotary-degas and flux the melt, skim dross, and keep the dosing/holding furnace supplying the casting machine at temperature.

Large secondary/cast-house remelt furnace: charge scrap bales, sows and alloying additions into a 100+ tonne reverberatory melting furnace, monitor bath temperature against the alloy recipe, adjust burner/power controls, skim dross, and tilt/tap the holding furnace to the casting machine on a continuous 24/7 cycle.

Small precision melt in a jewelry, dental or investment-casting shop: weigh a small charge of gold/silver/bronze or specialty alloy, melt it in a small induction or resistance crucible unit, judge readiness by color/pyrometer, hold at the pour temperature and cast into flasks.

Small art/jobbing foundry or repair shop kettle work: gas-fired crucible or kettle melting bronze, babbitt, solder, zinc or lead, tender judges the melt largely by eye/color, adds flux or deoxidizer, skims, adjusts the burner/thermostat by hand and lifts or tips the crucible to pour.

tasks.label: Weigh or measure specified amounts of ingredients or materials for processing, using devices such as scales and calipers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Chemical, soap or coatings kettle/reactor tender charges a batch: weighs 20-50 kg sacks of dry ingredients on a platform or hopper scale, meters liquids by weight or volume per the batch sheet, dumps them into the heated kettle and records the weights; tolerance about +/-0.5-1%. Setting: a company-controlled process plant with pallets, bag-dump stations and fixed vessels.

Glass, frit or refractory batch weighing: operator sets up and verifies weighing of sand, soda ash, limestone and cullet for the melting furnace, and hand-weighs minor colorants/oxides to close tolerance in the batch house before the mix goes to the melter. Setting: an industrial batch house with silos, weigh hoppers and conveyors.

Rubber/composite compound preparation for curing ovens or presses: weighing many small chemicals (accelerators, curatives, pigments) to gram accuracy into pre-weigh bags per recipe, plus bulk polymer and filler weights. Setting: a compounding room in a manufacturing plant.

Lumber dry-kiln operator measures the charge: selects kiln sample boards, weighs them on a scale, measures thickness/width with a caliper or rule and moisture with a meter, and computes moisture content to set or advance the drying schedule. Setting: sawmill kiln shed/yard controlled by the mill.

Small-shop, studio or laboratory-scale kiln/drier work: weighing gram-to-kilogram quantities of powders (glaze or body ingredients, compounds, sample materials) from open bags and buckets on a bench scale, and caliper-checking piece dimensions before and after firing. High mix, non-standard containers, frequent recipe changes.

Field or portable heated kettle work (roofing asphalt, sealant, tar, small mobile drier): measuring specified quantities of material or additive into the kettle using buckets, markings or a portable scale on a jobsite, outdoors, with variable footing, weather and layout.

tasks.label: Feed fuel, such as coal and coke, into fireboxes or onto conveyors, and remove ashes from furnaces, using shovels and buckets.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Hand-firing a small solid-fuel unit at a plant: through the shift the tender shovels coal, coke or wood waste from a nearby pile or barrow through the fire door of a boiler/kiln firebox, spreading fuel evenly over the grate by eye. Hot, dusty boiler house inside a plant.

Batch charging of solid fuel: carrying and dumping buckets or barrow loads of coke or fuel wood into a batch kiln, retort or furnace charge opening at prescribed intervals, weighing or counting charges, at a brick/lime/charcoal or process-heat plant.

Ash and clinker removal: raking and shovelling hot ash and clinker off the grate and out of the ash pit into buckets, cans or a wheelbarrow, hauling them to an ash bin or dumpster, and clearing spillage around the firing floor. Cramped, hot, dusty space under and around the furnace.

Moving bulk fuel from a stockpile or fuel bin onto the feed conveyor or into the boiler/kiln feed hopper - shovel and bucket work supplemented by a bucket loader - in the plant fuel yard or fuel house, keeping the conveyor supplied through the shift.

Firing and ash-clearing at an outdoor or field-erected unit (portable dryer, charcoal kiln, small field kiln, temporary heater): fuel piled on the ground, no fixed layout, weather and footing as found, ash raked out onto the ground and shovelled into containers.

tasks.label: Replace worn or defective equipment parts, using hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Thread-in or bolt-on sensing/metering parts on a kiln, oven or drier: operator locks out the unit, unscrews a failed thermocouple/RTD, burner tip, orifice or spray nozzle from its boss with wrenches, cleans the threads, installs the replacement with sealant or a crush gasket, reconnects the lead/plug and verifies the reading. Plant floor, access often at height or in a tight recess.

Consumable insert swap on driers, dust collectors, kettles or filter housings: unbolt or unclamp a housing lid/access door with hand tools, pull the fouled bag, screen, cartridge or strainer basket, drop in the new element, reseat and re-fasten the cover. Plant floor, part is dusty/wet but the fasteners are standard.

Drive-train wear parts on drier fans, mesh-belt ovens, kiln car drives and conveyors: remove guards, release a tensioner, strip off a worn V-belt, chain, sprocket, conveyor roller/idler or bearing, fit the new one, align pulleys and re-tension by feel. Work is in situ, under and around installed machinery.

Door seals and insulation: scrape out a baked-on, embrittled rope seal, silicone gasket or door gasket from an oven/kiln/kettle door channel, clean the surface, cut and fit new sealing material with adhesive or clips, adjust latches and check for leaks by closing the door on a strip. In situ, sooty, compliant materials.

Wired components: replace a burned-out electric heating element, igniter, solenoid valve, limit switch, contactor or small motor. Lock out, open a panel, tag and disconnect leads at screw terminals, withdraw the old component (often oxidized or seized in place), fit and rewire the replacement, then test-fire the unit. Plant floor, cabinet or element port.

Wet-end and piping parts on kettles, boilers and steam-heated driers: break a flanged or union joint, remove a leaking valve, steam trap, pump seal, hose or fitting, clean and dress the sealing face, fit a new gasket and part, torque bolts in pattern and leak-test on start-up. In situ piping, often overhead or in a pit, some seized fasteners.

tasks.label: Clean, lubricate, and adjust equipment, using scrapers, solvents, air hoses, oil, and hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Between-batch or end-of-campaign cleanout of the heated vessel/chamber itself: scraping burned-on soap, resin, pitch, carbon, glaze slag or product crust from kettle walls, oven hearth and racks, kiln furniture, or dryer plenum with scrapers, wire brushes, solvents and rags, on a cooled-down unit with confined, awkward access and deposits that vary in thickness and hardness. Setting: an operating plant (soap works, ceramic/brick plant, coating or curing oven bay, lumber dry-kiln shed).

Routine blow-down and housekeeping of the equipment periphery: air hose used to clear sawdust, lint, fines, ash or powder from burner assemblies, air registers, circulating fans, screens, filters, heat-exchanger fins, door seals and gauge faces, plus sweeping/vacuuming what falls out, done between cycles on the plant floor around the operator's own machine.

Scheduled lubrication round from a PM checklist: grease gun applied to zerk fittings on kiln-car wheels, conveyor and fan bearings, chain drives and door mechanisms; oil can on hinges, tracks and linkages; checking gearbox sight glasses and topping up oil reservoirs, on multiple pieces of equipment spread across the plant aisle.

Minor mechanical adjustment with hand tools: tensioning a drive belt or chain, tracking a conveyor belt or mesh, adjusting a damper linkage, burner air register or gas cock, repositioning a thermocouple or limit switch, snugging a leaking fitting or reseating a gasket, then running the unit and re-checking that temperature, airflow or belt travel is right.

Cleaning removable parts and tooling at a dedicated bench or wash bay: trays, racks, molds, kiln furniture, saggers, burner nozzles, filters and screens pulled from the unit and de-scaled with scrapers, solvent tank, steam/pressure wash or blast media, then dried and returned to service.

tasks.label: Discard or reject products, materials, or equipment not meeting specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Packaging/food or consumer-goods production line: inspector-weigher stationed at a moving conveyor pulls off-spec units (underweight or overweight packs, contaminated product, bad seals, discolored or damaged pieces) off the belt and drops them into a reject bin, hundreds to thousands of units per hour, in a plant with sanitation and line-speed standards.

Discrete-part quality check at a bench or in-process station (machine shop, plastics molder, electronics/assembly plant): inspector gauges or visually checks parts, then segregates the failing pieces into a red reject/scrap bin, marks or tags them nonconforming, and sets them aside on the MRB cart for later disposition.

Lot-level disposition in a receiving area, warehouse, or line-side staging: after a lot is failed by incoming or in-process inspection, the worker physically segregates it — moving flagged pallets, totes, or drums with a pallet jack/hand truck into the quarantine (hold) cage or the scrap area — keeping nonconforming stock physically separate from released stock.

Large, heavy, or bulk item rejection in a plant: a casting, weldment, coil, panel, tool, or piece of equipment fails inspection; the worker tags it, moves it with a hoist, crane, or forklift to the rework or scrap area, and in some shops defaces or cuts the scrapped item so it cannot be re-used.

Off-site or field disposition: inspector at a jobsite, supplier plant, delivery yard, or customer facility rejects delivered materials or condemns defective equipment, tagging it 'do not use'/'reject', setting it aside for return, or discarding it, under uncontrolled layout and weather.

tasks.label: Mark items with details, such as grade or acceptance-rejection status.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Discrete small/medium manufactured parts (machined parts, castings, moldings, electronic assemblies) marked at an inspection or test station on the plant floor: an ink dot, stamp, laser/dot-peen code or pass/fail sticker is applied to each part after test, at line rate, with parts arriving in trays, totes or on a conveyor.

Continuous grading/sorting line (planer mill lumber, flat glass, fabric roll, panel board): the worker applies a grade stamp, ink code or defect flag to each piece or at each defect location as material moves past at high speed.

Heavy semi-finished product in a mill or fabrication shop (steel coils, slabs, billets, plates, pipe, bundles): attaching a printed hang tag or metal tag, or stencil/paint-spray marking heat number, grade and accept-reject status, on hot, dirty, heavy items presented on roller tables or staged in the bay.

Marking individual defect locations on large complex assemblies or surfaces (painted car bodies, appliance panels, aircraft skins): the inspector circles or dots each flaw found at its precise location so a rework operator can find it, on units moving through the plant.

Lot- or batch-level marking after off-line/sample inspection in an inspection room or receiving area: applying QC acceptance stamps, serialized labels, colored 'hold/reject' tags or stickers to sampled units, cartons or pallets of mixed product handled manually.

Field or outdoor marking: paint-sticking or tagging rejected/accepted material in a lay-down yard, jobsite, scrap yard or at a customer site, where items are stacked as found and conditions (weather, layout, lighting) are uncontrolled.

tasks.label: Measure dimensions of products to verify conformance to specifications, using measuring instruments, such as rulers, calipers, gauges, or micrometers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Quality-lab / inspection-bench check of small-to-medium machined parts: inspector takes a tote or rack of one part number to a bench in the QC room or plant inspection area, measures 5-20 dimensions per sample piece with calipers, micrometers, bore and height gauges against the print, records results and dispositions the lot.

In-process / first-piece inspection at the machine on the shop floor: parts straight off a CNC, press or grinder (coolant, chips, burrs), checked for a handful of critical dimensions with hand gauges and comparators between cycles, with frequent part changeovers and immediate feedback to the operator.

High-volume production-line sampling: fixed inspection station beside a line producing stampings, moldings, turned parts or fasteners; every Nth piece pulled and gauged on a few critical dimensions, pass/fail sorting and SPC logging at line rate.

Large fabricated or assembled products: weldments, castings, sheet-metal or aerospace/automotive assemblies measured on the fabrication floor with tape measures, large calipers, height gauges, portable arms or trackers, with the part resting on a table, fixture or the floor.

Incoming / receiving inspection in a plant receiving-QC area: mixed low-volume purchased components and raw stock (bar, tube, sheet, fasteners, castings), a few pieces per lot, many different part numbers, print-driven dimensional layout and documentation.

tasks.label: Notify supervisors or other personnel of production problems.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Inspect, test, or measure materials, products, installations, or work for conformance to specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: At-line inspection of manufactured parts on a production floor (machined, stamped, molded or assembled parts): inspector takes parts off the line or from a bin at a workstation, checks surfaces for defects, takes caliper/micrometer/gauge dimensions against the drawing, accepts, tags or segregates nonconforming pieces, and records results.

Off-line measurement of sampled parts in a QC lab, gauge room or receiving area: first-article and in-process audits and incoming-lot sampling of purchased components and raw stock, using CMM, height gauge, optical comparator and hand metrology against drawings/GD&T, producing an inspection report and lot disposition.

Functional/performance testing of finished assemblies at a test bench or test floor: connect or load the unit into a tester (electrical/electronic test, leak, pressure, calibration check), run the test sequence to specification limits, and bin/pass/fail and log the unit.

High-volume sorting and grading of small items flowing on a conveyor (food product, plastics, fasteners, recovered materials): watch a moving stream, identify off-spec or foreign items and remove or divert them at line speed.

In-plant walk-down inspection of installed equipment and utilities: follow a route through the facility, read gauges and level indicators, check lever/valve positions, take thermal and vibration/acoustic readings, and log deviations from specified operating values.

Hands-on field inspection of installations and in-place work at an as-found site (job site, tank farm, erected structure, customer site): visual and contact NDT of welds, coatings and wall thickness, dimensional checks of installed work, with access, weather and layout as encountered.

instances.label: At an inspection bench in a plant QC area, the inspector zeroes/adjusts hand-held precision measuring instruments (micrometer, caliper, dial indicator, height gage) against gage blocks or a master: unlock and rotate the sleeve/adjusting nut with a spanner or turn a setscrew, re-check against the standard, repeat until readings fall within tolerance, then lock and tag.

On the shop floor or in the gage crib, the inspector resets adjustable gaging and check fixtures to a master ring, plug or setting disc — snap gage anvils, dial bore gages, comparator stands, go/no-go fixtures — turning setscrews and locking nuts by feel while watching the indicator, then verifying repeatability on the master.

After measurements show parts drifting, the inspector makes a minor in-place adjustment to the production machine or tooling in the plant: turns a setscrew on a stop or guide, nudges a fence/rail, shims or tweaks a tool holder, then runs and re-measures parts to confirm they are back in tolerance.

Adjusts in-line test/inspection equipment other than weighing gear in the plant: repositions or trims a sensor on a leak tester, torque tester, or vision station, adjusts a trim pot or micro-adjust screw, and re-runs a reference/master part until the instrument reads the certified value within tolerance.

Checks and adjusts weighing equipment in place — bench balance, floor scale, or in-line checkweigher — by running test weights, then performing the span/zero adjustment (internal calibration routine or external adjustment) until indicated mass is within tolerance, and documenting the result.

Field/on-site adjustment away from the controlled bench: calibrating and adjusting installed or portable equipment at a remote plant location, outdoor yard, jobsite, or customer facility (truck scale, tank gage, portable hardness tester, field instrument), with variable access, lighting, weather and clutter.

instances.label: High-volume CNC machining/turning production: the inspector pulls parts at set intervals, gauges critical dimensions with micrometers, bore gauges or a shop-floor CMM, tracks SPC trends, and adjusts tool offsets or calls a tool change when dimensions drift. Machine shop floor, standard fixturing, machines enclosed.

Filling/packaging line (food, beverage, pharma): the inspector monitors fill weight/level, seal integrity, cap torque, label placement and date codes on a running line, pulls samples, and adjusts filler/capper/labeler settings or takes a faulty filling valve out of service.

Continuous or converting process (injection molding, extrusion, paper/board, coating, rolling): the inspector monitors process readouts and product properties (part weight, thickness, basis weight, moisture, color), pulls samples for test, and changes machine setpoints to bring the process back within spec.

Electronics SMT assembly line: the inspector monitors printing, placement and reflow, reviews solder-paste and optical inspection results, and adjusts printer parameters, stencil cleaning frequency or placement offsets to hold the process in spec.

Mechanical/discrete assembly line (automotive, appliance, aerospace subassembly): the inspector monitors assembly stations and in-process checks (fit and gap, torque, sealant/adhesive bead, leak or function test), corrects misassemblies and adjusts fixtures, nutrunner settings or applicator paths.

Low-volume job shop, fabrication or heavy assembly: setups change daily, the inspector performs first-article checks against drawings, monitors welding, forming or machining of one-off or small-lot parts, diagnoses the cause of out-of-spec results and adjusts setup, feeds/speeds or weld parameters.

instances.label: Precision machine shop / CNC job shop: inspector checks machined metal parts at an inspection bench, finds burrs on edges, hole breakouts and cross-drilled intersections, and removes them with a hand deburring tool, file, scraper or small abrasive without altering tolerances; high part mix, small batches.

Foundry or forging finishing area: inspector finds residual flash, gate stubs, parting-line burrs and chips on castings/forgings during inspection and grinds them off with a die grinder or pedestal wheel, blending to the surrounding contour before the part moves on.

Sheet-metal fabrication / steel service center: inspector removes dross, slag, sharp edges and burrs from plasma- or laser-cut plate, stampings and weldments found at inspection, using belt sander, deburring wheel or grinder to a specified edge break.

High-value part finishing (aerospace engine parts, medical implants, molds, sealing faces): inspector finds a nick, scratch, pit or corrosion spot and blends/laps/polishes the localized defect to a specified depth and finish, then re-inspects to confirm the part is within limits.

Repair/reconditioning shop: inspector receives used or stored parts, tooling and fixtures with rust, corrosion or pitted surfaces and removes the corrosion by abrasive pad, wire wheel, blasting or laser cleaning, then rechecks the surface before return to service.

In-place work on items too large or too installed to move: inspector on a plant floor, tank interior, structural steel member or ship section abrades corroded/pitted areas or grinds off surface defects at the location where the item sits, on scaffolding or a lift.

tasks.label: Check arriving materials to ensure that they match purchase orders, submitting discrepancy reports as necessary.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-throughput carton/case receiving at a plant or distribution-center dock: floor-loaded or palletized uniform labeled cases come off a trailer; the worker counts and scans cases, verifies SKU/part number and quantity against the ASN/purchase order, watches for crushed or wet cases, and logs shortages/overages as receiving exceptions.

Manufacturing plant receiving dock with mixed pallet loads and non-carton goods: drums, banded bar stock, crates, castings in returnable bins, sheet stock. Worker matches paper packing slip/bill of lading to the PO, counts pieces or bundles, checks part/heat/lot numbers and visible damage, receives into ERP and files a discrepancy (DMR) report for wrong or short material.

Small plant or job-shop receiving of small-lot parcels and boxes: worker opens cartons, identifies loose parts (often unlabeled or hand-labeled), counts pieces, compares each line to the PO and drawing revision, and writes up shortages, wrong revisions, or substituted parts.

Receiving/incoming quality inspection: worker pulls an AQL sample from a received lot, verifies dimensions and visual attributes against the drawing/spec with calipers, gauges, or a CMM, reviews the certificate of conformance/material cert, and dispositions the lot with an accept tag or nonconformance/discrepancy report.

Bulk or liquid raw material receiving at a plant scale house: truck or railcar of aggregate, coal, resin, chemical or similar is weighed in and out, a representative sample is taken for lab analysis, net quantity is compared to the PO/BOL, and weight or quality variances are reported.

tasks.label: Inspect or test raw materials, parts, or products to determine compliance with environmental standards.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Incoming-inspection / QC area of an electronics or consumer-goods plant: inspector screens incoming parts, plastics, solder, cables and finished assemblies for RoHS/ELV/Prop-65 restricted substances (Pb, Cd, Hg, Cr, Br) with handheld or benchtop XRF, selecting measurement points per IEC 62321, judging pass/fail/inconclusive and logging lot results.

Plant QC laboratory: inspector receives raw-material, coating, process-water or effluent samples, prepares them (dilution, digestion, homogenization, extraction) and runs titration, IC/GC-MS, pH/conductivity or VOC-content tests against environmental limits, then reports compliance results.

End-of-line test station on a production line: inspector performs environmental-compliance testing of finished products - helium/refrigerant leak-tightness of HVAC-R units and fuel-cell or fuel-system modules (F-gas/EPA 608), evaporative-emission leak tests, or exhaust-emission drive cycles on a dynamometer - connecting the unit, running the test and dispositioning failures.

Receiving/sorting area of a scrap yard, foundry or recycling facility: inspector examines incoming scrap or recycled feedstock loads on the sort line for prohibited and hazardous contaminants (copper, wires, trash, sealed containers, batteries) and removes off-spec material so the stream meets purity and environmental permit requirements.

Walking survey rounds through an operating chemical, gas or manufacturing plant to check for fugitive emissions and gas leaks at flanges, valves, seals and tanks (LDAR-style checks with gas detectors/acoustic or optical imaging), recording readings and flagging exceedances.

Collecting physical compliance samples in the plant: grab or flow-paced composite samples from outfalls, tanks, sumps or process streams, bottling, preserving, labeling and handing off with chain-of-custody for permit reporting.

tasks.label: Compare colors, shapes, textures, or grades of products or materials with color charts, templates, or samples to verify conformance to standards.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-line / at-line inspection on a manufacturing production line: inspector picks parts or packages coming off the line (molded plastic parts, painted components, printed cartons, labels) and compares color, shape and surface appearance to a master 'gold' sample or color chip, then passes or routes nonconforming units to a reject bin. Standard plant lighting, high throughput, repeated part families.

Bench/QC-lab comparison of samples: swatches, coupons, resin pellets, coating draw-downs, or extruded samples judged under a standardized light booth against physical color standards, texture/gloss boundary samples and grade charts; verdict is a pass/fail or a shade/grade classification recorded on a QC form.

Continuous grading/sorting of bulk or web material at a sorting line: scrap metal and recycled streams, lumber, ceramic tile, fabric rolls — the worker stands at a moving belt or grading chain and classifies items by color, shape, texture and grade, pulling off or diverting off-grade material at high throughput.

Whole-unit appearance inspection of large assembled goods (finished vehicle bodies, appliances, cabinets, furniture): the inspector walks around the unit under inspection lighting, checking paint/stain color match between panels, gloss, grain and texture against approved standards, and marks defects for rework.

Receiving/field inspection outside a fixed inspection station: sampling incoming lots at a dock, in a warehouse aisle, at a supplier plant or on a job site — cutting or pulling a sample from a bale, roll, pallet or delivered batch and comparing it to a color chart or retained sample under whatever light is available, then accepting or rejecting the lot.

instances.label: Start-of-shift/end-of-shift care of hand instruments at an inspection bench or gauge station on the shop floor: wipe coolant, chips and fingerprints off digital calipers, micrometers and dial indicators, oil the faces, check zero against a gauge block or setting standard, re-zero, and log the check.

Scheduled in-house calibration in a gauge crib or measuring room: dial indicators, plug/ring gauges, micrometers, height gauges and gauge blocks checked against masters on a calibration bench or comparator, deviations recorded at several points, pass/fail decided, sticker and certificate issued.

Cleaning removable fixed gauges, master parts and check fixtures brought to a wash-up area: thread and plug gauges, ring gauges, gauge-block sets, snap gauges and detachable fixture details degreased, rinsed, dried and rust-preventive applied before return to the crib.

In-situ cleaning and upkeep of installed test equipment on the floor or in the lab: granite surface plate wiped and stoned, optical comparator screen and lenses cleaned, hardness-tester anvil and indenter cleaned, leak-test bench and gauging fixtures blown out and wiped where they stand.

Adjusting and repairing instruments: replacing a dial indicator crystal, bezel or contact point, swapping batteries and worn fingertips, freeing a sticky spindle, lapping/deburring worn gauge members, tagging out-of-tolerance gauges and packaging them for the outside calibration house.

Verification/calibration of the automated measuring equipment itself: qualifying CMM probe styli against the reference sphere, re-mastering a shop-floor comparative gauging system with its master part, checking bore-gauge and air-gauge setting masters, and recording the results.

Correcting defects away from a controlled plant: at a customer site, construction/erection site, outdoor storage yard or on installed equipment, where layout varies site to site, access is awkward and conditions (weather, clutter, unknown fixtures) are taken as found.

tasks.label: Compute usable amounts of items in shipments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Receiving inspection of a homogeneous, high-volume piece-part shipment at a plant or DC (fasteners, stampings, turned or molded parts): verify piece counts (count-by-weight or piece count), check for damaged/out-of-tolerance units, and compute and record the usable quantity in ERP.

Receiving inspection of a mixed / low-volume shipment (assorted SKUs, cartons of diverse goods, assemblies, kits): open and check cartons against packing list, judge condition and conformance of varied items, compute usable quantity and post short/damaged amounts.

Sorting or containment of a suspect or mixed lot of small manufactured parts: 100% inspect each piece, separate conforming from nonconforming, and tally the number of usable pieces returned to inventory with a certified count report.

Bulk raw-material lot received at a mill or plant (lumber packs, metal coil/bar, sheet stock, resin): weigh/measure the lot, grade or inspect it, deduct off-spec, damaged or wet/rusted portions, and compute usable weight, board footage, or length.

Roll or web goods shipment (fabric, paper, film, foil, nonwovens): inspect along each roll, map and point-score defects, and compute usable yardage/footage per roll and for the shipment for invoicing or claims.

Delivery received in the field or an unstructured outdoor site (jobsite laydown yard, salvage/damaged-freight assessment): assess a heterogeneous load taken as found and compute how much of it is usable for a claim or work order.

Discrete manufactured parts (fasteners, machined, stamped, molded parts, glass/plastic containers) presented in bins, trays or on a line: worker gauges dimensions with calipers/gauges, checks surface finish and color, classifies each part pass/rework/scrap and places it in the correct bin, logging counts. Materials recovery / waste / scrap facility picking line: worker stands at a moving belt of mixed, dirty, heterogeneous material and sorts by material type, grade and size into chutes - heavy contamination, unpredictable object mix, loud and dusty but institution-controlled premises.

Distribution center or parcel hub: mixed packaged goods and parcels arriving in gaylords, totes or on belts are classified by size, weight and SKU/destination class and placed into the correct sack, tote or lane; over-size and off-weight items diverted; counts and weights recorded.

Outdoor yard or non-line setting (scrap yard, salvage/C&D operation, steel or pipe yard, transfer station): worker classes bulky heterogeneous material or stock into grades and piles as it is found - loose in heaps or on the ground, weather and layout varying by site.

tasks.label: Disassemble defective parts or components, such as inaccurate or worn gauges or measuring instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Plant inspection station: a unit or subassembly of a known, recurring product model fails in-process or incoming inspection, and the inspector removes screws, clips and covers with hand/power tools to expose and pull the out-of-spec component for measurement. Same product family repeatedly; standard fasteners; unit may be damaged.

Gauge crib / calibration lab: an inaccurate or worn measuring instrument (micrometer, dial indicator, caliper, torque wrench, bore or plug gauge, checking fixture) is stripped down to inspect and replace worn anvils, spindles, springs, gear trains or contact points. Mixed makes and models in ones and twos, small delicate parts, galled or staked threads, judgment on how far to strip.

Failure-analysis / warranty-returns teardown: a returned or field-failed unit of variable model and vintage is opened non-destructively to find root cause. Unknown damage, seized, stripped or corroded fasteners, adhesive or crimped joints; must preserve evidence and stop when the defect is exposed.

Destructive or mechanical separation of a sampled part for internal inspection: pressing a bearing or bushing off a shaft, cutting open a housing, sectioning a weld or crimp coupon, breaking a bonded joint, removing potting - done at a bench, press or saw in a lab or shop on a repeating sample part.

In-situ partial disassembly at a plant, customer site or field location: removing a cover, meter, valve internal or instrument from installed equipment so it can be inspected, working at the equipment as found, sometimes at height or in a confined space.

instances.label: Packaging/filling line in a food, beverage or consumer-goods plant: at set intervals the inspector pulls filled packages off the line, places them on a bench scale or checkweigher, tares packaging, compares net weight to target and tolerance, records on a control chart and signals the filler operator to adjust. Plant floor, standard equipment, institution-controlled.

Pharma/nutraceutical/chemical dispensary or batching area: verify ingredient quantities against the batch record - tare drums, kegs or bags on platform/floor scales in a weigh booth, weigh out or check-weigh each raw material, sign/second-verify the record. Indoor GMP facility, controlled access, mixed container sizes up to sacks and drums.

QC laboratory bench: weigh samples and aliquots on analytical/precision balances - tare vessel, transfer powder or liquid sample, check balance calibration with test weights, record result to LIMS/logbook. Indoor lab, standard human labware, controlled premises.

Receiving/shipping or process area of a plant or warehouse: weigh drums, totes, IBCs, pallets, coils or bulk containers on floor scales, pallet-jack or forklift scales; compare to bill of lading, spec or tare weight; record and flag discrepancies. Handling done with material-handling equipment.

Shipping/packing area of a distribution center: weigh finished cartons or parcels to verify contents against the packing list and to confirm shipping weight, diverting or re-working under/over-weight packages. Conveyorized or bench-scale workstation in a controlled facility.

Outdoor/field sampling at a scrap yard, quarry stockpile, jobsite or customer site: collect a sample or load, weigh with a portable scale, hanging scale or truck scale under weather and variable footing, record against the ticket or spec. Layout differs site to site.

tasks.label: Clean and polish metal items and jewelry pieces, using jewelers' tools, polishing wheels, and chemical baths.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench jeweler in a retail store or trade shop finishes a one-off customer repair: after sizing/soldering a ring shank or chain, the piece is pickled in an acid bath, then pre-polished and buffed on the polishing lathe with tripoli and rouge, then ultrasonic- and steam-cleaned for same-day pickup. Pieces are unique, frequently stone-set, and must come back bright with no rounded edges or loose stones.

Counter/back-room service cleaning: batches of customer rings, chains and bracelets checked and run through the ultrasonic bath and steam cleaner, dried, and given a light rouge-cloth buff, often while the customer waits during a routine inspection/cleaning visit.

Production finishing in a jewelry manufacturing shop: batches of newly cast, stamped or laser-cut sterling silver and 10K/14K gold rings, pendants and chain, sprue areas cleaned up and pieces run through tumblers, magnetic pin/disc/drag finishers and buffing wheels, then ultrasonically cleaned before plating or shipping.

Delicate and heirloom work: antique silver hollowware or filigree restoration, engraved or hallmarked pieces, enamel, and items with pearls, opals or emeralds. Selective hand polishing with brushes, thread, tips and cloths, deciding which areas to leave alone, keeping ultrasonic/chemical baths away from soft or porous gems and glued settings.

Larger or bulkier metal items: silver hollowware, trophies, flatware, belt buckles, watch cases and bracelets, cut down and buffed on larger polishing wheels with several compounds, then dip/ultrasonic cleaned and dried.

tasks.label: Smooth soldered joints and rough spots, using hand files and emery paper, and polish smoothed areas with polishing wheels or buffing wire.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail/trade-shop bench: after sizing a plain, unset gold or platinum wedding band, the jeweler files the solder seam flush inside and outside the shank, works through emery paper, then buffs on a polishing lathe with tripoli and rouge to match the band's original bright finish.

Retail bench: finishing the sizing/shank solder joint on a customer's stone-set ring (pave, channel, prongs, sometimes heat-sensitive or antique). The joint must be filed flush and blended without touching stones, hallmarks, engraving or an existing satin/hammered finish; buffing done with small wheels and hand pressure around settings.

Fine repair work: soldered chain links, clasps, jump rings, earring posts, retipped prongs and bezel repairs. Tiny joints on thin wire are cleaned with needle files and abrasive points, then polished with small buffs, bristle brushes or buffing wire, working around set stones and delicate links.

Custom/artisan studio: a one-off fabricated pendant, bracelet or ring with several solder seams in different orientations and mixed textures (matte panels, bright edges, mixed metals). The maker files and emeries each seam by eye, then selectively polishes only the areas that should be bright.

Production/manufacturing shop: batches of identical cast or soldered components (rings, findings, charms) - sprue stubs, parting lines and seam roughness removed and the batch brought to a uniform high polish before stone setting or plating.

Silversmithing/holloware and larger objects: a repaired teapot handle joint, trophy seam or flatware repair - larger soldered joints filed and emeried, then buffed on large wheels, matching the surrounding finish or patina on a one-off, often antique, piece.

tasks.label: Make repairs, such as enlarging or reducing ring sizes, soldering pieces of jewelry together, and replacing broken clasps and mountings.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Ring sizing at a bench in a retail jewelry store's back shop or a wholesale trade shop: measure the ring, saw the shank, remove metal or insert matching sizing stock, align and torch- or laser-solder the joint, file, emery and polish the seam invisible, then check stone tightness and clean. Metals and shank profiles vary piece to piece (14k/18k yellow, white, rose, platinum, silver); some rings carry heat-sensitive stones or engraving that constrain the method.

Chain and link soldering: rejoining a broken fine gold necklace or bracelet chain (rope, box, herringbone, cable), closing and soldering a jump ring, or soldering two pieces/charms together under magnification with tiny solder chips, flux, tweezers and a micro-torch or laser welder, then re-polishing and cleaning without melting surrounding links.

Replacing broken findings: fitting a new lobster claw, spring ring, box or fold-over clasp on a necklace or bracelet, replacing earring posts, backs or a bail; selecting a matching finding from stock, attaching by solder or laser weld, and testing the mechanism at the store bench with same-week turnaround.

Mounting and prong repair: retipping worn prongs, rebuilding or replacing a head, repairing a bezel or cracked mounting, tightening or resetting stones displaced by the damage; requires removing or protecting heat-sensitive gems, judging how much metal remains, and finishing so the repair is invisible to a customer inspecting the piece.

Non-standard repairs: bent or crushed hollow bands, antique or mixed-metal and enameled pieces of unknown alloy, pieces with missing parts that must be fabricated, plus incidental soldering repairs to eyeglass frames, silverware or watch bracelets brought to the counter; each item is unique and the method is decided case by case.

Production wax setting for stone-in-place casting at a manufacturing facility: melee stones are placed into the seats of wax/resin models per the CAD layout (heated wax pen or vacuum tweezer), stones held for casting-in-place; high volume, identical models, standardized stone sizes.

Fashion / costume / mass-market setting: stones are press-fitted or glue-set into stamped or molded standardized mountings, hardware and findings on a production line; hundreds to thousands of identical parts, uniform machine-cut stones, tolerance requirements lower than fine jewelry.

Jeweler realigns bent or splayed prongs, a twisted head, or a knocked-over setting on a ring or earring with the gemstone still in place, working under a microscope/loupe with fine chain-nose and prong pliers, applying just enough force to move the metal without cracking the stone.

Repair-shop jeweler straightens kinked fine chain links, bent earring posts and hoops, distorted jump rings, clasps, brooch pins and other findings on finished pieces using needle-nose/chain-nose pliers, often on thin, plated, or hollow wire that work-hardens and snaps if over-worked.

Silversmith/jeweler reshapes a crushed hollow bracelet, hollow bead, or dented/bent silver hollowware or flatware: straightens a twisted handle, raises dents, and restores contour with mallet, stakes, and pliers while preserving chased or engraved decoration.

Jewelry manufacturing/production setting: worker straightens batches of identical components (posts, wire forms, pin stems, thin cast bands) that came out of casting, tumbling, or handling slightly bent, correcting each to the same nominal geometry against a gauge or fixture before assembly.

tasks.label: Plate articles such as jewelry pieces and watch dials, using silver, gold, nickel, or other metals.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail/trade repair shop bench: rhodium-plating a single white gold ring, pendant or earrings after sizing/repair. Jeweler ultrasonically cleans and steams the piece, electrocleans it, wires it to a cathode, dips it in a heated rhodium beaker at set volts for seconds-to-minutes, rinses, dries and inspects for uniform coverage with no bleed onto stones. One or a few mixed pieces at a time, stones in place.

Repair/trade shop re-plating assorted customer items in gold, silver or nickel: worn gold-plated chains and bracelets, silver flatware/hollowware, watch cases and bracelets. Requires identifying the base metal, sometimes stripping old plate, masking areas, choosing bath and time, then plating, rinsing, drying, buffing and inspecting. Highly varied one-off items.

Jewelry manufacturer or plating job shop: batch plating of hundreds of identical castings, findings or fashion-jewelry pieces (copper/nickel underplate, gold flash, rhodium, silver) on rack or barrel tank lines. Worker racks or loads parts, runs the clean/rinse/plate/rinse/dry sequence to specification, unloads, and QCs thickness and color.

Watch dial / small watch-component plating in a component manufacturing facility: brass dial blanks and small parts held on dedicated fixtures, nickel and gold baths to a specified thickness, very high cosmetic standard (no spots, handling marks or fingerprints), batch quantities, controlled bath chemistry and inspection.

Selective / brush ('pen') plating and touch-ups on one-off pieces: spot-plating a repaired or worn area, restoring two-tone finishes by masking parts of a finished piece, touching up plating near set stones or on an antique silver-plated article. Each item differs; the worker decides where to mask and how long to plate by eye.

tasks.label: Soften metal to be used in designs by heating it with a gas torch and shape it, using hammers and dies.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail/repair bench in a jewelry store or trade shop: the jeweler anneals a customer's ring shank with a gas torch, then hammers it round on a steel mandrel, hammers a band up half a size, or trues a bent/out-of-round shank. Every piece is unique (unknown alloy, worn profile, often stones in place); the original finish must survive and the final size must be exact.

Custom fabrication at the bench: anneal wire, sheet or ingot with a torch and forge it by hand into a bespoke form - tapering a band, forging a cuff or bangle, forming a bezel over a mandrel, hammer-texturing a surface - repeatedly re-annealing as the metal work-hardens, with the shape judged by eye against a sketch or customer's wishes.

Bench forming with dies of repeatable components in ones-to-dozens: anneal cut discs/blanks and dome them in a dapping block, press them into a pattern/impression die in a small hydraulic press, swage or stamp findings, bezel cups, charms; blanks are identical and the die fixes the resulting shape.

Manufacturing/production shop: anneal rolled sheet, wire or struck blanks and die-strike or press-form batches of identical components (ring shanks, settings, findings, stamped charms) on drop hammers or hydraulic presses, with re-annealing between strikes; output must match a fixed pattern to gauge.

Forming simple hollow shapes (bowls, cups, wide domed bangles, spun cones) in silver or gold: repeated anneal-and-form over a mandrel/stake or in a forming die until the geometric form is achieved; the accepted output is a smooth, geometrically correct hollow form.

Studio silversmithing/art metal: raising and planishing a one-off hollowware or sculptural piece through many torch-annealing cycles, with hammer marks, asymmetric profiles and surface character that are the artistic point of the piece and judged by eye.

Purpose-built industrial cell; aircraft-scale parts, not jewelry-scale finish work.

It is the machine analogue of 'soften metal by heating and shape it with hammers and dies', but at aircraft-part scale and tolerance, so it substantiates heat-and-form cells generally rather than jewelry-quality bench work.

tasks.label: Pour molten metal alloys or other materials into molds to cast models of jewelry.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small custom/repair jewelry shop or one-person studio: for a one-off ring or a repair part, the jeweler melts 10–100 g of sterling silver or 14k/18k gold (torch-and-crucible or small benchtop induction caster) and pours/casts it into a single invested flask taken hot from the burnout kiln; a few casts per week, cosmetic-grade result required.

Mid-size production casting department (in-house casting for a manufacturing jeweler): batches of invested flasks with wax trees are carried from the burnout oven, alloy grain plus scrap is weighed, and each flask is cast on a vacuum-pressure or centrifugal casting machine; several casts per hour of gold/silver, porosity and fill quality tracked.

High-volume casting house / large jewelry manufacturer: continuous shifts of flask after flask, standardized alloys and casting programs, automatic metal feeding, documented temperatures and cycle records for quality certification.

Platinum or other high-temperature / specialty alloy casting (Pt, Pd, high-melting alloys) at a dedicated casting station: small flasks, melt temperatures 1,600–1,800 °C, tight temperature control, inert gas, high metal value at risk.

Non-flask pours in the workshop: pouring reclaimed or fresh metal into ingot/bar molds for later rolling or drawing, and artisanal open-mold work (delft clay, cuttlefish bone, sand or open-face molds) where the mold is improvised and fragile.

tasks.label: Design and fabricate molds, models, and machine accessories, and modify hand tools used to cast metal and jewelry pieces.

instances.label: Custom/production shop: create a master model (pattern) for a new piece — a ring, pendant or signet — either hand-carved in wax at the bench with files, wax pens and gravers, or designed in CAD and produced as a castable wax/resin master. Output must be dimensionally correct, castable, and detailed enough for pave/prong work.

Manufacturing shop: fabricate a production mold for wax injection from a design the shop already holds digitally (CAD), including designing the parting line, gates and vents, and proving the mold by injecting test waxes that shoot clean and hold size.

Shop with a physical master only (a customer's ring or a metal master model): pack raw rubber/silicone around the master in an aluminum frame, vulcanize under heat and pressure, then hand-cut the cured block open along an interlocking wavy parting line with a scalpel while flexing the rubber, and test-inject.

Casting room: build the investment mold — sprue and attach wax/resin patterns to a tree or rubber base, seat the flask, mix investment powder and water, pour and de-air under vacuum, let set and load for burnout, at flask sizes and wall detail suited to gold/silver.

Bench: shape or modify hand tools for a specific job — grind and hone a graver's face and heel angles, reshape plier jaws or a bezel pusher face, make a custom punch, burnisher, stake or dapping tool from tool steel, then harden/temper and polish the working face.

Shop floor: fabricate a machine accessory or fixture — a custom mandrel, holding jig for a laser welder or setting machine, polishing-lathe attachment, or a stop/fixture that positions a piece repeatably — machined from bar stock or plate to fit existing equipment.

Cutting open a vulcanized rubber or RTV silicone mold around a master model with a fresh scalpel: working around the block by feel and sight, cutting interlocking zigzag keys and reliefs, freeing the master without tearing the cavity, and cutting the sprue gate so injected waxes release cleanly.

Cutting a design into hard tooling: sinking a relief design into a steel or brass hub, master die, or metal/graphite mold cavity used to strike or mold jewelry parts, in a manufacturer's tool room, to tolerances that will reproduce fine detail in struck metal.

Reworking an existing model or mold at the bench: recutting or sharpening details on a cast or milled master, cutting air vents, gates and register cuts into an existing mold, and hand-finishing the cut surfaces so the mold or model performs in production.

tasks.label: Rout out locations where parts are to be joined to items, using routing machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Manufacturing/production shop: a CNC mill, mill-turn lathe or router cuts stone pockets, prong seats and recesses into cast or turned precious-metal components (bands, mountings, findings) from CAD data, so stones or heads can later be set/joined. Retail/trade shop bench: jeweler routs a seat or recess into a new mounting or shank with a flex-shaft handpiece, burs or a benchtop micro-mill so a head, bezel, bail or clasp sits flush before soldering; piece is new (CAD model or standard catalog finding), geometry known.

Routing channels/pockets for channel-set stones or for an inlay (wood, opal, meteorite, enamel) in a ring or watch band, on a benchtop mill or CNC engraving machine with a ring fixture, from a defined design.

Larger or awkward items: routing a recess in hollowware, a trophy, a locket lid or a box to seat an applied nameplate, hinge or ornament, using a rotary engraving/router machine with a fixture or vacuum table.

tasks.label: Weigh, mix, and melt metal alloys or materials needed for jewelry models.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench jeweler in a retail/repair shop back room: weighs a customer's scrap gold or a few grams of casting grain on a gram scale, adds master alloy, melts it in a crucible or melting dish with a hand-held oxy-propane torch, stirs/fluxes it and pours an ingot or fills a flask for a model.

Casting department of a jewelry manufacturer: weighs out a precise charge of fine gold/silver plus master alloy and a controlled fraction of returned sprue, loads it into an induction vacuum/pressure casting machine, sets the melt program and casts investment flasks of models.

Custom/studio jeweler alloying specialty metals: calculates and weighs the constituent metals for a non-standard karat or color (rose/green gold, palladium white gold, sterling), melts and homogenizes the mix in a small induction unit or torch, pours an ingot for rolling or a model.

Model-making materials: melting and conditioning injection wax (or pewter/white-metal and other low-temperature model materials) to the right temperature and consistency in a wax pot/injector before shooting jewelry model patterns from rubber molds.

Scrap consolidation/refining prep: weighing collected lemel, filings and polishing sweeps, mixing with flux, melting the batch in a crucible furnace and pouring a bar that is weighed and sampled for assay before refining.

sources.system: AlloyBot automatic weighing and arc-melting system

sources.claim: AlloyBot is a purpose-built robotic cell that autonomously dispenses and weighs pure elemental metal feedstock (pellets and cut wire) to better than 1 at.% against a closed-loop balance, stacks the charge into a copper crucible with a rail-mounted robot arm, and arc-melts and remelts it into a homogeneous bulk alloy button or cast rod, one alloy per hour with no human assistance except about one hour of maintenance per day.
sources.transferJustification: Same task elements as the jeweler's: weigh constituent metals to a target composition, combine them, and melt/homogenize them into an alloy. Batch masses (>100 g) and dosing accuracy exceed what karat-alloy mixing for jewelry models requires.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: weighing, mixing and heating solid materials in crucibles. It shows closed-loop gravimetric dosing, mixing and crucible handling/heating chained autonomously in a fixtured cell, the same sequence a jewelry charge requires.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small custom/repair jewelry shop: jeweler loads an invested, burned-out flask into the arm of a spring-wound or benchtop centrifugal caster, places a few pennyweights of gold or silver in the crucible, torch-melts it, and releases the arm so the spinning mold fills completely without porosity; one-off ring or custom piece.

Production casting department of a jewelry manufacturer: operator loads flasks and metal charges into an induction vacuum/centrifugal casting machine that spins the flask during and after injection; dozens of flasks per shift in standard karat golds, silver and platinum, with programmed rpm/acceleration per alloy.

Spin casting of vulcanized rubber molds for base-metal/pewter findings, charms, buckles and models: mold clamped between platens of a spin caster, machine spun up, molten low-melt alloy fed into the center sprue, repeated many times per shift on a production floor.

Bench work with small non-centrifugal molds: hand-rocking or tilting ingot molds, charm, cuttlebone or delft-clay molds while pouring, and swirling/rotating the filled mold to drive out trapped air; varied, sometimes improvised mold shapes at the bench.

Home-based studio or itinerant art-jeweler setting: casting done on a bench in a garage/spare-room studio taken as found, with a hand-cranked or improvised broken-arm caster, mixed mold sizes and no standardized layout.

tasks.label: Assign polish, symmetry, and clarity grades to stones, according to established grading systems.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Grading laboratory bench (GIA/IGI/GSI/GCAL-type lab): a grader takes a loose round-brilliant polished diamond of common size (roughly 0.2–5 ct), cleans it, examines it with tweezers under a 10x binocular microscope and darkfield/overhead lighting, plots inclusions, and assigns clarity, polish and symmetry grades for a report.

Cutting/manufacturing factory or wholesale trading office QC bench: loose polished round stones coming off the polishing wheels are graded and sorted in-house at production speed, assigning clarity, polish and symmetry so parcels can be priced, re-polished, or matched to buyer specs.

Harder stones in the lab or factory: fancy shapes (oval, pear, princess, emerald cut), tiny melee, very large or very high-value stones, and borderline calls (IF vs VVS, heavily included SI/I stones, lab-grown), where inclusion type/position and finish defects must be weighed judgmentally.

Mounted stones: a diamond already set in a ring or other finished jewelry is graded at a retail store bench, appraisal office, or lab, viewing around prongs and metal, with limited access to the pavilion and girdle, to estimate clarity, polish and symmetry.

Colored and non-diamond gemstones (emerald, sapphire, ruby, other faceted gems) evaluated at a lapidary shop or gem lab for clarity type/grade and finish (polish and meet/symmetry quality), using loupe and microscope under the applicable colored-stone grading system.

tasks.label: Identify and document stones' clarity characteristics, using plot diagrams.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Grading department / gem lab bench: a loose polished round brilliant (natural or lab-grown, ~0.2–5 ct) is taken from a parcel with tweezers, cleaned, examined at 10x under a gemological microscope and darkfield/overhead lighting, its inclusions and blemishes identified by type (crystal, feather, cloud, needle, naturals, extra facets) and their positions plotted in red/green on crown and pavilion diagrams in grading software for the report.

Same lab bench work, but on loose polished fancy shapes (oval, pear, emerald, cushion, marquise, princess) or on stones outside routine size/color ranges; the grader must select the correct facet diagram for the shape and plot characteristics that reflect differently in step cuts and elongated outlines.

Jewelry store back bench or appraisal office: clarity characteristics of a diamond mounted in a finished ring or pendant are identified and plotted for an insurance appraisal or identification record; prongs, bezels and the mounting block portions of the stone, the stone cannot be removed, and cleaning/orientation must be done in the setting.

Colored-stone identification at a lab or appraiser's bench: inclusions in a loose sapphire, ruby or emerald (silk, healed fissures, three-phase inclusions, flux residue) are identified with microscope, fiber-optic and immersion, and plotted on a shape diagram as part of an identification/origin/treatment record.

Diamond cutting/manufacturing facility: rough, sawn or blocked stones are examined and their internal features mapped and documented so cutting can be planned, and finished production is graded and its clarity characteristics recorded for in-house sorting before sale.

instances.label: Diamond cutting/polishing plant, in-process check by a blocker/brillianteer: a semi-polished (blocked) round brilliant still on its dop is taken off the wheel and examined with a 10x loupe/microscope and a bench proportion scanner to verify table size, crown and pavilion angles, girdle thickness and culet centering; the stone is returned to the wheel with a correction or passed on.

QC/inspection bench in a diamond manufacturing house or grading operation: parcels of finished or near-finished stones are examined one by one under loupe, microscope and shadowgraph/proportion scanner for facet misalignment, off-center table, extra facets and symmetry deviation; each stone is accepted, sent for re-polish, or downgraded and sorted into the right lot.

Colored-stone lapidary/faceting workshop: during faceting of sapphire, tourmaline, garnet or quartz the cutter stops the machine, wipes the stone and inspects meetpoints, facet angles, girdle placement and pavilion depth under a loupe or binocular scope (sometimes an optical comparator), then adjusts index/angle settings and continues cutting.

Industrial diamond/tool shop: verifying the angle, position and concentricity of bores in diamond wire-drawing dies, or the geometry of diamond tool blanks, dressers and bearings, using a measuring microscope, shadowgraph/profile projector and gauges between drilling and lapping operations.

One-off custom faceted work in a home studio or jeweler's back bench: recutting or repairing a customer's faceted stone to standard proportions, checking angles and symmetry with a loupe against a target design under variable bench conditions.

Freeform/artistic lapidary in a home studio or store back room: checking hand-cut cabochons, carvings, inlay pieces and opal freeforms for dome symmetry, girdle line and fit to a mounting, judged by eye and loupe against templates rather than a numeric standard.

tasks.label: Examine diamonds or gems to ascertain the shape, cut, and width of cut stones, or to select the cuts that will result in the biggest, best quality stones.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Rough diamond planning at a manufacturer or dealer: the worker takes rough stones (roughly 0.3–5 ct) from a parcel, examines each with loupe/microscope and scanner for shape, grain, and inclusions, and determines the cut(s) that yield the biggest, best-quality polished stones; done at a planning desk in a secured diamond factory.

Examination of finished polished diamonds for QC or grading: stone held in tweezers/holder, shape identified, table/depth/crown/pavilion proportions, girdle width and symmetry measured, cut grade assessed; done in a factory QC room or gem laboratory with standard equipment.

In-process examination at the cutting bench: the worker stops during blocking/brillianteering, inspects the semi-polished stone (often on the dop) under loupe/microscope, gauges girdle thickness and facet symmetry, checks remaining inclusions, and decides the next cut or a recut of a finished/broken stone.

Melee and small-stone parcels: hundreds to thousands of small cut stones examined and sorted by shape, cut quality and dimensions (diameter, height, corner angles) for matching and setting; done at a sorting bench in a jewelry manufacturer or diamond dealer.
Colored gemstone rough (sapphire, tourmaline, aquamarine, etc.) examined in a lapidary shop to judge shape and orientation and select the cut that will produce the largest, best stone(s).

Finished/cut colored gemstones examined in a jewelry workshop or gem lab: identify shape and cutting style, measure length/width/depth, judge cut quality (symmetry, windowing, meet points, polish) for appraisal, matching, or a recut decision; wide variety of species and fancy cuts.

tasks.label: Examine gem surfaces and internal structures, using polariscopes, refractometers, microscopes, and other optical instruments, to differentiate between stones, to identify rare specimens, or to detect flaws, defects, or peculiarities affecting gem values.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Diamond grading laboratory: a grader takes loose polished diamonds (mostly round brilliants, some fancy shapes) from parcels, cleans them, and examines each under microscope, loupe, colorimeter, fluorescence/spectroscopic units to assign clarity and color, plot inclusions, and flag treatments or laboratory-grown origin for a report.

Melee and parcel screening: a worker at a lab, manufacturer, or retail intake desk screens hundreds to thousands of small stones (0.001-0.20 ct) for laboratory-grown diamonds, HPHT treatment, and simulants, separating referred stones for further optical/spectroscopic testing.

Diamond manufacturing or dealer facility: examining rough stones for internal inclusions, cracks and clouds to plan cutting, and inspecting polished output for surface blemishes, chips and defects affecting value, using microscopes and scanning/imaging instruments at a bench.

Retail jeweler bench or appraisal office: identifying colored gemstones and separating natural from synthetic or assembled stones and detecting treatments, using refractometer with contact fluid, polariscope, dichroscope, spectroscope and microscope; many stones are mounted in finished jewelry and must be examined in the setting.

Off-site or field examination: estate appraisal at a client's home or bank vault, pawn/buy counter, trade-show booth or mine-site buying office; mixed and unfamiliar mounted goods, portable loupe and handheld testers, variable lighting and no fixed bench setup.

tasks.label: Advise customers and others on the best use of gems to create attractive jewelry items.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Locate and mark drilling or cutting positions on stones or dies, using diamond chips and power hand tools.
Secure gems or diamonds in holders, chucks, dops, lapidary sticks, or blocks for cutting, polishing, grinding, drilling, or shaping.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Diamond polishing bench in a cutting works: worker cements/clamps a sawn or blocked diamond into a dop held by a tang, centers it and sets the angle under a loupe so the stone presents correctly to the scaife for blocking or brillianteering; repeated dozens of times a shift, remounting the stone for each facet group.

Rough diamond preparation in a manufacturing shop: worker cements or clamps a rough or partly worked stone into a sawing/laser holder or a bruting chuck, aligning it to the marked plan before laser sawing, shaping or girdling.

Custom colored-stone faceting in a small lapidary/custom-cutting shop: worker studies a unique piece of rough for color zoning, pleochroism and inclusions, chooses the orientation, heats wax and dops the stone on a dop stick, then transfers it to a second dop after the pavilion is cut, keeping alignment within a fraction of a degree.

Production run of calibrated stones or synthetics (melee sapphire, cubic zirconia): worker mounts batches of like-sized preforms onto dops, plates or machine cassettes with wax/adhesive so an automatic faceting machine can cut them to a fixed pattern.

Cabochon, bead and carving work in a lapidary shop: worker attaches a sawn preform or slab piece to a dop stick or block with wax or epoxy (or loads it into a jig) for grinding, sanding, drilling and polishing on a lapidary unit.

Industrial diamond/gem work in a tool plant: worker secures diamonds or hard-stone blanks in chucks, blocks or holders for drilling, grinding or shaping components such as wire-drawing dies, single-point dressers, styli and tool inserts, meeting tight orientation tolerances.

tasks.label: Select shaping wheels for tasks, and mix and apply abrasives, bort, or polishing compounds.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Lapidary shop bench, cabbing/shaping colored stones: worker picks the correct diamond grinding/sanding wheel or lap for the stage (80 → 220 → 600 → 1200 → 3000 grit), mounts it on the arbor, and applies diamond spray/paste or cerium-oxide slurry to felt or leather laps, keeping water/coolant feed going and avoiding grit cross-contamination.

Diamond cutting/polishing bench in a diamond plant or workshop: worker chooses the right cast-iron scaife (grit grade, surface condition, wheel zone), dresses/scores it, mixes diamond bort powder with oil to the needed consistency, charges the scaife, and re-charges it during the shift as it wears; roughing versus final-polish laps kept separate.

Finishing/buffing station in a jewelry or gem-products shop: worker selects the buff (muslin, felt, bristle, leather) and the compound (tripoli, rouge, diamond compound) for the material and finish stage, loads the wheel with compound repeatedly during the run, and switches wheels between cutting and coloring stages.

Industrial diamond/abrasive-products facility: preparing tooling for shaping industrial diamonds, dies, and diamond/carbide tool blanks — selecting and mounting resin- or metal-bond diamond grinding wheels, truing/dressing them, and charging lapping plates with metered diamond slurry and lubricant.

Consumable preparation and changeover in the shop: mixing a fresh batch of abrasive to spec (grit size, concentration, oil or water carrier), loading dispensers/spray bottles, cleaning laps and plates between grits to prevent contamination, and labeling/storing the batches.

tasks.label: Measure sizes of stones' bore holes and cuts to ensure adherence to specifications, using precision measuring instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-process/final dimension check at a cutting bench: worker takes a diamond or colored stone (often just off the dop/tang, semi-polished or finished) and checks girdle diameter, total depth, table size and crown/pavilion angles against the cutting spec with a Leveridge gauge, digital caliper, loupe or benchtop scanner; result decides whether to keep polishing.

Parcel of melee/calibrated stones in a manufacturing or jewelry-supply sorting room: worker measures and verifies each small stone (0.6-3 mm) against calibrated size tolerances for setting, using sieves, a computerized melee gauge or micrometer, and separates out-of-spec stones.

Grading-lab or factory QC station: a polished diamond is measured for full proportions and symmetry (table %, depth %, crown/pavilion angles, girdle thickness, culet) against cut-grade or customer specification using an optical proportion scanner, and a report is issued.

Industrial diamond tool shop: worker measures the bore hole of a wire-drawing die, nozzle or orifice — hole diameter, roundness, taper/entrance angles and bearing length — after drilling or repolishing, using a measuring microscope, projector or plug/wire method, to confirm the finished hole matches the ordered size.

Bench work on drilled stones, beads and pearls in a jewelry shop or findings supplier: checking drill-hole diameter, depth and centering with pin gauges/calipers and checking a cut stone's dimensions for fit in a mounting seat.
