tasks.label: Count, sort, and weigh processed items.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In a wafer fab cleanroom, verifying the wafer count and slot map of cassettes/FOUPs of processed wafers at a tool or sorter station: confirming 25 wafers present, finding empty slots, cross-slotted or broken wafers, and recording the count against the lot record in the MES.

Sorting processed wafers between carriers: reading wafer IDs/laser marks, consolidating partial lots, splitting a lot for different downstream processing, pulling engineering/monitor wafers or rejects into a separate cassette, and updating lot composition in the tracking system.

Weighing processed material in the crystal-growth/ingot area or wet-process bay: placing a grown boule, sawn ingot segment, crucible charge or chemical/consumable lot on a scale, reading the weight and logging it for yield and material accounting.
On the test/probe or assembly floor, sorting processed devices or dies into bins/trays by test or inspection result (pass, downgrade, reject) and counting the quantity in each bin for lot accounting.

In a staging area or fab stockroom, counting and sorting boxed wafer lots, trays, empty cassettes/carriers and consumable items for inventory, kitting or shipment, and reconciling the counts with the inventory system.

instances.label: High-volume production singulation in an assembly/test or advanced-packaging cleanroom: technician retrieves cassettes of tape-frame-mounted 200/300 mm wafers, loads them to a fully automatic blade dicing saw's load port, selects the product recipe, the tool aligns to street patterns and full-cuts the wafer, spin-rinses it, and the technician unloads and moves the lot on. Runs 24/7 under gowning, ESD and particle controls.

Laser scribing / stealth dicing / laser grooving of thin, brittle or low-k wafers (SiC, GaN, sapphire, ultra-thin Si) on a laser saw in the same cleanroom: load cassette, run recipe, verify groove/kerf position and chipping, unload for subsequent break/expand.

Setup and changeover on a dicing tool: mount/replace the correct hub blade for the incoming product, dress it, set blade height relative to the chuck, teach or verify the alignment target, run test cuts, inspect kerf width, offset and front/back chipping under the microscope, adjust and release the tool to production.

Preparation and post-singulation handling framing the dicing step: mounting the thinned wafer onto dicing tape and a ring frame (lamination, trimming, UV), verifying mount quality, and after cutting UV-curing and transferring the diced frame to inspection or die attach, in a production cleanroom.

Low-volume, R&D or specialty work in a pilot line or university/company lab: scribing and breaking or dicing partial wafers, coupons, laser bars and exotic substrates (InP, GaAs, glass) of varying size and shape, with a one-off setup for nearly every sample on a bench dicing saw or scriber-breaker.

Exception and rework handling: a wafer cracks or the tape delaminates mid-cut, a frame jams in the handler, kerf goes out of spec or the blade breaks; technician opens the tool, recovers broken silicon fragments and debris, cleans the chuck and nozzles, salvages or manually breaks out remaining good die, and requalifies the tool.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume 300mm logic/memory fab, class-1 cleanroom: a plasma dry-etch step. A FOUP of 25 patterned product wafers arrives at the etcher load port; the technician verifies lot/recipe against the MES, starts the run, monitors chamber parameters and endpoint traces, unloads the FOUP, and sends the lot to in-line CD/defect metrology for disposition.

300mm fab CMP (chemical-mechanical planarization) module: FOUP of oxide/tungsten/copper wafers is polished on a multi-platen polisher with post-CMP clean and dry; technician confirms pad/slurry/conditioner status, runs the lot, checks integrated thickness metrology and scratch/defect results, and adjusts or holds the lot when removal rate drifts.

Legacy 150/200mm fab (power, analog, discrete, MEMS): batch wet chemical etch or spin etch. Technician moves cassettes/SMIF pods on carts between tools, loads cassettes into the wet station or single-wafer etcher, runs timed baths (BOE, phosphoric, KOH) with rinse/dry, and verifies etch depth/step height afterwards.

Silicon/SiC substrate manufacturing plant: ingot outer-diameter and flat/notch grinding, then wafer lapping, double-side polishing and caustic/acid batch etch. Technician loads ingots into the grinder and wafer batches into lappers, polishers and etch lines, and checks TTV, flatness, thickness and surface finish against spec.

Back-end / thinning module at an OSAT or fab: tape-mounted device wafers are back-ground and dry- or CMP-polished to target thickness (sometimes below 100 um). Technician loads cassettes/frame carriers into the fully automatic grinder, sets the thinning recipe, and verifies final thickness, TTV and absence of chipping/cracks.

R&D, pilot line or low-volume specialty work (university nanofab, compound-semiconductor or MEMS development): manual wet etching or hand lapping/polishing of odd-sized pieces, quarter wafers and non-standard substrates in a fume-hood wet bench, with one-off chemistries, frequently changing recipes, tweezer handling and visual endpoint judgement.

instances.label: High-volume 300 mm fab (logic, memory, or analog): technician runs the litho module — production lots arrive in FOUPs, are coated on a track linked to a DUV/EUV scanner, the scanner aligns to prior-layer marks and exposes, and the track does post-exposure bake and develop; technician sets up lots/reticles, monitors alarms, verifies CD/overlay.

Legacy/specialty 150–200 mm fab (analog, power, RF, MEMS, discretes): technician loads wafer cassettes/SMIF pods onto the coat-develop track and i-line/KrF stepper or mask aligner, selects recipe and reticle, runs the align–expose–develop sequence, and checks resist patterns under a microscope.

Rework, engineering, and hot lots inside a production fab: partial-cassette lots, send-ahead wafers, re-exposure after a failed overlay/CD check, alignment-offset adjustments and requalification runs on the same track/stepper cell.

Advanced packaging / thick-resist / MEMS lithography line (bumping, fan-out, WLP, deep cavities) on 200–300 mm wafers using a proximity or projection aligner with thick photoresist and coat/develop modules.

R&D, pilot line, or university cleanroom: small batches of standard 100–200 mm whole wafers on a contact/proximity mask aligner, frequent recipe and mask changes, develop by automated developer or bench puddle/dip, followed by microscope inspection.

Non-standard substrates in R&D/prototype work: diced pieces and fragments, compound-semiconductor or thin/warped/bowed substrates mounted on carriers, backside/double-sided alignment, one-off tooling and hand-mounted parts.

instances.label: Retail photo department (drugstore/big-box/camera store): customer brings a phone, memory card, or places an online/in-store order; worker sets size, crop, quantity, borders and finish, runs the dry minilab or kiosk, applies auto/manual color and density correction, cuts prints, checks them against the order and sleeves them in an order envelope. Includes ID/passport prints made to official specification.

High-volume centralized photofinishing lab (online/mail-order photofinisher, school and portrait volume lab): batches of thousands of 4x6 to 8x10 prints on roll-fed silver-halide or inkjet photo printers; worker loads media, runs calibration/control strips to lab protocol, monitors print queues, cuts and sorts prints by barcode into customer orders, pulls defective prints and reprints.

Professional lab standard output: portrait, wedding, sports and school package prints and enlargements up to about 12x18 on specified pro papers (lustre, metallic, deep matte); printed to the lab's calibrated color standard from the photographer's files, machine-trimmed to size, sorted per order, spot-checked for color/density and surface defects.

Fine-art / display / specialty output: large exhibition prints on sheet fine-art paper or canvas, direct prints to rigid board, gallery wraps, mounted and face-mounted pieces; requires proofing and matching a customer-supplied proof or brand color, hand-loading sheet or rigid media, precise trimming, mounting/stretching and inspection of the finished piece.

On-site / event printing: instant print stations and booths at weddings, parties, festivals, sporting events, theme parks and picture-day locations; prints made on the spot from a chosen template/size while the customer waits, in whatever venue the event occupies.

Traditional darkroom/analog printing at a custom or fine-art lab: enlarger-made black-and-white or color prints from negatives, test strips, dodging and burning, wet-chemistry processing in trays or a roller processor, judging the print against the customer's instructions; includes alternative-process and hand-finished work.

Digital imaging / digitization station: operator sets scanner or film-processing machine controls per material — resolution, bit depth, exposure/density, color balance, crop presets for negatives, slides, prints; or chemistry temperature, replenishment rate and transport speed on a film processor. Lab, studio or archive room with standard equipment.

On-location / event printing (weddings, private parties, mobile portrait and photo-booth work): operator sets dye-sub or inkjet printer controls at the venue — media/ribbon type, print size and finish, color and density tweaks for the lighting and ambient conditions — in a space taken as found with no institutional control of layout, power or environment.

Archive, library, museum or government imaging unit: item-level digitization of collection material — loose photographic prints, glass plate and film negatives, oversized aerial photos, bound albums — captured with colour targets to FADGI/Metamorfoze-style specifications, with condition handling, file naming and metadata capture. Dedicated institutional imaging lab.

On-site or in-house ad hoc digitization: technician takes a portable scanner or copy stand to a client's home, small office or event venue to digitize an album, framed print or fragile items that cannot be shipped; space, lighting and work surface are whatever is available.

High-volume commercial/professional lab (dip-and-dunk C-41/E-6/RA-4 lines, motion-picture or industrial processors): dedicated mix room with drums, cubitainers and mixing tanks; multi-part concentrates blended in sequence with tempered water and pumped into the processors' several working and replenisher tanks, including full refills after a drain-and-clean.

Freelance or home-based darkroom / on-location processing setup: an as-found room or improvised bench, mixed and non-standard vessels, no fixed plumbing or layout; solutions mixed from concentrates and poured into tanks and trays.

instances.label: Retail photo counter (drugstore, big-box, one-hour lab): a customer hands over an SD card, USB flash drive, phone or disc at the order station; the worker inserts it into the reader, imports the images into the lab's order/print system, confirms all images arrived, ejects and returns the media, often with customers waiting.

Commercial/professional lab ingest station: memory cards arrive from photographers in wallets or envelopes with job tickets; the worker inserts each card into a multi-slot reader at a dedicated ingest workstation, copies files into job folders on the server, verifies file counts and integrity, makes a backup copy, then ejects and returns or reformats the cards.

High-volume school/sports/event portrait production lab: dozens of cards per day from shoots, ingested in batches against job barcodes or shoot IDs, downloaded, verified, logged into the workflow system, and the cards reformatted for reuse. Highly repetitive and standardized work at a fixed bench.

Studio tethered or direct-from-camera download: the worker connects a camera body to the workstation with a USB cable (or seats it in a dock/cradle) and imports the shoot directly from the camera into the computer at a studio capture station.

On-location ingest at an event venue (wedding, trade show, sports field, green-screen event setup): laptop on a folding table, cameras and cards handed over between shoots, cramped and variable lighting/space, media of several types downloaded and backed up on the spot.

Non-standard media and troubleshooting: legacy or damaged media (old CompactFlash, microSD in an adapter, a phone needing its own cable and unlock, a scratched CD, a card that mounts but reports errors); the worker diagnoses the device, finds the right adapter/cable, and recovers the images with recovery software before loading them.

tasks.label: Examine developed prints for defects, such as broken lines, spots, or blurs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail photo counter / drugstore or camera-store minilab: operator takes 4x6s and enlargements from the dry-lab output tray, fans through them under counter lighting looking for dust spots, streaks and broken lines from dirty rollers or clogged heads, color casts and soft or blurred output, culls bad prints and re-runs them before bagging the customer order.

High-volume commercial photofinishing plant (photo books, cards, calendars, bulk prints): operator monitors sheets and rolls coming off production presses and cutters on the finishing line, pulls sample sheets and defective pieces showing banding, ink spots, streaks or missing image, and signals reprint while the line keeps running.

Professional / fine-art custom lab: large-format inkjet or silver-halide prints laid on a light table or viewing wall and examined closely for head strikes, banding, dust specks, scratches, gloss differential and sharpness; operator decides reprint, spotting or retouch before mounting and shipping.

School, sports and portrait production lab: packaged print sets checked before packing - each sheet compared with the order (right subject, crop, orientation) and screened for blur, spots and lines; defective sheets pulled and reprinted, then packages assembled.

On-location event printing (weddings, conventions, race and sports venues, photo-booth operations): operator runs a portable dye-sub or inkjet printer at a temporary setup, inspects each print immediately under the venue's ambient light for dye-ribbon lines, smudges, spots and blur, and reprints on the spot.

Analog darkroom / film-based lab: fiber or RC prints from an enlarger inspected wet and dry under inspection light for dust spots and scratches carried from the negative, uneven development, chemical stains and unsharpness, deciding whether to spot and retouch by hand or reprint.

It transfers to examining developed prints because the objects are the same class (printed paper sheets, including photo-quality output), the defect classes named (spots/dust, stains, streaks and lines, faint or blurred areas) are those this task lists, and the system also completes the worker's downstream act - culling the bad print and reprinting it.

tasks.label: Reprint originals for enlargement or in sections to be pieced together.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail photo department / minilab counter: customer brings an original print (or file/negative) and orders an enlargement (5x7 to 16x20). Worker or kiosk scans the original, crops and scales it, prints on a dry minilab or kiosk printer, checks density/color, trims and sleeves the print. Store is a controlled retail premises with standard equipment.

Commercial/professional photofinishing lab: enlargement ordered from a digital file or scanned negative, output on silver-halide printer-processor (e.g., laser imager) or fine-art inkjet at 16x20 to 40x60; color matched to the original, printed, processed/dried, inspected for banding and color, trimmed to size and packed.

Wide-format lab: image larger than the media width is tiled by the RIP into sections/panels, printed on roll media with overlap allowances, panels trimmed square, sequence-labeled, checked for color consistency panel to panel, then rolled/packed for the customer or installer to piece together.

Custom wet-darkroom enlargement (fine-art, restoration, archival reprint): original negative or copy negative in an enlarger, test strips, exposure/contrast judgment, hand dodging and burning, tray or processor development, wash, dry and flatten to a specified interpretation.

Lab itself pieces the printed sections together: dry-mounting/laminating multiple printed panels onto a board or substrate, aligning seams to sub-millimeter registration across the composite, trimming the assembled piece to final size and inspecting the joins.

Sections delivered and pieced together at the customer's premises (mural or trade-show graphic): panels hung/applied on an as-found wall, aligned and overlaps trimmed on site under variable lighting and access conditions.

tasks.label: Clean or maintain photoprocessing or darkroom equipment, using ultrasonic equipment or cleaning and rinsing solutions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Weekly wet-lab minilab maintenance at a retail or professional photofinishing lab: lift developer, bleach-fix and stabilizer roller racks and crossovers out of the processor, scrub off chemical crystals, sludge and gelatin residue with brush/sponge and rack cleaner, rinse thoroughly under running water, dry, check gears/belts, and reinstall without contaminating adjacent tanks.

Periodic deep clean of a film/paper processor's tanks and circulation system: drain spent chemistry to waste containers, wipe and scrub tank walls, circulate a tank-and-transport cleaning solution through the lines and filters, flush and rinse with water, then refill with fresh chemistry and verify levels.

Dry-lab (inkjet) minilab and large-format printer upkeep in a store or commercial print lab: run nozzle checks and head-cleaning cycles, wipe the nozzle plate/wiper and capping station with cleaning fluid and lint-free swabs, feed cleaning sheets to clean paper-path rollers, empty waste-ink trays, and vacuum dust.

Washing darkroom/wet-side accessories in the lab sink: processing trays, tanks, film reels, hangers, graduates and mixing vessels are washed with cleaning solution, rinsed free of chemistry, dried and returned to shelves at the end of a ....

Benchtop ultrasonic cleaning of small precision parts (spray-bar nozzles, jets, film clips, negative carriers, printhead components): load parts into a basket, run the ultrasonic cycle in detergent solution, rinse, blow/air dry, inspect for remaining residue and return the parts to the machine.

Cleaning optical and imaging surfaces without damage: enlarger lens and condenser, negative carriers and film gates, scanner platen glass and mirrors, printer sensors — using blower, lens tissue and cleaning solution, checked visually for streaks, dust and scratches.

tasks.label: Monitor equipment operation to detect malfunctions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail/drugstore or big-box photo department: operator runs a dry minilab/kiosk print system (e.g., Fuji Frontier/Noritsu drylab) during order runs, watching for paper jams and misfeeds, low media/ink alarms, error codes on the console, and streaks, banding or color casts on prints as they drop into the sorter; work is interleaved with customer service at the counter.

Professional/commercial photo lab production room: operator tends several wide-format and dry-lab photo printers plus mounting/laminating gear, checking nozzle-check patterns and test prints, listening for transport or head-strike problems, watching ink/media levels, and catching banding, head clogs, roll tracking and lamination bubbles before a job is spoiled.

High-volume photofinishing / photobook production plant: operator monitors a continuous web or sheet-fed print-and-finish line (printer, cutter, collator, binder) at speed, watching for registration drift, color shift across the run, missing jets, paper breaks, jams at the finishing stations, and unusual machine noise or heat.

Wet-process film/print processing lab: operator monitors C-41/E-6/RA-4 processors and dip-and-dunk lines for temperature deviation, replenishment pump and circulation failures, chemistry leaks or crystallization, dryer faults, and film/paper transport jams; runs periodic control strips and reads densitometry to catch process drift before it damages customer film.

On-location/event operation: portable printers and a laptop-based workflow set up in a hotel ballroom, gym, school cafeteria or event trailer; operator monitors the printers during a live event for jams, ribbon/media exhaustion, overheating, power/cabling faults and print quality, in a space taken as found with crowds and variable temperature and lighting.

instances.label: Volume film processing at a commercial lab/minilab: worker loads dozens of exposed 35mm/120 rolls onto leader cards or hanger racks in the dark and runs them through the C-41/E-6/B&W sequence (developer, bleach, fixer, wash, stabilizer) at controlled temperature and time, with control-strip QC.

Small-batch hand tank development of roll film at a boutique lab, school, or portrait studio: load reels in total darkness, pour and agitate developer on a timed schedule, stop, fix, hypo clear, wash, wetting agent, hang to dry.
Print processing of RC papers in a lab darkroom (B&W RC or RA-4 color): exposed sheets immersed in developer, stop/bleach-fix, and wash, then dried; standard sizes, repeated many times per shift.
Sheet/large-format film and custom push-pull work: 4x5–8x10 sheets in hangers-and-tanks or trays, non-standard development times per the customer's instruction, one small batch at a time.

Technical/industrial film immersion processing: medical or dental radiographic film, NDT industrial X-ray film, graphic-arts/PCB film run through developer, fixer, wash and dry in a facility darkroom.

Fine-art fiber-based and alternative-process work in a custom or artist's darkroom: FB or hand-coated papers developed by inspection in trays under safelight, extended fixing, hypo clear, long archival wash; varied paper sizes, weights and chemistries taken as found.

tasks.label: Examine quality of film fades or dissolves for potential color corrections, using color analyzers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail/consumer photofinishing lab: developed C-41 roll film is fed through the minilab's negative carrier and scanned; the operator watches the analyzer/monitor frame by frame for color casts, density shifts and washed-out (faded) frames, sets red/green/blue corrections, then prints the order. High volume, standard 35mm/120 stock, fast turnaround.

Professional/custom still lab or mail-in scanning service: customer's older, dye-faded negatives, slides and mixed stocks are examined on the scanner's color analyzer for fading and crossed curves, and color-restoration settings are determined before scanning/printing. Lower volume, higher quality bar, one-off originals.

Consumer film-reel digitizing service: 8mm/Super 8/16mm home-movie reels with in-camera fades, splices, and varying exposure are loaded on a frame-by-frame scanner; the technician monitors the analyzer during the scan for color/exposure problems across transitions and applies corrections to the delivered video files.

Photochemical motion-picture lab color timing: the cut negative is run on a video color analyzer (Hazeltine-type); the timer checks each fade and dissolve for a smooth ramp and matched color across the transition and assigns RGB printer-light values scene by scene for the answer print, which the client must approve.

Archive/restoration or post facility: severely dye-faded film or a scanned intermediate is reviewed on a grading system with waveform/vectorscope 'analyzers', with particular attention to fades and dissolves that must match across the transition; correction decisions are made for a preservation master or mastering deliverable, often under supervision of an archivist or client.

tasks.label: Thread filmstrips through densitometers or sensitometers and expose film to light to determine density of film, necessary color corrections, or light sensitivity.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Shift/daily process control in a photofinishing minilab or commercial C-41/RA-4 lab: the operator takes a pre-exposed control strip, runs it through the film processor, then threads the wet-or-dry strip into a transmission densitometer, reads R/G/B densities of the D-min, LD, HD and stain patches, plots them against the aim values and decides replenishment or chemistry corrections. Lab room with benches, processor and densitometer.

Printer/paper balance and color-correction determination: the worker exposes and processes a printer balance strip or test print, threads it through the densitometer, reads the patch densities, and derives the filter-pack/channel corrections that are entered into the printer or scanner. Same lab, standard strip formats.

Sensitometric testing in a professional or motion-picture film lab: in the darkroom the worker loads a strip of raw stock into a sensitometer, exposes it through a calibrated step tablet, processes it, then threads the wedge through the densitometer to obtain the D-log E curve, speed, contrast and printer-light corrections for that emulsion/batch.

Radiographic film processor QC (hospital/dental darkroom or industrial NDT film room): expose a sheet of X-ray film with a sensitometer, run it through the processor, read the step densities on a densitometer, compare speed/contrast/base-plus-fog to baseline and flag processor corrections.

Ad-hoc, non-routine density work in a small custom lab or archive: odd-size or hand-cut strips, sheet film, older or damaged material and customer negatives are placed on a bench densitometer between other jobs to read specific highlight/shadow densities and judge printing corrections.

tasks.label: Place sensitized paper in frames of projection printers, photostats, or other reproduction machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail/commercial minilab: in a light-tight darkroom or dark bag, the operator opens a fresh roll of color photographic paper, loads it into the printer's light-tight paper magazine, threads the leader onto the feed rollers, closes the magazine and slots it into the roll-fed printer/processor (e.g. Noritsu/Fuji Frontier), then runs a test print to verify feed and registration.

Custom/professional lab darkroom: under safelight, the printer takes single sheets of enlarging paper from a light-tight box or paper safe and positions each sheet emulsion-up in the blades of the easel (frame) beneath a projection printer/enlarger, one sheet per exposure, for test strips and final prints; sheets must be square in the frame and unfogged.

High-volume photofinishing/production lab: mounting large rolls of sensitized paper into the paper magazines of production printers and processors on the line, splicing the new web to the trailing leader and re-threading the transport, in a light-controlled bay.

Reprographic/large-format shop: loading sheet or roll sensitized/coated media into large reproduction machines (photostat descendants, diazo/blueprint machines, large-format copier-printers), registering sheets against the frame or copyboard and feeding the machine.

Small studio or home-based/on-location darkroom: improvised light-tight space (converted bathroom, closet, changing tent) with non-standard equipment; loading paper into contact-printing frames or an easel under an enlarger, with clutter and varying layouts site to site.

tasks.label: Produce timed prints with separate densities or color settings for each scene of a production.

instances.label: Retail/consumer photofinishing lab (drugstore, camera store, mail-order print service): a customer order of many images from one shoot or film roll is run on a minilab; each frame/scene needs its own density and color-balance setting before exposure onto paper, then wet or inkjet processing, cutting and sorting into the finished order.

Professional high-volume lab handling a shoot 'production' run (school, sports league, portrait studio, event): hundreds to thousands of frames printed as packages, with per-pose/per-scene density and color settings applied against a lab standard, printed, cut, collated and QC'd against turnaround deadlines.

Custom/professional or fine-art lab work: technician individually judges and adjusts density, contrast and color for each negative or file to the photographer's or gallery's stated intent (test strips or soft proofs, iterative approval), then produces exhibition- or portfolio-quality prints.

Motion-picture film laboratory, printing side: technician receives the scene-by-scene timing/light values (RGB printer-light cue list) from the timer or DI grade, loads the cue data and threads the cut negative and raw print stock on an additive contact printer, runs the print and the continuous processor, and checks the resulting timed daily/check/release print.

Motion-picture/commercial color-timing session: technician analyzes each scene on a color analyzer or projector, decides the density and RGB light values for every scene to realize the cinematographer's intent, produces successive timed prints, screens them with the DP/director and re-times until the answer print is approved.

tasks.label: Splice broken or separated film and mount film on reels.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume commercial film lab (C-41/E-6): technician pulls leaders from batches of 35mm cassettes, trims and tapes/splices roll after roll end-to-end (or onto a leader card) keeping customer order sequence, and winds the resulting strip onto the processor take-up reel before threading it into the roller-transport/long-roll processor. Standard, mostly undamaged 35mm and 120 stock, clean lab bench, repetitive.

Small custom / black-and-white or pro lab: in total darkness or a changing bag, exposed roll film is cut free of the 135 cassette or 120 backing paper, the leading edge trimmed, and the film hand-loaded onto stainless-steel or plastic developing spirals ('reels') that are stacked in a tank or Jobo drum. Done by feel; kinks, buckles and re-loads are common.

Motion-picture / archival / home-movie transfer lab: a reel of 8mm, 16mm or 35mm film is inspected on a rewind bench, broken or separated cement/tape splices and torn perforations are repaired with a splicer (perforations aligned), and the film is wound onto a reel or core for projection, printing or scanning.

Scan/print prep in a lab: developed uncut rolls or strips are spliced together or onto a leader and mounted on the scanner's or printer's feed and take-up reels/magazine so the machine can run them continuously; film that separates mid-run is re-spliced and re-wound.

Bulk media changeover on lab machines: the tail of an expiring bulk roll of film or photographic paper stock is spliced to the start of a new roll and the heavy roll is mounted on the machine's spindle/unwind so production continues without a gap.

Damaged / odd-case rescue: brittle, torn, vinegar-syndrome or fungus-damaged film, film torn off the spool inside a camera, jammed film pulled out of a processor, or obsolete formats (110, 126, 127, disc, APS) that must be judged, hand-spliced and mounted on a reel without further loss.

Hand retouching on the physical artifact itself at a lab bench: spotting white specks on a fiber-based silver-gelatin exhibition print with Spotone dye and a 000 brush, or pencil/dye/airbrush work and knife etching on a large-format negative, matching tone without marring the emulsion.

tasks.label: Measure dimensions of finished workpieces to ensure conformance to specifications, using precision measuring instruments, templates, and fixtures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-mix job shop: after a short run or prototype comes off a CNC mill or lathe, the operator takes the part to the bench beside the machine and checks 3-10 dimensions from the print with digital calipers, micrometers, bore and thread gauges, deburring and wiping chips/coolant first; the part and features are different at nearly every setup.

Repeat production run: the operator gauges every Nth part of an identical family with dedicated hard gauges, snap gauges, plug/thread gauges, air gauges or a shop-floor comparator, logs results to SPC, and adjusts tool offsets when the trend drifts; done at a gauge bench on the shop floor next to the machine.

First-article or final dimensional inspection of a machined part at an inspection station or QC room: the part is clamped in modular fixturing on a CMM (or checked on an optical comparator/height gauge), a measurement routine is run against the drawing/CAD, and a dimensional report is produced for sign-off.

On-machine verification: before the finished workpiece is unclamped, the operator runs a spindle touch-probe cycle to measure bores, bosses, depths and true position, compares against tolerance, and applies wear/tool offsets or re-cuts; performed inside the machine tool enclosure.

Large or awkward workpiece: a large weldment, casting, long shaft, sheet-metal panel, plywood panel or stone slab from a CNC router/waterjet/machining center is checked with tape measure, straightedge, square, templates, height gauge and hand-held gauges, sometimes with crane or a second person to reposition it on the shop floor.

tasks.label: Set up and operate computer-controlled machines or robots to perform one or more machine functions on metal or plastic workpieces.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production run on a CNC lathe or vertical machining center in a machine shop: operator repeatedly loads blanks from a tote into a chuck or vise, cycle-starts, unloads and deburrs finished parts, blows off chips, gauges every few parts and nudges wear offsets, keeping the machine fed through the shift.

Changeover to the next short-run job: swap soft jaws/vise or fixture, load pre-assembled tools into the magazine, call up the program, set tool and work offsets, run and inspect a first article, then run a batch of 20-500 pieces.

Tending several machines at once across a cell or shop floor: walking between three to six CNCs, loading/unloading, hauling totes of blanks and finished parts, taking parts to a gauge or CMM, restarting cycles and keeping all spindles running.

Running a CNC sheet/plate machine (laser, waterjet, plasma, router) on metal or plastic sheet: load the sheet, run the nest program, break out parts from the skeleton, sort and stack them, clear scrap.

Difficult or one-off work: large, heavy, thin-wall or high-value parts needing a custom fixture built and indicated in, first-piece prove-out with feed/speed tweaking by sound and finish, and rescue of a marginal setup.
Exception handling on the cell: a dropped or mis-seated part, chip nest or coolant problem, broken tool or crash alarm that must be diagnosed and cleared before production resumes.

instances.label: Production run on a CNC lathe or VMC in a metal machine shop: operator repeatedly loads raw blanks (bar slugs, sawn billets, small castings) into a chuck, vise or dedicated fixture, seats the part against stops/parallels, secures it (wrench, handle or actuated clamp), verifies seating, and unloads the finished part each cycle.

Job changeover on a machining center: bolt a vise, tombstone or fixture plate to the table, indicate it parallel/locate it with a dial indicator or spindle probe to a few thousandths, torque the T-nuts, clamp the first workpiece, and establish work offsets before the run.

Cutting-tool setup: assemble cutting tools into holders (collet/ER, shrink-fit, set-screw), tighten to spec, measure length and diameter on a presetter or in-machine, load holders into the lathe turret or machining-center ATC magazine, and enter tool offsets.

Heavy or awkward setups and machine attachments: strap-clamping large castings, weldments or plate to an HMC pallet or large VMC table with step blocks and a hoist; installing a rotary/4th-axis table, changing lathe chuck jaws or a steady rest; indicating the setup in before cutting.

Non-metal CNC work: in a cabinet/plastics shop or countertop fabrication shop, loading a full sheet of panel stock onto a CNC nesting router's vacuum table (or a stone/quartz slab onto a bridge saw/router bed), squaring it to stops or pods, and securing it by vacuum or clamps.

tasks.label: Listen to machines during operation to detect sounds such as those made by dull cutting tools or excessive vibration, and adjust machines to compensate for problems.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Repeat production run of metal parts on a vertical/horizontal machining center in a job or production shop: operator stands at or near the enclosed machine, hears the cut change as an end mill or insert dulls (rising pitch, rubbing/squealing, load change), and responds by dialing back feed/speed override or stopping the cycle to index or swap the tool.

Chatter / excessive vibration during milling or turning (thin wall, long tool overhang, unfavorable rpm harmonic): operator hears the characteristic squeal or rattle mid-cut and adjusts spindle speed, feedrate or depth of cut on the control to kill the chatter and save the surface finish.

Small or fragile tooling and long-cycle work (Swiss-type lathe, small drills/taps, deep holes, aerospace/medical parts): operator listens for the change in sound or the snap of a breaking tool during the cycle and stops the machine, retracts, and replaces the tool before scrap or a crash occurs.

Operator tending several CNC machines across a shop floor (cells, bar-fed lathes, pallet pools, run-up to unattended/lights-out shifts): while walking the floor, notices an off sound from one machine's cutting process, goes over, confirms the problem, and adjusts feeds/speeds or halts that machine's cycle.

Non-metal CNC work — wood nesting router / panel processing center, stone or solid-surface router, plastics sheet machining: operator listens for the dull-bit sound, burning or screeching from a worn router bit or blade and adjusts feed rate or swaps the cutter.

Abnormal machine (non-cutting) noise: spindle bearing whine, coolant pump cavitation, air leak whistle, tool-changer or chip-conveyor clunk, loose fixture rattle. Operator notices the sound, investigates, and derates or stops the machine, adjusting parameters or flagging maintenance before damage.

instances.label: Machining center in a job/production shop: an endmill, drill or reamer dulls mid-run. Operator stops the cycle, pulls the toolholder from the spindle or magazine, removes the worn cutter from the holder (collet/press/shrink), installs a fresh cutter, re-presets length and diameter offsets, returns the holder to the magazine and verifies with a check cut.

Turning center / lathe: worn carbide inserts in turret toolholders or boring bars. Operator loosens the torx screw, indexes or swaps the insert, cleans the pocket seat, torques the screw to spec, and adjusts the wear offset before resuming the part.

High-volume FMS or pallet cell with tool-life management: worn tools are retired to sister tools by the control; the magazine must be replenished with fresh, preset tools from central tool storage and out-of-life tools removed and routed to the tool room, often during unattended/lights-out running.

CNC router / woodworking / plastics shop: dull spiral router bit, drill or saw blade swapped in a collet or shrink-fit HSK holder; dusty environment, larger machine footprint, moderate precision requirements, offsets re-zeroed after the change.

Heavy or multi-edge tooling: face mills with many inserts, large boring bars, big HSK/Capto holders needing a hoist, or grinding wheel packs on a CNC tool grinder; change requires handling weight and careful seating/balancing.

Abnormal removal: cutter snapped off in the holder or spindle, galled/seized insert screw, chip-packed pocket or damaged threads; the worn tool must be extracted and the holder repaired or scrapped before a replacement can be fitted.

tasks.label: Check to ensure that workpieces are properly lubricated and cooled during machine operation.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Start-of-cycle verification at a VMC/lathe: after loading and starting the program, the operator watches the first cuts through the window to confirm flood and through-tool coolant is actually striking the tool/workpiece, then opens the door and bends or re-aims coolant lines, or edits coolant position/M-codes, before letting the cycle run.

Periodic in-run checks while tending several machines on the shop floor: glancing at coolant streams and chip color/smoke through splash guards, listening for dry cutting or chatter, spotting chip nests that block coolant, blowing/washing chips off the part and fixture, confirming the part is not running hot or discolored.

Coolant fluid condition checks at the machine sump: verifying level, topping off with correctly mixed coolant, checking concentration with a refractometer and adjusting the mix, watching for foam, tramp oil, or an over-warm sump during a long production run.

Machine lubrication checks during operation: confirming way-lube/spindle-lube reservoir level and pump cycling, responding to low-lube or low-lube-pressure alarms on the control, adding way oil, and verifying lube actually reaches ways and ballscrews so the machine keeps cutting to size.

Tight-tolerance or heat-sensitive job (aerospace alloy, deep-hole drilling, grinding): verifying high-pressure through-spindle coolant pressure/flow at each tool, confirming coolant chiller/temperature control is holding, and checking that the part is not thermally growing before in-process gaging.

tasks.label: Adjust machine feed and speed, change cutting tools, or adjust machine controls when automatic programming is faulty or if machines malfunction.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Mid-cycle correction of cutting conditions on a production machining center or CNC lathe in a job/production shop: the operator hears chatter, sees spindle-load spikes, blue chips or a poor finish, and turns the feed/speed override or edits the F/S values so the cut comes back into range and the part is saved.

A cutting tool dulls or breaks part way through a job: the operator stops the cycle, opens the door, pulls the holder, fits a fresh insert/endmill (or a preset spare tool), re-establishes the tool length/wear offset, and restarts the program at the right block.

Prove-out of a newly posted CAM program where the automatic feeds/speeds and sizes are off: the operator runs at reduced rate, then trims feeds and spindle speeds and dials in tool/work offsets until the first article measures in tolerance.

The automatic program itself is faulty (wrong tool call, gouging toolpath, bad approach/retract, wrong work offset): the operator diagnoses the error at the control, edits the NC program or has it re-posted, and re-runs the affected section.

Machine malfunction on the shop floor: tool-changer arm jam, chip nest or coolant/hydraulic failure, servo or spindle alarm, chuck/tailstock fault, or a tool snapped off in the workpiece. The operator diagnoses it, clears the obstruction by hand, resets or adjusts parameters, and restarts or calls maintenance.

High-volume or lights-out running inside a fenced automated cell/FMS: tools reach end of life or the process drifts during unattended hours, and the response is a redundant (sister) tool call, adaptive feed control, magazine restocking with preset tools, and automatic offset compensation.

tasks.label: Monitor machine operation and control panel displays, and compare readings to specifications to detect malfunctions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine in-cycle monitoring of a single CNC mill or lathe during a production run on a job-shop/production floor: watching the control screen (spindle load, feed/position, alarms, part counter), listening for chatter or tool squeal, watching chip formation and coolant flow, and comparing what is seen to the setup sheet/spec limits; stopping the cycle when something deviates.

Multi-machine attendance: the operator runs 3-8 machines and walks a route around the shop floor, glancing at each control panel/stack light, checking cycle counts, alarm history, tool-life counters and coolant/hydraulic status against expected values, and identifying which machine is faulting or drifting.

Heightened monitoring during first-article or new-program proveout and after a setup change: running single-block/reduced feed, watching distance-to-go and position readouts against the program and print, listening and watching for crash risk, chatter, workholding slip, poor finish, and unanticipated problems on an unproven process.

Monitoring a fenced, robot-tended or bar-fed automated cell / lights-out run: overseeing the cell HMI and machine-monitoring dashboard, tool-life and load-trend data, alarm logs and part counts, and detecting faults (tool wear/breakage, misload, chip build-up) that require stopping the cell.

Monitoring a CNC laser or plasma cutting machine in a sheet-metal fabrication shop: watching cut quality, pierce failures, dross, tip-ups and head collisions on the control display and at the table, comparing gas/power/feed parameters to the cut chart, and halting the nest when cuts go bad.

Monitoring a CNC router, waterjet or stone/wood machining center in dusty, wet or slurry-laden conditions: watching for tool breakage, burning/smoke, dust-extraction failure, abrasive feed problems, workpiece shift on vacuum tables, and comparing machine readouts to job specs.

tasks.label: Maintain machines and remove and replace broken or worn machine tools, using hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Machining center / lathe on a job-shop or production floor: dull or broken cutting tool assemblies are pulled out of the machine's tool magazine or turret and replaced with fresh preset assemblies (grab wrench, release holder, load new holder, enter/verify tool length and diameter offsets, restart the program).

Indexing or replacing worn carbide inserts and their tiny torx screws on face mills, boring bars and turning holders, at the machine or on a bench; clean the seat, index or fit a new edge, torque to spec, re-check runout.

Rebuilding the tool assembly itself: pull the worn end mill/drill out of a collet, ER or shrink-fit holder with hand tools or an induction heater, clean the taper and holder, install a new cutter, tighten, and preset length/diameter on a presetter.

Housekeeping at the machine between jobs/shifts: blow and rake chips off the fixture, chuck, table and way covers, hose down the work zone, and keep the coolant sump topped up to level and concentration.

Scheduled preventive maintenance checklist on the machine: check/refill way-lube and hydraulic oil, grease fittings, clean or swap coolant and air filters and chip-conveyor screens, drain and clean the sump, replace way wipers, check air pressure and door interlocks, wipe windows and doors.

Breakdown or crash recovery: diagnose the fault, extract a snapped tap or drill from the workpiece, replace a damaged toolholder, collet, chuck jaws, vise or worn belts/seals, re-align and re-qualify the machine with indicators, using hand tools in a cramped machine enclosure.

tasks.label: Insert control instructions into machine control units to start operation.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Repeat production run at a CNC machining center or lathe in a job shop: the part program is already resident in the Fanuc/Haas/Siemens control; for each piece the operator confirms the active program and mode at the panel and presses cycle start, dozens of times per shift, with feed/rapid overrides in hand.

Job changeover with a proven program: operator brings the NC file into the machine control unit (DNC/Ethernet transfer from the shop network, or USB/CF card inserted at the control), navigates the control's program directory, selects and activates the program, then starts the cycle.

Keying corrective data into the control before restarting: entering or adjusting tool-length/wear and work offsets, spindle/feed parameters or M-code settings at the MCU keypad after a measurement, then restarting the cycle.

Hand-entering instructions at the control (MDI): the operator types G-code blocks directly into the control for a one-off facing, drilling or re-cut operation, or edits lines of the resident program based on a print and judgment, then starts the machine.

Multi-machine tending: operator responsible for 3-6 CNC machines (mills, lathes, routers, saws) spread over the shop floor, walking machine to machine, calling up the right program at each machine's own control and starting its cycle as each finishes.

Automated/lights-out cell: in a fenced or scanner-guarded robotic machine-tending cell the operator queues the jobs, and for each part the program is selected in the machine control and the cycle started automatically between load/unload moves; operator initiates and monitors the batch.

Sheet, plate, slab or panel stock loaded onto a flat-bed machine: steel sheets onto a CNC laser/punch/waterjet table, MDF or plywood panels onto a nesting router, plastic or composite sheet onto a router, moved from a stack with a vacuum lifter, fork truck or crane and squared against stops.

Operator prepares the paperwork and metrology side of the next job while the machine runs: transfers/verifies the NC program at the control or over the network, reviews the setup sheet and print, gathers gauges, gauge blocks, probes and inspection fixtures, and lays out first-article inspection documents at the machine.

tasks.label: Control coolant systems.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: During a running job on a CNC mill/lathe in a job or production shop: starting and stopping flood, through-spindle/through-tool and air-blast coolant for each operation, and selecting flow/pressure appropriate to the tool and material as the cycle proceeds.

At setup and at each tool change: establishing where coolant is delivered - positioning the nozzle/spigot so the stream reaches the cutting edge for each tool length, and re-aiming as tools change during the job.

Shift/daily fluid checks in the shop: reading sump level, checking concentration with a refractometer, mixing concentrate with water at the right ratio and topping off the machine sump (or diluting a rich sump) to bring it back in spec.

Keeping the coolant fit during production: skimming tramp oil, filtering fines and chips out of the coolant, flushing chips out of the work zone and off sump screens so flow is maintained during long or unattended runs.
Periodic changeover: draining a spent charge, cleaning settled swarf and sludge out of the machine sump/chip pan, and recharging the machine with fresh, correctly mixed coolant.

Hands-on fault response mid-job: a nozzle plugged with a chip or knocked out of aim, a leaking hose or fitting, excessive foam or mist, coolant blowing out of the enclosure - diagnosing and physically correcting it, then restoring the cut.

tasks.label: Clean machines, tooling, or parts, using solvents or solutions and rags.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Between cycles/setups at a CNC mill or lathe: flush chips out of the work zone with the coolant gun, blow off and wipe the chuck jaws, vise, fixture and locating pads with a rag and cleaner so the next part seats correctly. Cleaning machined parts: removing coolant, cutting oil, and chips from finished or in-process parts by spraying/dipping in a cleaning solution or solvent, wiping with rags, and blowing dry before inspection, secondary operations, or packing. Done at a wash sink or bench in the shop.

Cleaning tooling: wiping toolholder tapers, collets, pull studs, cutter bodies and inserts with solvent-dampened rags, degreasing tools before presetting or return to storage, cleaning the spindle taper. Done at a tool crib bench or at the machine.

Periodic (end of shift/weekly) deep clean of the machine itself: wiping down enclosure interior, way covers, windows, sheet metal, control panel and handwheels with solvent, degreaser and rags; wiping oil and coolant film off the machine exterior. Cluttered space around and inside a machine built for human access.

Cleaning ancillary equipment and coolant system: scrubbing coolant tank/sump and filters, cleaning chip conveyor and chip pans, clearing and wiping coolant nozzles and lines with cleaning solutions and rags during coolant changes.

tasks.label: Enter commands or load control media, such as tapes, cards, or disks, into machine controllers to retrieve programmed instructions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Machining center operator at a job shop selects an existing part program already resident in the CNC control's memory (e.g., Fanuc/Haas/Siemens MCU), calls it up on the pendant keypad, checks the program header and offsets on screen, and sets it as the active program for the next run.

Operator loads a new or revised program into the controller from portable media: inserts a USB flash drive (or, on legacy machines, a floppy disk or a floppy-to-USB emulator) into the control's port, navigates the control's file menu, and copies the program file into machine memory.

Operator retrieves a program over a network/DNC link: from the CNC control panel (or via a barcode scan of a job traveler) requests the file from the shop server over Ethernet/wireless or RS-232, or drip-feeds a large program, with no physical media handled.

Operator keys in short commands directly at the control in MDI mode - tool changes, spindle/coolant commands, single blocks of G-code - or types brief edits/parameter values into a resident program at the keypad to recall and run a specific routine.

Production operator on a repetitive cell (e.g., CNC lathe or router running a family of parts) recalls a stored program number for the scheduled job at shift start or changeover, sometimes via a job number entered on an HMI touchscreen tied to the ERP/scheduling system.

tasks.label: Lay out and mark areas of parts to be shot peened and fill hoppers with shot.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Aerospace/MRO job-shop bench work: operator reads the peening spec and part drawing, lays out and marks the boundary of the peen zone on a small-to-medium machined part (bracket, gear, shaft, blade root) with layout dye, marker or template, then applies masking tape/plugs to protect adjacent surfaces. Mixed part numbers, few pieces of each, parts arrive on carts and benches in varying orientations.

Refilling the shot hopper on a peening cabinet between or during runs: fetch 50-lb bags or pails of steel shot, cut wire or ceramic/glass bead from media storage, verify size/type against the job traveler, cut and pour into the machine hopper, and watch the level through the run.

Large, heavy parts (landing-gear cylinders, large gears, forgings, weldments) craned onto a bench or positioner: lay out peen zones over curved/3D geometry from drawing dimensions using templates, height gauge and scribe/marker, marking long boundaries the peening operator will follow.

High-volume repetitive batch of one part number: mark the same peen zone on dozens to hundreds of identical small parts using a template or fixture, and top off the cabinet's shot hopper between lots.

Bulk media handling on a large automated peening system: hoist 1,000–2,000 lb bulk bags or drums of shot into the machine's media replenishment hopper or storage silo, sieve/classify, and top off the circulating media charge.

instances.label: Hybrid microelectronics plant: after a laser-trim run, the operator takes a carrier of thick-film resistor networks on ceramic substrates to a bench stereo/measuring microscope and checks each trim kerf (length, width, placement relative to conductor, cut-through, spatter, micro-cracks), sorting substrates pass/fail.

First-article / setup verification: after a new job setup or trim-parameter change on the laser trimmer, the operator examines the first pieces under the microscope to confirm the trim cuts are complete, correctly located and correctly shaped per the trim program before releasing the run.

Small-lot hi-rel / defense hybrid shop: operator inspects a handful of varied, frequently changing part numbers under a stereo microscope against MIL-spec workmanship criteria (trim completeness plus chips, cracks, contamination, bonds), signing the traveler; no pre-programmed inspection recipe exists for these one-off jobs.

Reject review: operator examines flagged or electrically failed parts at higher magnification to characterize the anomaly (over-trim/cut-through, substrate crack, spatter in the kerf, wrong trim path) and record/report the defect type for corrective action.

Plastics/film and packaging heat sealing (pouch, tray, blister, medical device packaging): worker positions films, webs, pre-formed pouches, trays or components into the sealing station/tooling so the seal lands on register marks and the components are correctly nested; cleanroom or food-plant conditions, moderate-to-high volume.

Wood products plant (plywood/LVL layup, panel and laminate bonding): worker aligns veneer sheets onto the glue spreader and squares the layup stack, or positions decorative laminate over a glued substrate before the press. Large limp/rigid sheets, dusty mill floor, conveyorized line.

Rubber and rubberized-fabric parts (tire components, hose, belting, gaskets): worker aligns plies, tread, or rubber-coated fabric onto a drum, mandrel or mating part so splices and overlaps are correct before bonding/vulcanizing. Tacky, stretchable stock; dedicated building station in a rubber plant.

Shaped flexible goods (footwear cementing, foam/fabric/leather soft goods, some medical assemblies): worker positions curved, deformable parts—upper to lasted sole, foam to fabric, gasket to housing—by eye or against marks so the cemented joint is accurate, then presses. Frequent style/size variation within a running model.

Small-batch, high-mix custom bonding/sealing at a bench-top press, RF/impulse sealer or glue station in a job shop: short runs of odd-shaped or one-off parts, improvised jigs and marks, several changeovers a day, alignment judged by eye to layout lines.

instances.label: Attentive monitoring of a running gluer/laminator (folder-gluer, flexo folder gluer, veneer glue spreader, laminator) during a production run: watching glue tracks/beads, listening for abnormal noise, checking temperature, pressure and speed readouts, and reacting immediately to a developing fault (glue skips, streaks, misregister) by adjusting settings or stopping the line. Plant floor, standard equipment, run in shifts.

Clearing a jam or misfeed: crumpled blanks or sheets wadded in the folding/transport section, a glue-soaked board hang-up, veneer jammed in a spreader, or a web break. Operator stops the machine, opens guards, reaches into the machine, pulls out damaged and glue-covered material, re-threads or re-feeds and restarts.
Keeping the adhesive supply going: noticing a low or empty melter tank/glue pot and refilling or switching supply so the run is not interrupted.

Adhesive-system faults requiring hands-on repair: clogged or dripping nozzles/guns, charred or hardened hot melt, plugged filters and hoses, dirty glue wheels/pots; operator wipes, purges, probes or swaps the applicator and cleans up before resuming.

A malfunction beyond the operator's own repair (bearing noise, drive fault, electrical alarm, air leak, smoke/odor): operator stops the machine, tags/locks it out as required, notifies maintenance or the supervisor, and logs the downtime and symptom.

Catching bond-quality drift downstream — open/weak seams, blisters or dry spots in plywood or laminate, insufficient glue coverage found on pull tests or spot checks — and correcting it by adjusting glue volume, pattern position, roller gap, pressure or temperature.

instances.label: Plywood/veneer plant: operator starts the glue spreader and hot press line, opens valves to admit mixed resin from the glue mixing tank to the spreader, and sets platen temperature, press pressure and press (cure) time on the press control panel for the panel thickness being run; adjusts during the shift as glue and moisture conditions change.

Paper/board converting (folder-gluer, corrugator, case sealer): operator starts the machine, brings the hot-melt melter or cold-glue pot to temperature, sets air/fluid pressure and glue gun timing (on/off distances) for the blank, opens supply valves to the application heads, and starts the run.

Coating/laminating line for film, foam, rubberized fabric or simulated leather: operator admits adhesive to the coater head or hot-melt slot die, sets coating-head gap/coat weight, oven zone temperatures, nip pressure, and line speed/dwell, then starts the web running.

Standalone shop machine (shoe cementing/sole press, edgebander, small platen laminator, bench dispenser): operator charges the machine with cement or hot-melt, dials in temperature, pressure and dwell time on the machine's controls, and presses start for each cycle.

Startup, changeover and re-supply: purge and prime adhesive lines after a product or adhesive change, swap a drum/tote or refill the melter hopper, re-enter or recall the parameter set (temperature, pressure, timing) for the new job, and verify the first bonded pieces before releasing the run.

tasks.label: Fill machines with glue, cement, or adhesives.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Packaging/converting plant: operator keeps hot-melt melter tanks on case sealers, cartoners and labelers topped up during a shift — carrying boxes/bags of EVA pellets or slats to the machine, opening the hot tank lid and pouring in adhesive, watching the level gauge and avoiding overfill, char and burns.

Corrugated/folding-carton or laminating plant running cold, water-based adhesive (PVA, dextrin, starch): operator refills glue reservoirs and pump supply containers from pails, drums or totes, primes lines, tops off during the run and flushes/cleans the supply at product changeover.

Bindery/print-finishing shop: operator keeps the glue pot/wheel of a perfect binder or the tanks of a small gluing machine supplied — filling a floor-standing pre-melter or pot with hot-melt chips or PUR, several fills per shift, in a fixed spot beside the machine.

Plywood/LVL or panel mill glue kitchen: operator batches the adhesive to formula (liquid phenolic or urea resin, extender flour, water) by weight, mixes it, and charges the glue mixer/spreader supply tank, then washes out tanks and lines between batches.

tasks.label: Perform test production runs and make adjustments as necessary to ensure that completed products meet standards and specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Folding-carton or corrugated plant: at job changeover on a folder-gluer/box-gluer, the operator sets glue heads, guides and speed, runs a short trial of blanks, pulls sample boxes, checks glue bead placement, coverage and adhesion (pull/fiber-tear), squareness and gap, tweaks glue-gun timing/volume and mechanical guides, re-runs and releases the job.

Plywood/veneer/panel or wood-laminating plant: for a new panel spec, the operator runs test panels through the glue spreader and hot press, checks glue spread rate (weighed sheets) and bond quality (knife/shear/boil test), adjusts spreader roll gap and pressure, glue mix and press time/temperature/pressure, re-runs until panels pass.

Web coating/laminating line (tape, film, foam, rubberized fabric, simulated leather): at startup the operator runs the web slowly, checks coat weight/adhesive thickness, wrinkles, bubbles and adhesion on cut samples, adjusts applicator/slot-die settings, nip pressure, tension and temperature, then brings the line to speed.

Automated adhesive dispensing/bonding station or cell (electronics, medical device, appliance, automotive part): first-article parts are dispensed and bonded, bead volume/position and bond are checked against spec with gauges or vision, dispense volume, path, pressure and cure settings are corrected, and parts are re-run until in spec.

Small shop or high-mix short run: an unfamiliar or custom bonded product (prototype, specialty laminate, cemented rubber/leather goods) with no fixed recipe; the operator improvises trial pieces, destructively pulls them apart by hand to judge bond and squeeze-out, iteratively changes adhesive, temperature and dwell, and decides when it is good enough.

tasks.label: Examine and measure completed materials or products to verify conformance to specifications, using measuring devices such as tape measures, gauges, or calipers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Plywood/veneer plant: after the hot press, saw line and sander, the tender pulls finished panels from the line or a stack, measures thickness at several points with a caliper/micrometer, checks length, width and squareness with a tape, and inspects edges and faces for delamination, glue skips and blows before the lot is released.

Paper/paperboard converting (folder-gluer, corrugated plant, board laminator): operator pulls sample glued cartons or laminated sheets off the delivery, checks glue-lap position and coverage, squareness and fishtail, and measures panel/box dimensions with a tape or gauge against the job spec, repeatedly through the run.

Rubber/plastic bonding: laminated rubberized fabric, simulated leather, foam/film laminates, flocked or spliced sealing profiles. Operator measures bonded thickness and width with calipers or a dial gauge, checks bond line, edge trim and surface for bubbles or adhesive squeeze-out on samples taken from the running line.

Furniture/laminated panel work: hot-press laminating, edgebanding or countertop lamination. Operator measures finished panel length, width and thickness, checks overhang/flushness and glue-line tightness at edges with a gauge or straightedge on panels coming off the machine.

Small adhesive-bonded assemblies (medical device components, electronics, gaskets, footwear soles/uppers): operator takes sampled parts to a bench, verifies critical dimensions, gaps and bond-line thickness with calipers, pin/go-no-go gauges or an optical comparator, and records results on an inspection sheet.

tasks.label: Remove and stack completed materials or products, and restock materials to be joined.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Corrugated / folding-carton plant: operator works the delivery end of a folder-gluer or litho-laminator, taking shingled runs of finished glued cartons off the delivery, squaring and bundling them, stacking bundles on a pallet; at the feed end, lifts lifts of blanks off pallets brought by forklift into the machine hopper. Job changes several times per shift; box sizes vary.

Plywood / engineered-panel or edge-glue plant: operator pulls pressed panels or glued-up boards off the press or glue line, stacks them on carts or pallets with stickers, and restocks veneer sheets, core stock or lumber strips into the spreader/layup station. Heavy, large-format sheets; hot press cycles set the pace.

Rigid-component bonding cell in a durable-goods or automotive/appliance plant: operator unloads bonded assemblies (plastic, metal or composite panels, trim, filters) from a press or bonding fixture, sets them in racks/dunnage trays, and reloads the fixture with components taken from racks and bins staged beside the station on an active line.

Molded rubber/plastic parts bonding: operator unloads small bonded parts (grommets, gaskets, seals, plastic sub-assemblies) from a bench-side bonding machine or heated press, counts and stacks them in totes or on trays, and refills the machine's parts trays from bins of adhesive-coated components.

Roll-fed gluing/laminating line (bag, envelope, book-binding, corrugator): operator removes finished glued stacks/bundles from the delivery or downstacker and skids them, and restocks the machine with heavy paper reels or sheet lifts using a hoist/roll cart at reel changes.

Limp-material bonding (rubberized fabric, simulated leather, foam, footwear uppers and soles): operator peels finished bonded pieces off the press or roller, stacks them flat with interleaving, and restocks cement-coated flexible blanks into the machine, often in a small high-mix shop where sizes change constantly.

tasks.label: Remove jammed materials from machines and readjust components as necessary to resume normal operations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Carton folder-gluer or case sealer in a packaging/converting plant jams: crushed, glue-smeared board wedges in the folding, transfer or compression section. Operator e-stops the line, opens a guard, pulls out the deformed board and torn fragments by hand, scrapes wet glue off belts and rails, resets guide rails/hold-downs, and restarts, checking the first cartons for bond quality.

Plywood/veneer glue line: a torn, overlapped or curled veneer sheet jams in the glue spreader rollers, lay-up feeder or press infeed. Operator stops the line, reaches into the spreader or between platens to free heavy, glue-coated sheets, removes squeeze-out and broken pieces, realigns the feeder/conveyor chains, and resumes lay-up.

Web-fed laminator, labeling machine or perfect binder jams: film/paper web tears and wraps up on a heated nip roller, or labels pile up at the applicator. Operator strips glue-bonded material off the rollers with a scraper/knife, cleans hot-melt residue, re-threads the web, resets tension and registration, and runs test pieces.

Light misfeed at a feeder, transfer or exit stacker: a skewed sheet, double feed or tipped part hangs up at the hopper or discharge without deforming. Operator reaches in from the operating side, pulls the piece clear, nudges a side guide or sensor, presses reset, and the machine resumes within a minute.

Rubber/plastic or panel bonding press, roll laminator or edgebander: a tacky part sticks to a heated platen or roller, or a panel jams in the bander. Operator pries the adhered part off, cleans cured/uncured adhesive from the platen or rollers, readjusts pressure, gap or temperature settings, and runs a sample to confirm the bond before resuming production.

tasks.label: Clean and maintain gluing and cementing machines, using solutions, lubricants, brushes, and scrapers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: End-of-run/end-of-shift cleaning of the glue application components on a production line (spreader/applicator rolls, glue pot or pan, doctor blades, nozzles and application heads): scraping off skinned or cured adhesive, brushing, and washing with water or solvent so the line can restart in spec. Plant floor, machine stopped but in place, other workers and lift trucks around.

Purging, flushing and unclogging the adhesive delivery circuit at adhesive changeover, startup or shutdown: draining the tank/melter, running solvent or wash water through hoses, manifolds and heads, clearing plugged nozzles/tips with cleaning solutions and probes, verifying clean flow.

Scheduled lubrication rounds on the gluing/cementing machine: oiling and greasing bearings, chains, slides, gearboxes and conveyor components at listed points per the PM schedule, and topping up reservoirs.

Machine wipe-down and housekeeping: scraping cured glue off machine frames, guards, feed tables, conveyor belts and catch pans, wiping surfaces with solvent rags, emptying drip trays and clearing adhesive spills and waste around the machine.

Periodic deep maintenance during scheduled downtime: partial disassembly of glue heads/rolls, soaking and scrubbing components in cleaning solution, inspecting and replacing filters, seals, screens and worn wear parts, reassembly, lubrication and a test run.

tasks.label: Measure and mix ingredients to prepare glue.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Wood-panel plant (plywood/LVL) glue kitchen: operator works to a resin recipe, doses liquid phenolic or urea resin, water and caustic, weighs and dumps 25-50 lb bags of extender flour/filler into the batch mixer, runs the mixer for a set time, checks viscosity, temperature and pH, and pumps the batch to the glue spreader.

Corrugated box / paper converting plant starch glue kitchen: prepares repeated batches of Stein-Hall or no-carrier starch adhesive (starch, caustic soda, borax, water) to a target viscosity and gel point, checks each batch with a viscosity cup and thermometer, and feeds the corrugator or gluer storage tanks through a shift.

Machine-side small batch of a two-component adhesive: operator weighs or measures resin and hardener/catalyst (epoxy, urethane, rubber cement plus curing agent) in the specified ratio into a pot or the machine reservoir, stirs with a paddle or drill mixer, and must use the batch within its pot life.

Adjusting and replenishing adhesive on a running bonding line: adds water, solvent/thinner or fresh premix to the reservoir or mix tank to bring solids/viscosity back to spec, verifies with a viscosity cup or inline gauge, and re-mixes without stopping the line.

Small job shop (bindery, cabinet/laminating shop, upholstery, small footwear or specialty products maker): operator mixes glue by hand in buckets from bags of powder and jugs of liquid on a general-purpose bench, with recipes and batch sizes varying by job and no dedicated mixing plant.

tasks.label: Add specified amounts of chemicals to equipment at required times to maintain solution levels and concentrations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Beverage/food plant: operator tending a returnable-bottle washer or CIP set, titrating the caustic bath each shift and adding caustic soda and additive from a bulk tank or drum, plus water make-up, to hold concentration (e.g., 1.8-2.5% NaOH) and tank level while the line runs.

Metal pickling line / acid dip tanks in a steel or metal-finishing plant: operator samples the bath and adds hydrochloric or sulfuric acid, inhibitor, or regenerated acid at set intervals to keep free-acid and iron concentrations within spec, and tops the tanks back to level.

Job-shop / manufacturing aqueous parts washer or bay washer: operator checks the wash tank with a refractometer or titration kit once a shift, pours alkaline detergent concentrate from a pail or drum and adds water to restore level and concentration in an open-top tank.

Institutional warewashing or industrial laundry machine: operator keeps detergent, destainer, rinse aid and sanitizer at required concentration each cycle, replacing solid blocks or drums and verifying dose with test strips.

Coal preparation, pulp, or mineral washing plant: operator makes up and adds reagents (powdered flocculant, lime, magnetite, surfactant) to washing/thickening circuits at required times to hold reagent dose and slurry chemistry.
