instances.label: Precast/architectural concrete plant: worker bores holes and cuts blockouts, vent holes and pour openings in plywood, timber or steel side forms sitting on casting beds, using a hand drill, hole saw or circular saw; layout marked from shop drawings, forms of varying size lying flat on the plant floor.

Ceramic / sanitaryware / pottery mold shop: worker cuts the pouring spout (sprue) and bores vent, spare and air-line holes in plaster or resin case molds at a bench, using a drill press, hand drill or rotary tool; molds are one to several feet across, plaster is soft and chips easily.

Foundry-type non-metal mold shop (bonded-sand, plaster-mold or ceramic-mold casting): worker cuts gates, runners, risers and pouring basins/spouts into bonded sand or plaster molds and cores with a router, die grinder or drill, following rigging layout for the casting.

Cast stone, concrete pipe or terrazzo plant: worker drills holes through steel or fiberglass (GRP) production molds for lifting anchors, inserts, bolts and drainage/vent openings, using a magnetic drill or hand drill with hole saws; molds are heavy, reused, and positioned wherever the crew set them.

Field/jobsite work: worker bores holes and cuts pouring spouts or chute openings in erected wooden formwork or field-built molds for cast-in-place or on-site cast elements, using a cordless drill and circular saw amid clutter, weather and other trades.

Small craft/artisan shop (candles, figurines, soap, plaster ornament): worker bores wick or vent holes and cuts a pouring spout in a one-off silicone, plaster, wood or aluminum mold with a drill press or rotary tool, judging placement by eye against the cavity.

tasks.label: Tap or tilt molds to ensure uniform distribution of materials.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Precast/architectural concrete plant: after a steel mold or form on the shop floor is filled with fresh concrete, the worker vibrates, taps or shakes the mold (vibrating table, clamp-on external vibrators, rubber mallet) so the mix flows into corners and around reinforcement and voids rise out; heavy molds, varying element sizes, dusty noisy plant.

Concrete products plant (block, paver, pipe, terrazzo/cast stone tile): mold boxes filled with stiff mix are vibrated/tapped so material distributes evenly and fully fills every cavity before pressing or curing; high-repetition production of standard shapes.

Food-product molding in a food plant (chocolate/candy bars and pralines, molded cheese, baked/confection goods): filled molds are tapped or run over a vibrating section to level the fill, settle inclusions and release air bubbles; sanitary environment, standard mold trays.

Ceramic/plaster works (tableware, sanitaryware, figurines, art pottery): slip or plaster is poured into plaster or resin molds, then the mold is tapped and tilted/rotated so material reaches fine detail, then drained of excess; molds of many shapes handled on benches and racks.

Small craft or custom shop (artisan chocolatier, candle maker, resin/gypsum figurine or soap maker, concrete countertop shop): small batches of varied benchtop molds are hand-tapped on the bench or set on a small vibrating table between frequent product changeovers.

On-site or outdoor casting (job-site tilt-up panels, cast-in-place decorative elements, site-cast GFRC): forms built or set up in place are rodded, tapped with a mallet or worked with a poker/form vibrator under variable weather, footing and access conditions.

sources.transferJustification: The machine performs the same function as tapping/tilting a mold by hand: mechanically shaking the filled mold so the concrete distributes uniformly and air is expelled, on the same workpieces (steel molds of precast elements).

tasks.label: Construct or form molds for use in casting clay or plaster objects, using plaster, fiberglass, rubber, casting machines, patterns, or flasks.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Ceramics plant mould shop (tableware/sanitaryware): repetitive production of working plaster moulds from existing case moulds — weigh and mix pottery plaster to consistency, pour into the clamped case mould, strike off, wait for set, strip the case, sponge/trim edges, number and rack the mould to dry. Standard shapes, high volume, fixed benches.

Model-and-mould development at a plant or commercial mould supplier: from a master model, block and case the shape — build the block mould, fabricate the fiberglass or plaster case (mother) mould with registration natches, and pull the first working mould for trial casting. Skilled, one-off per new product.

Small pottery/art-casting studio or giftware shop: build a new multi-part plaster mould around a prototype or found pattern — bed the object in clay, set coddles/boards, cut keys, apply size, mix and pour each half in turn, flip, separate, clean and dry. Objects vary constantly.

Flexible-mould work in a statuary/ornamental shop: brush or pour silicone/latex rubber over a pattern to capture undercut detail, build a fiberglass or plaster mother shell over it with keys and flanges, then de-mould, trim flash and register the shell for casting plaster or clay bodies.

Large or awkward mould work: heavy multi-part moulds for large sanitaryware or garden statuary, and taking moulds off existing architectural ornament in the field (site plasterwork, restoration) — non-standard supports, restricted access, mould sections handled with hoists or by hand.

instances.label: High-volume concrete products plant (block, paver, pipe, hollowcore): batched mix is fed into steel molds/forms, vibrated and pressed/compacted, struck off; the same product repeats thousands of times per shift on a fixed machine line.

Food, candle, wax or soap plant: molten chocolate/confection/wax dosed into moving molds, vibrated to release air, cooled and demolded on a continuous line.

Small custom shop or studio (statuary, ornamental plaster, cast stone, cultured marble, art casting): worker hand-mixes small batches, brushes a face coat into a one-off or short-run mold, packs stiff mix in by hand and tool, tamps around undercuts and inserts, strikes off and patches voids.
Mold and model shop: packing sand or refractory around a pattern/model, or pouring plaster or ceramic slurry around a model, to build the working molds and shells used for later production.

tasks.label: Verify depths and dimensions of cuts or carvings to ensure adherence to specifications, blueprints, or models, using measuring instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Monument/memorial shop: after sandblast carving or etching of a granite headstone or marker, the worker checks letter and ornament depth with a depth gauge/rule and checks overall height, width, thickness, and margin layout against the order drawing; piece lies on a padded bench or leans on a rack, wet stone dust present.

Architectural stone fabrication plant: verifying finished cut and profiled pieces (panels, sills, treads, cornice/molding runs) against shop drawings using tape, framing square, calipers and plywood/zinc profile templates before crating; pieces sit on carts, pallets or A-frames.

Countertop/slab shop: checking a cut and edged quartz or granite top for overall length/width, squareness, miter and edge thickness, sink and cooktop cutout position and radius, and hole depths, against the digital template/layout, using tape, square, calipers and templates.

In-process check at the machine (bridge saw, CNC router, lathe, splitter): between operations the worker measures remaining stock, cut depth, groove or rebate depth and workpiece thickness on the machine bed and adjusts the setup or program before continuing.

Hand-carved sculptural or restoration work: comparing carved depths and contours of an ornament, capital or figure to a plaster/clay model or historic profile using calipers, pointing machine, depth needles and profile gauges, judging where more stock must come off.

sources.system: ZEISS ScanBox (ATOS sensor on robot module)
sources.date: 2026-07 (page retrieved; product line in production use since 2010s)

sources.claim: ZEISS ScanBox is a commercially established robot-based optical 3D measuring machine (robot-manipulated fringe-projection sensor plus rotary table, up to 2000 kg part load) used for automated production quality control, comparing scanned parts to CAD and reporting deviations.

tasks.label: Move fingers over surfaces of carvings to ensure smoothness of finish.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Memorial/monument shop: after polishing and sandblast lettering, the cutter runs fingertips over the flat polished or honed granite face, margins and eased edges of a headstone or marker to feel for rough spots, chatter marks, scratches and unpolished areas before the piece is accepted for shipment.

Architectural/commercial stone fabrication plant: worker hand-checks machine-cut and hand-ground profiles, moldings, curved edges, sills and column elements for tool ridges, unblended transitions and grit lines after grinding/polishing, deciding whether another abrasive pass is needed.

Hand-carved sculptural or ornamental work in a carving studio/shop: the carver repeatedly passes fingers over drapery, undercuts, deep relief and modeled figurative surfaces of a statue, capital or ornament, judging by feel whether the intended texture is even and free of rasp or chisel marks; acceptance is a craft judgment iterated with rasps and abrasives.

On-site or restoration work: checking smoothness of carved stone in place on a building facade, in a cemetery, or at an installation site after patching, dressing or re-cutting, in weather and with scaffolding or uneven ground.

Bench inspection of small pieces: incised lettering, plaques, small carvings and samples are held or set on the bench and felt over for burrs, chipped letter edges and uneven honed texture before delivery.

sources.system: Adaptive robotic stone surfacing / carving system (US patent 12,397,472)
sources.developer: academic inventors (Automation in Construction paper; patent granted 2025)
sources.title: Device and method for adaptive robotic stone surfacing (US 12,397,472)
sources.claim: A robotic stone-carving system evaluated its own carving outcome autonomously between iterations by scanning the worked stone with a depth camera and comparing to the target model, but only at 1-2.5 mm accuracy - far coarser than a fingertip smoothness check - in lab experiments.

tasks.label: Lay out designs or dimensions from sketches or blueprints on stone surfaces, freehand or by transferring them from tracing paper, using scribes or chalk and measuring instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Countertop/slab fabrication shop: a granite or quartz slab is set on the saw table and the fabricator transfers the job's paper or digital template onto it — marking cut lines, seam locations, sink and cooktop cutouts with chalk/marker and a straightedge/tape, positioning the pieces to use the veining and dodge flaws.

Monument/memorial shop: laying out an approved inscription and emblem sketch on a polished granite headstone face — snapping/scribing centerlines and baselines with chalk and rule, spacing and centering the lettering, and positioning the sandblast stencil to the marks.

Architectural dimension-stone shop: transferring dimensions and profiles from shop drawings or zinc/plywood templates onto rough blocks and sawn slabs for sills, treads, coping, cornice and arch stones — scribing cut lines, bed and joint reference marks on several faces with square, rule and scribe.

Ornamental/sculptural carving: laying out a design freehand or from a scaled sketch/full-size cartoon on an irregular rough block for a capital, rosette, gargoyle or figure — plumb and centerlines, key points, adapting the design to the block's actual shape and flaws.

Yard or on-site layout: marking a stone where it lies (in the yard, on the truck, or at an installation) to trim it to an irregular existing condition — scribing from a field template or off the adjoining work, on uneven ground and in weather.

sources.system: Monumental Labs robotic stone carving cells (7-axis KUKA arms)
sources.title: AI robots can already carve stone statues. Entire buildings are next
sources.claim: Monumental Labs runs seven-axis KUKA robotic carving arms in its New York workshops; architectural ornament for Carnegie Hall and the Frick was cut by the robots from digital models and only hand-finished afterwards, i.e. the design geometry is transferred onto the stone by machine.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic milling/carving of the design into the stone. Layout is the registration of a drawing's geometry onto a particular stone; a cell that registers a scanned block and cuts the design to it necessarily performs the marking step, on the same objects (marble/limestone blocks) in the same shop, at tighter precision.

sources.system: Quarra Stone robotic carving cells (KUKA arms with rotating tables)

sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic cutting/carving of architectural stone from CAD. It subsumes laying out the same dimensions and profiles on the block: the machine indexes the workpiece on its table and applies the drawing geometry to the stone faces, which is exactly what scribed layout achieves.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous robotic carving of a design into a rough block. The hard part of freehand layout — fitting a design from a sketch/model onto an irregular block and putting its lines in the right place on the stone — is performed by the scan-to-toolpath registration this system uses before it cuts.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine execution of a slab layout. The layout task's output — the job's lines placed correctly on this slab, with veining and edges accounted for — is produced digitally and applied to the physical slab by the imaging station plus the machine, the same objects and precision as chalk-and-tape layout.

This is the same transfer of a sketch's geometry to the stone surface that chalk/scribe layout accomplishes, on the same workpieces, but done by machine after the stone is positioned and leveled under it.

tasks.label: Drill holes and cut or carve moldings and grooves in stone, according to diagrams and patterns.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Countertop fabrication shop: granite/quartz slab is craned or vacuum-lifted onto a work table; worker drills faucet and sink-anchor holes, cuts the sink opening, and routes edge moldings, flutes and drainboard grooves to a digital template/diagram.

Monument/memorial shop: granite die, base or marker sawn to size; worker cuts margins and decorative grooves, runs a molded (ogee/bevel) edge, and drills dowel/vase/anchor holes per the approved production drawing.

Architectural dimension-stone shop: limestone/marble cornice, sill, baluster or panel; worker cuts profiled moldings, rebates, deep slots and anchor/dowel holes to shop drawings and full-size profile templates.

Ornamental/art carving bay of a stone works: irregular block or rough-cut element; worker carves a molded capital, relief, fluting or a match-carved restoration profile using pneumatic chisels and diamond tools, guided by drawings, rubbings and templates.
Jobsite/field work on staged pieces: replacement or shipped stone element laid on horses at the site is trimmed, a groove or rebate is cut and anchor holes drilled to the diagram before it is set.
Jobsite work on stone already set in the building: cutting a groove/relief or drilling anchor and pin holes into masonry that is in place, on scaffold or in a confined location.

tasks.label: Remove or add stencils during blasting to create differing cut depths, intricate designs, or rough, pitted finishes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Monument shop sandblast room: standard flat, bevel or slant granite marker with rubber stencil applied; blaster blasts lettering, then peels the stencil off the panel/border area for a second, shallower pass so letters are deeper than the frosted panel. Dusty enclosed booth, stone set on a trolley or table.

Upright monument with decorative emblems (crosses, scrollwork, praying hands, wheat, halftone photo emblem): multi-stage work where sections of stencil are peeled and sometimes replaced between passes to get two or three depths and gray shades in one face.

Sculptural 'shape carving': roses, drapery, hands or figures blasted with steel shot into rounded, three-dimensional contours; the carver progressively peels and re-tapes stencil and works the nozzle by hand and eye, judging contour and shading. Highly skilled artisan work in the blast room.

Producing rough, pitted or textured finishes on selected areas — steeled/frosted backgrounds, simulated rock-pitch or pitted panels, textured borders on polished granite or on shaped/curved stone — by masking areas and blasting with coarse abrasive at varied pressure and standoff.

On-site cemetery work: adding a death date or second name to an installed monument using portable blast equipment and a small mask, taping off surrounding stone, peeling the mask sections to match the existing depth and texture; outdoors, weather and grave-side access constraints.

tasks.label: Guide nozzles over stone, following stencil outlines, or chip along marks to create designs or to work surfaces down to specified finishes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Monument shop blast room: worker mounts a cut rubber stencil on a granite die/marker and guides the sandblast nozzle over the stone to blast names, dates, verses and standard emblems to uniform depth, then inspects and cleans up ragged lines.

Monument shop: 3D 'shape carving' with fine sandblast nozzles - roses, praying hands, scenery - where the carver varies nozzle distance, angle and dwell freehand inside stencil openings to model depth and shading on a polished granite face.

instances.label: Production job set-up in an architectural/monument stone shop: from drawings or a 3D model of a piece (panel, moulding, capital blank, base), the carver picks the cutting, profiling, grinding and polishing tools/bits to use and orders them roughing → shaping → finishing, mounting them as the job proceeds. Hand and pneumatic finishing/touch-up at the banker: as the stone reveals veins, seams, hard spots or a chipped arris, the carver re-chooses chisels, rasps, rifflers or a small air scribe on the fly and re-orders the steps so the repaired area matches the surrounding hand-tooled texture on the finished piece.

Surface-finish selection on slabs and architectural units: deciding among bush-hammer, chisel/nicked, flamed, sandblasted, honed or polished treatments and setting the coarse-to-fine sequence of heads, pads and abrasives to reach the specified finish, on stock brought to the finishing machine or bench in the shop.

Field/site work on an installed piece (facade element on scaffolding, cemetery monument in place, museum installation): choosing portable pneumatic tools, hand chisels or a portable blast pot and nozzle and sequencing them under whatever access, weather and surrounding fabric exist at the site.

tasks.label: Load sandblasting equipment with abrasives, attach nozzles to hoses, and turn valves to admit compressed air and activate jets.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production blast-room setup in a granite monument shop: hauling and dumping 50-100 lb bags of silicon carbide or steel grit into the pressure pot / feed hopper, sealing and pressurizing the pot, checking that the blast hose is coupled to the pot and the venturi nozzle is seated in its holder, then opening the compressed-air ball valve and abrasive metering valve and testing the jet before blasting a batch of stencilled monuments.

Setup of a CNC / automatic sandblasting table or booth used for inscriptions and portraits on tombstone slabs: topping up the machine's abrasive hopper, confirming the nozzle is attached to the machine's blast hose at the correct standoff, opening the air supply and pot valves, and starting the programmed blast cycle.

Nozzle and hose changeover or maintenance on shop blast equipment: unscrewing a worn venturi nozzle from the nozzle holder and threading on a new or smaller-bore one for fine lettering, swapping hose quick-couplings and gaskets, reconnecting the deadman/control line, then re-admitting air and testing the jet.

Abrasive changeover between jobs: blowing down and emptying the pot of the previous media, screening/reclaiming it, charging the pot with a different abrasive (e.g., aluminum oxide for fine detail versus steel grit for deep carving), resetting the metering valve, and admitting air to activate the jets at the new setting.

Small siphon-feed blast cabinet or hand detailing blaster in the shop: refilling the cabinet media hopper from a bag or bucket, attaching the small gun/nozzle to the air and media hoses, opening the air valve and triggering the jet for touch-up, frosting or shape-carving work.

Field setup at a cemetery or building site for on-site lettering/restoration: unloading a portable blast pot and towable compressor, filling the pot from bagged abrasive on uneven ground, running and coupling air and blast hoses, attaching the nozzle, and opening the valves to blast a death date onto an installed monument.

instances.label: Scientific/laboratory glassblower in a university or company glass shop softens borosilicate tubing at a bench torch or on a glass working lathe — rotating the tube steadily in the flame until the working zone is uniformly pliable — to make a one-off joint, seal, or repair on custom apparatus of varying diameter and wall thickness.

Artistic hot-shop glassblower reheats a gather/parison on a blowpipe or punty in the glory hole, rotating the pipe continuously to keep the mass centered and uniformly at working temperature before the next shaping step; judgment of colour, sag and timing is visual and continuous.

Production glass shop running repeat items (lab glassware runs, lighting/technical components): tubing or blanks preheated in ovens/kilns and heated at fixed burner stations or a semi-automatic lathe, with set-up parameters repeated across a batch.

instances.label: Specialty/production hot-glass plant or hand shop: worker takes a gather from the furnace on a blowpipe, blows and rotates it in a metal or paste mold (or rolls/shapes it on a board or block) to a fixed catalog shape — tumblers, lighting globes, jars, heavy-wall containers — repeating the same piece dozens to hundreds of times per shift to standard dimensions.

Technical / laboratory-glass production shop: lampworker or lathe operator blows borosilicate or neutral glass tubing with compressed air (through a swivel or blow hose) to keep the bore from collapsing while forming standard repeat catalog items — vials, ampoule and thermometer bulbs, sight glasses, lamp shells, tube-to-bulb transitions — in batches to fixed drawings.

Custom scientific glassblowing shop (university, national lab, or industrial R&D): one-off apparatus built to a sketch — blowing a bulb onto a manifold, forming ring seals, joints and side-arms on a bench torch or lathe, blowing by mouth or air line to prevent collapse, with the shape judged by eye and adjusted job-to-job.

Studio/art hot shop: one-off or limited-edition blown piece; the gaffer inflates the gather by breath, rotates it constantly, blows into an optic or wooden mold, shapes on a board/block and reheats, with size and form judged continuously by the maker.

Neon / luminous-tube bending shop: a section of glass tubing is heated over a ribbon or crossfire burner and bent to a paper pattern laid on a board, while the bender blows through a latex hose to keep the bore round and prevent collapse; each sign's letterforms differ.

tasks.label: Inspect, weigh, and measure products to verify conformance to specifications, using instruments such as micrometers, calipers, magnifiers, or rulers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Container-glass plant (bottles/jars): at the cold end the worker pulls sample ware from the line at set intervals, weighs each container on a balance, checks finish bore/height/diameter and body dimensions with gauges and calipers, checks wall thickness, and inspects for checks, blisters and seeds against the spec sheet; results logged for process control.

Pharmaceutical/technical small glassware (vials, ampoules, cartridges, cut tubing): measuring outer diameter, wall thickness, length and flange dimensions with micrometers/calipers, inspecting under a magnifier or loupe for chips and cracks, verifying against tight documented tolerances in a QC area beside the forming line.

Scientific/custom glassblowing shop: a one-off or small-batch lab apparatus (joints, condensers, manifolds) checked against a customer drawing - tube OD/ID and length with calipers and rulers, joint and angle conformity, annealing strain checked with a polariscope, magnifier check for cracks and seeds; rework decided on the spot.

Glass bending / flat and curved glass fabrication (architectural, automotive, neon tubing): the finished bent or heat-treated piece is laid on a template or checked against a full-size pattern, radii, angles, overall size and squareness measured with rulers, tapes and gauges, distortion/curvature judged against spec.

Hand/art/studio glass and tableware production: finished blown or pressed pieces compared to a master sample and spec - height, rim and base diameter and wall with calipers/rulers, weight on a scale, and a magnifier/visual check for bubbles, cords and shape defects before the piece is accepted or rejected.

Semi-automatic or hand-press station in a hot shop: worker takes a gather/gob of molten glass (from a ladle, shear drop, or punty) and drops it into the die of a small mechanical or hydraulic press, cycles the press, opens the mould and removes the pressed component (handles, feet, discs, lens-shaped blanks, lighting parts). Optical blank pressing / precision glass moulding at an optics plant: place a cleaned preform or reheated glass slug into a polished tooth/die set, close the press, run the heat-press-cool recipe under vacuum or nitrogen, unload the blank without scratching it, and verify form and thickness to tight tolerance. Clean, temperature-controlled production room.

Technical / scientific glass shop: short-run pressing of custom components from reheated stock or gathers in a die on a bench press; the die is changed several times a shift, first articles are gauged, and press temperature/force are dialled in for each job.

Art or giftware studio production pressing: hand-gathered glass dropped into varied one-off or short-run moulds on a small press (paperweight bases, tiles, ornaments, jewelry components), pressed and then reheated or hand-finished; gob size and timing judged by the maker.

tasks.label: Repair broken scrolls by replacing them with new sections of tubing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Sign-shop bench repair of a standard neon unit returned by a customer with a broken decorative scroll: bender lays the unit on the paper/asbestos pattern, cuts out the fractured curved section, heats fresh tubing on ribbon burner and crossfires, bends it freehand to match the pattern, splices it into the existing tube with a blow hose to keep the bore open, then re-processes (electrode check, bombarding, evacuation, gas fill, tip-off) and tests the section lights evenly.

Shop bench repair of an ornate or script scroll: tight-radius multi-bend section in colored or phosphor-coated tubing on a vintage or art piece; the replacement section must match glass color/coating, wall thickness and the original curvature so the repair is invisible, and must fit existing mounting standoffs; joints made freehand at the burner and re-pumped.

Whole-scroll replacement at the shop: rather than splicing mid-run, the bender re-bends an entire new scroll unit from a fresh length of tubing on the pattern table, welds on electrodes, processes it, and swaps it into the sign frame.

Field repair at the customer's premises: technician goes to a storefront, bar interior or building facade with a lift or ladder, de-energizes and removes the damaged scroll unit from its standoffs and GTO wiring, and either fits a pre-made replacement section on site or performs a torch splice on site, aligning the new tubing to the housing and re-testing.

Studio repair of decorative non-sign glass scrollwork (art glass piece, chandelier arm, decorative tubing element): the broken curl is cut away and a newly bent section of tubing is fused in at the torch, annealed, and finished to match the surrounding piece.

instances.label: Custom neon sign shop, in-process check: the bender heats a 10-15 mm soda-lime tube on a ribbon burner and repeatedly lays the hot, pliable tube down on the full-scale pattern (fire-resistant pattern paper on the bench) mid-bend, sighting fit, flatness and twist against the drawn lines and correcting in the fire before the glass sets.

Production neon / channel-letter shop: batches of repeated standard letters and border shapes; each bent section is laid over the printed full-scale pattern to confirm it matches the layout and the housing hole positions before electrode work and processing.

Scientific / laboratory glassblowing shop (university or industrial glass shop): 6-25 mm borosilicate or quartz tubing bent for manifolds, coils and apparatus; the bent tube is superimposed on a full-scale drawing or template on a heat-resistant board, often for complex three-dimensional one-off geometries.

Final dimensional QC on cooled/annealed work: the finished bent tube is placed over the pattern on a flat bench to verify overall dimensions, planarity and fit to the sign housing or apparatus, and is accepted, reworked in the fire, or scrapped.

Field or private-studio work: an artist's home studio or an on-site repair where a pattern is traced from the existing sign or apparatus at the customer's premises and the replacement bent tube is checked against that traced pattern on whatever flat surface is available.

tasks.label: Set up and adjust machine press stroke lengths and pressures and regulate oven temperatures, according to glass types to be processed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Job change on a press or press-and-blow line in a container/tableware plant: after tooling is mounted, the operator sets plunger/press stroke and press force (pneumatic or hydraulic pressure levels), mold and plunger cooling, and the machine timing for the new article and glass composition, then runs first ware and tweaks until the ware is acceptable. Hot end of a production plant, high heat, fixed layout.

Regulating oven/lehr and conditioning temperatures in a production plant: setting the annealing lehr temperature curve and zone setpoints (and forehearth/feeder temperatures) according to glass type, ware weight and wall thickness, then adjusting zones as throughput or job changes.

In-run adjustment during a production run: operator watches ware for incomplete fill, thin walls, checks or distribution faults and tweaks press pressure/dwell, plunger-up timing, mold cooling and lehr temperatures to bring the process back into spec.

Bending/tempering setup: setting multi-zone bending or tempering furnace temperatures and the press-bend stroke/pressure for a given glass type, thickness, coating and shape (automotive, architectural or appliance glass), then checking shape and stress on first parts.

Studio, lampworking or scientific glass shop: setting furnace/glory hole setpoints and programming the annealing kiln ramp, soak and cool schedule to match the glass being worked (soda-lime, borosilicate, quartz) and the piece thickness; loading ware and running the anneal.

tasks.label: Operate gas or electric kilns to fire pottery pieces.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small/medium production pottery: worker stacks a batch of bisque or glazed ware in a computer-controlled electric kiln — setting shelves on posts, spacing glazed pieces so they cannot touch or stick, checking kiln wash — then selects a cone-fire or ramp/hold schedule, fires overnight, and unloads the cooled ware. Setting: the shop's kiln room/production floor.

Mid-size ceramics plant with a gas shuttle/car kiln: worker stacks glazed ware and kiln furniture on the kiln car, rolls it in, starts burners, runs a cone 9–10 firing with reduction periods, watches cones through spyholes and the pyrometer, trims damper/gas as needed, then cools and unloads/sorts the ware. Setting: factory kiln bay.

Higher-volume plant with a continuous tunnel or roller-hearth kiln: ware is set onto kiln cars/batts and fed continuously; the operator monitors the kiln control panel and zone temperatures, loads/changes firing curves for product changeovers, and oversees setting and de-hacking of fired ware. Setting: a continuous firing line on the plant floor.

Repeat-production heavy or awkward items (large planters, lamp bases, big platters, sinks): loaded into a shuttle kiln with props and setter plates chosen for the known model, fired on a long schedule, then unloaded hot-ish with care and inspected for warping or shelf sticking. Setting: factory or larger studio kiln bay.

One-off sculptural or architectural commission: an oversized, irregular piece requiring bespoke propping and kiln-furniture arrangement invented for that piece, a custom slow schedule, and periodic judgment during firing/cooling to avoid cracking. Setting: studio or plant kiln room.

Test and trial firings: loading cone packs and glaze test tiles to check kiln evenness or qualify a new glaze/clay body, firing the trial schedule, and unloading the tests. Setting: the same kiln room, small load.

tasks.label: Mix and apply glazes to pottery pieces, using tools, such as spray guns.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Spray glazing standardized production ware (mugs, plates, vases, insulator/whiteware pieces) in a downdraft spray booth at a ceramics plant: worker sets the bisque piece on a turntable, sprays an even glaze coat with a hand-held spray gun, checks coverage/thickness, cleans the foot, and racks the piece for firing.

Dip and pour glazing of batches of bisque hollowware in a production pottery's glaze shop: stir/adjust the glaze tank, check specific gravity, dip or pour-fill pieces, drain, wipe glaze off feet and rims, and rack; repeat for hundreds of like pieces.

Mixing glaze batches: weighing dry frits, oxides, clays and stains to a recipe, blunging/ball-milling with water, sieving and de-ironing, then adjusting specific gravity/viscosity and verifying the slip before release to the glazing station.

Small-batch/artisan production run: varied hand-thrown or hand-cast ware with frequent glaze and shape changes; multi-layer application, wax resist on feet, brushed accents and banding, and hand touch-up of drips and thin spots to an aesthetic standard.

Glazing large, heavy or internally complex pieces (one-piece WCs, washbasins, large sculptural or garden ware): maneuvering the piece, spraying inside cavities and hidden surfaces, siphon/interior glazing, and heavier handling between racks and booth.

tasks.label: Raise and shape clay into wares, such as vases and pitchers, on revolving wheels, using hands, fingers, and thumbs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Repetition throwing of standard small open tableware in a production pottery: weighed balls of pugged clay (1-3 lb) centered, opened and pulled into mugs, cups, bowls and tumblers to a fixed height/width template, dozens to hundreds per shift, at a fixed wheel station with standard studio equipment.

Throwing open, tapered or flared hollowware to a template: cylinder and flared vases, wide-mouth jars, canister and casserole bodies, small planters/flowerpots, thrown in short repeat runs to catalog dimensions.

Throwing necked or closed forms: bottle vases, narrow-mouth jars and bud vases where the potter must collar the wall inward and shape the interior by feel with the wall no longer visible, keeping wall thickness even.

Throwing pitchers/jugs and altered wares: raising the body, then hand-forming a pouring lip or spout with thumb and fingers, flaring or darting the rim, faceting or altering the still-soft wall before it is set aside for handling.

Throwing large, heavy wares from 10-25+ lb of clay: big planters, large serving bowls, lamp bases and umbrella stands, sometimes thrown in sections and joined; requires heavy centering force and control of a tall, soft wall.

One-off, custom or prototype work: throwing a new form to a designer's drawing, model or client sample, short runs and frequent shape changeovers, often with test pieces adjusted for shrinkage and profile before acceptance.

tasks.label: Adjust wheel speeds according to the feel of the clay as pieces enlarge and walls become thinner.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production pottery / small ceramics manufacturer: potter throws a repeat run of standard hollow ware (mugs, bowls, cups) to set clay weights and dimensions on an electric wheel, easing the foot pedal down as the piece opens out and the walls rise and thin; ware must match the run for size and wall thickness.

Ceramics plant jigger/jolley station: operator drops a clay bat into a plaster mould on the rotating head, brings down the roller/template, and modulates head speed as the clay spreads and the wall thins, judging by feel and drag on the tool; output is mould-formed cup/plate/bowl bodies at line rate.

Larger vessels: 10-30 lb pieces (vases, pitchers, large planters) thrown on the wheel, where the wheel must be slowed markedly as diameter grows and walls thin to avoid wobble, torque-driven distortion, or collapse; often formed in stages over a session.

Wheel finishing/trimming: leather-hard pieces re-chucked on the wheel head; the worker varies wheel speed by feel of the stiffened clay while trimming the foot, refining the profile, and smoothing the rim before drying.

One-off or bespoke work in a small owner-operated studio, often a converted home/garage space: custom shapes, prototype samples, varied and unstandardized clay bodies and moisture; the hand-thrown character of the piece is itself the product.

sources.system: SACMI-SAMA NCC numerical controlled jiggering / roller machine for cups
sources.date: 2024-2026 (product page and 2024 jiggering catalogue; site footer 2026)
sources.title: Roller Machine for Cups | SAMA MASCHINENBAU
sources.claim: SACMI-SAMA's NCC numerically controlled jiggering (roller) machine forms cups, bowls and flowerpots from plastic clay in an automatic cell that includes clay feeding belt, dosing pug ... slicing, and mould feeding/discharge belts - i.e., a purpose-built machine that performs the rotating-spindle forming of hollow ware with programmed head speeds.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine jiggering/roller-forming of plastic clay hollow ware. tasks.label: Position balls of clay in centers of potters' wheels, and start motors or pump treadles with feet to revolve wheels.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production tableware shop: worker takes a pre-cut clay bat/slug from a spreader or rack, throws it centered onto the plaster mould on the jigger/jolley head, and starts the rotating head with a pedal or lever; repeated hundreds of times per shift on the factory floor.

Small-batch production studio/pottery manufactory: worker takes 1-5 lb wedged clay balls from a nearby table or scale, slams each firmly onto the wheel head (or a bat) so it adheres roughly centered, and presses the foot pedal to bring the electric wheel up to speed; dozens of repetitions of the same product per day.

Large-form work (planters, vases, large bowls): heavy 10-40 lb clay mounds must be lifted, thrown down hard and squarely on the wheel head or bat so they stick, then the wheel is started at low speed; lower repetition, higher force and mass.

Varied setup/changeover work in a craft-manufacturing shop: attaching bats or plaster chucks of different sizes, positioning clay for throwing off the hump, and switching among products and clay-ball sizes several times a day; presentation of clay and wheel setup differs run to run.

Traditional/treadle or kick-wheel station (heritage production, demonstration or teaching-adjacent production work): clay ball positioned on a non-motorized wheel head and rotation supplied by pumping a treadle or kicking the flywheel, with periodic re-kicks while working.

tasks.label: Move pieces from wheels so that they can dry.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production pottery / small ceramics manufacturer: the potter throws mugs, bowls or small vases directly on the wheelhead, wire-cuts each freshly thrown piece free and lifts it by hand (soft, wet, easily deformed walls) onto a ware board, then sets the board on an open drying shelf a few steps away. Shared shop floor with other workers, wet tools and racks of varying height.

Jigger/jolley or roller-machine work in a tableware plant: the operator lifts the plaster mould holding the just-formed plate, saucer or cup off the machine head every few seconds and sets it on a drying rack, trolley or dryer conveyor, returning an empty mould to the head. High repetition, standard mould sizes, factory floor.

Throwing on removable bats: the potter releases the bat (with the wet piece still attached) from the wheelhead pins, carries bat and piece to a drying shelf or ware cart, and fits a fresh bat. The handled object is a rigid disc, but the unsecured wet pot must not be jarred.

Large or awkward ware: big vases, wide platters, planters or sectional forms cut off the wheel, needing two hands or a board/helper, carried slowly to a dedicated slow-drying area and sometimes tented with plastic or turned to control drying.

Clearing accumulated boards of freshly made ware from the wheel area to the drying room: loading multiple boards onto a ware cart or multi-tier rack, moving them across the shop, and sliding them onto shelves, shuffling existing boards to make space.

Small artisan/one-off workshop (including converted garage or home studio) with irregular layout, mixed furniture, cluttered shelves and idiosyncratic one-off forms; pieces come off the wheel onto whatever surface is free and are later rearranged for even drying.

tasks.label: Smooth surfaces of finished pieces, using rubber scrapers and wet sponges.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production pottery/dinnerware shop: sponging the rims, feet and outer walls of a batch of dozens to hundreds of identical leather-hard jiggered or pressed mugs/bowls/plates at a bench or whirler, using a damp sponge and rubber kidney to remove tooling marks and round the rim.

Slip-cast hollowware (mugs with applied handles, pitchers, teapots with spouts, figurines): fettling and wet-sponging the mould seams and the joints where handles/spouts are luted, working around delicate attachments and compound curves at leather-hard.

Wheel-thrown production ware: while the piece turns on the wheel head (or after trimming on a chuck), compressing and smoothing walls and rim with a rubber rib and damp sponge, wiping away slurry and throwing lines before the piece stiffens.

Large, irregular or one-off pieces — hand-built or altered art pottery, oversized planters, sculptural and custom-order ware — where geometry differs piece to piece and the potter smooths by eye and feel with scrapers and sponges on a bench or banding wheel.

Final touch-up pass over dry greenware/bisque on ware boards before glazing: damp-sponging dust, chips and burrs and scraping stray clay off a mixed assortment of shapes staged on boards and racks in the shop.

sources.system: SACMI RobotClean
sources.title: SACMI RobotClean, fully automated sanitaryware finishing
sources.claim: SACMI RobotClean is an articulated-robot station that automates 'white finishing' (green finishing) of cast sanitaryware — the sponging/scraping of leather-hard cast clay surfaces, rims, sub-rims, interiors and exteriors — with force-compensated tools and offline programming; already installed at customer plants.
sources.transferJustification: Green/white finishing of cast sanitaryware is the same physical act as the potter's task: smoothing leather-hard clay surfaces and mould seams with sponges and scraper-type tools before firing, judged by surface-quality acceptance. Material state, tool contact force, fragility of the greenware and the accepted finish standard are comparable; sanitaryware pieces are larger but geometrically more complex than mugs and bowls.

tasks.label: Pull wires through bases of articles and wheels to separate finished pieces.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Repeat production throwing in a small/mid-size ceramics manufacturer: after throwing a mug or bowl on a power wheel, the potter holds a taut cut-off wire flat against the wheel head (or plaster bat) and pulls it under the base to free the piece, then lifts it to a ware board. Dozens to hundreds of identical pieces per shift, wheel head at a fixed position, clay body and stiffness standardized.

Throwing off the hump: many small items (cups, cereal bowls, lids, knobs) formed in sequence from a tall mound of clay; the potter undercuts each finished piece with a needle tool and pulls a wire (or twisted wire) through the narrowed neck at the base to separate it from the column, repeatedly and quickly, without deforming the soft rim.

Jigger/jolley machine operation: the operator wire-cuts slices/slugs of pugged clay from the extruded column to feed the machine, and pulls a wire across the chuck or mold base to free the jiggered article and any excess clay from the machine head; standardized molds and slug sizes, machine-paced cycle.

Large repeat ware (planters, large bowls, tall vases) thrown on a wheel or bat: a longer, heavier wire is pulled through a wide, soft base, often in two passes with a helper or a support board, sometimes after a short stiffening period, before the piece is lifted off.

One-off, custom or sculptural work: altered or off-center forms, footed or undercut bases, pieces cut with a twisted wire for a decorative shell pattern, or ware stuck to bats that must be re-wired after partial drying; the potter judges timing, wire angle and support case by case.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: separating formed clay pieces from a clay column/base with a taut wire. Same material (plastic clay), same tool (tensioned wire pulled through a base), same required precision (a flat cut at a set plane), performed under machine control in a purpose-built line.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: wire-cutting pieces off a continuous clay body, the same act a potter performs when cutting items off the hump or cutting throwing balls from a pugged column.

tasks.label: Design spaces to display pottery for sale.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Outdoor craft fair, art festival or farmers'-market booth: the potter hauls in a canopy, tables, cloths, crates, risers, shelving and lighting to an assigned 10x10 patch of grass or asphalt, levels and stabilizes the setup for wind and slope, then composes 100-300 handmade pieces into groupings by form, glaze and price, adds signage, price tags and payment station, and strikes the whole display at the end of the show.

Own studio/home showroom or open-studio sale: the potter lays out the salable area of an idiosyncratic working studio or garage - moves work tables, builds or repositions plank-and-block shelving and pedestals, sets sight lines and traffic flow around wheels, kilns and clay bins, arranges pieces by collection and price point, adjusts lighting, and reworks the layout seasonally.

Gallery, museum shop or consignment retail store: the potter brings a collection to a shop, negotiates the allotted shelf, pedestal or vitrine space with the buyer, unpacks and composes the pieces on the shop's fixtures with spacing, height variation, cards and price labels, working around customers and existing merchandise during store hours.

In-house potter/designer at a production pottery: designs and builds a factory-outlet showroom section or a trade-show/market booth (e.g., a wholesale gift show) - plans the fixture layout and planogram, assembles risers, backdrops and graphics in the hall or showroom, and arranges dinnerware and giftware lines with lighting and signage.

Routine upkeep of an already-designed display: refilling and re-facing shelves in the studio shop or the store's pottery section as pieces sell, replacing sold work with new ware in the established arrangement, dusting and straightening, and swapping in a few new items - a repetitive placement job against an existing layout plan.

sources.system: TX SCARA (Telexistence)

sources.claim: Telexistence's TX SCARA autonomously replenishes beverage shelves in FamilyMart convenience stores in Japan, scanning shelves with cameras, deciding what is low and placing bottles and cans, with remote operators only intervening on the ~2% of failures.

It is the closest deployed analogue to the upkeep portion of display work, but it handles uniform rigid bottles from a rail-mounted arm behind a fixed refrigerated case with a known planogram; it does not compose or design a display.

tasks.label: Verify accuracy of shapes and sizes of objects, using calipers and templates.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Tableware/pottery plant, in-process check at the forming machine: operator lifts a jiggered, rolled or pressed greenware plate/bowl off the ware board, checks rim diameter and foot height with spring calipers and lays a profile template against the section, then adjusts the jigger tool; soft, fragile greenware, tolerances of roughly 0.5-1 mm, done every few pieces on a running line.

Small production/studio pottery: potter throwing a repeat set on the wheel stops and sets calipers to rim diameter and height on the wet, rotating pot, and checks lid galleries against a caliper/template so lids fit the matching pots; deformable wet clay, cluttered but owner-controlled workshop bench, judgement by feel and eye.

Fired-ware quality bench in the plant's QC area: sampled fired plates, bowls and mugs pulled from kiln cars are checked with calipers for diameter/height after shrinkage, with go/no-go rings and profile templates for warpage and flatness, results logged and out-of-spec lots flagged.

Model and mould shop / slip-casting area: new block-and-case models, working plaster moulds and cast greenware are checked against profile templates and calipers with shrinkage allowance before the mould goes into production.

Technical/industrial ceramics (insulators, refractory shapes, extruded tubes): pressed or extruded parts are measured with calipers and gauge templates against a spec sheet at the machine and again after firing, tighter tolerances and higher documentation requirements.

sources.system: Plate Quality Inspection System (PQIS), Coleman Technologies
sources.developer: Coleman Technologies (with National Instruments hardware/software, Teledyne DALSA cameras)
sources.title: SPOTLIGHT - Detecting Defects in Dinnerware
sources.claim: Coleman Technologies' Plate Quality Inspection System, installed for a large dinnerware manufacturer, inspects earthenware plates travelling on a conveyor at 60 items/minute; one station builds a 3-D laser-triangulation map of each plate and checks its dimensions against a stored reference template, i.e. verifies shape and size of pottery without human involvement.
sources.transferJustification: Same task on the same objects (dinner plates), but performed on fired ware inline: dimensional/shape verification against a stored template rather than a hand-held template, at the same millimetre-level tolerances a potter checks with calipers.

sources.system: Robotic measurement cell (Mitutoyo MiSTAR CMM + handling robot by Engineering Data)
sources.developer: Mitutoyo and Engineering Data, for Méca-Précis
sources.title: Robotic measurement cells removes bottleneck in parts inspection process | Engineer Live
sources.claim: Méca-Précis runs a robotic measurement cell in which an articulated robot takes fixtured parts from a 20-pallet store, loads them onto a Mitutoyo MiSTAR shop-floor CMM and runs dimensional inspections unattended, day and overnight.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated dimensional verification of machined parts. It transfers because the act judged here is the same - present a workpiece, measure defining dimensions, accept or reject - at far tighter tolerances than pottery calipers, in a fixtured cell.

sources.system: Renishaw Equator gauging system with FANUC M20iA robot and EZ-IO software

sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic gauge-tending and pass/fail sorting of production parts. Transfers because the robot itself performs the whole verify-and-decide loop - load the piece to a gauge, compare to master, accept or divert - which is what caliper/template checking delivers.

sources.system: Clay 3D printing with real-time model re-calibration (KUKA 6-axis arm + laser sensor)
sources.developer: Institute for Advanced Architecture of Catalonia (IAAC)
sources.title: Clay 3D Printing of Spatial Lattices Using Real-Time Model Re-calibration - IAAC Blog
sources.claim: An IAAC robotic clay-printing experiment used a KUKA 6-axis arm with a laser distance sensor to measure the deflection/geometry of freshly printed wet clay lattices in real time and re-calibrate the tool path in a closed loop, showing autonomous dimensional measurement of soft, wet clay geometry in a robot cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: closed-loop control of clay deposition. It transfers because the measurement step is the same - sensing the actual geometry of unfired, deformable clay to millimetre accuracy and comparing it to the intended form, which is what calipers on wet thrown ware do.

sources.system: Sensorised vacuum and impact grippers for ceramic ware handling
sources.developer: Ferreira et al. (published in Electronics, MDPI)

sources.claim: Purpose-built robotic grippers (a rotary vacuum gripper and a three-finger impact gripper with load sensing) were shown to grasp and manipulate fragile unfired ceramic ware - a coffee saucer and a coffee cup - with controlled, low grip forces for glazing and polishing operations.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic handling of green ceramic cups and saucers. It transfers because presenting fragile pottery to a measuring station without damage is the handling half of caliper/template checking, on the same objects and fragility class.

sources.system: Strip-projection 3D scanning service for ceramics (beamer, two cameras, turntable)
sources.title: 3D Scanning for Ceramics 3D Printing | WZR ceramic solutions
sources.claim: WZR ceramic solutions uses a strip-projection 3D scanner with a turntable to scan ceramic parts before and after firing and compare them with CAD data, determining shrinkage and warpage of ceramic ware.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: post-firing dimensional/shrinkage verification of ceramic parts against a digital master. Supporting context only; loading appears operator-driven, so it is not relied on for a positive judgment.

tasks.label: Examine finished ware for defects and measure dimensions, using rule and thickness gauge.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Glost-fired standard tableware (plates, bowls, mugs, saucers) at a mid- to high-volume ceramics plant: worker at the sorting bench/line picks up each fired piece, examines it for cracks, chips, pinholes, glaze blisters, stains and warp, spot-checks diameter and height with a rule and rim/wall thickness with a gauge, and grades first quality / second / reject.

Scheduled dimensional QC of finished ware: worker pulls samples each shift from the kiln output, measures diameter, height, foot-ring depth and wall thickness with rule, calipers and thickness gauge against the spec sheet, records the readings, and flags out-of-tolerance drift back to the forming department.

Finished decorated/specialty ware (decal or machine-lined porcelain, relief patterns): worker checks decoration presence, alignment and completeness and back-stamp quality along with body and glaze defects, and verifies key rim dimensions against the standard.

Small production pottery / short-run workshop: hand-thrown or jiggered art ware in varied shapes, sizes and glazes; worker judges whether surface and shape irregularities are acceptable handmade variation or true defects, and measures height/diameter/thickness against a master piece.

Large, heavy or complex finished ware (big vases, planters, basins/sanitary-type pieces, thick refractory or technical ceramics): worker lifts and rotates the piece on a bench or trolley, taps it to listen for hidden cracks, inspects hard-to-see interior surfaces, and measures overall dimensions and wall thickness with rule and gauge.

sources.system: PQIS (Plate Quality Inspection System) by Coleman Technologies / Sciotex
sources.developer: Coleman Technologies Inc. (now Sciotex), with National Instruments hardware/software
sources.title: Using LabVIEW and the Vision Development Module to Create a Plate Quality Inspection System - NI
sources.claim: Plate Quality Inspection System (PQIS), a conveyor-based three-camera plus laser-triangulation machine installed at a major dinnerware manufacturer, inspects tops and bottoms of 50+ styles of plates and bowls for trim gouge/bulge, glass adhesion and warp at 60 plates/min, 24/7, and drives a PLC that automatically sorts the plates; it replaced manual inspection of every plate.

sources.system: Optomachines CV3G tableware inspection machine

sources.claim: CV3G is a commercially sold, robot-equipped tableware inspection and sorting machine (third generation of a line built since 2001-2004) that inspects glazed tableware of all shapes at 800-900 pieces/hour for geometry (general dimensions, completeness, deformation), cracks, chips, fractures, pinholes, grains, stains, glaze gloss/texture and back-stamp presence, then sorts good from bad parts and interleaves paper sheets.

sources.system: Creaform MetraSCAN 3D-R / CUBE-R automated inspection cell
sources.title: R-Series Automated Inspection | 3D Scanners for Quality Control - Creaform
sources.claim: Creaform's R-Series (MetraSCAN 3D-R robot-mounted optical CMM scanners and the turnkey CUBE-R measuring cell) performs automated full-surface dimensional inspection of manufactured parts at-line on the shop floor, replacing manual gauging and CMM measurement of production samples.

sources.claim: A deep-learning surface-defect detection system with a fixed industrial camera station was installed in the production flow at Grestel S.A., a Portuguese tableware and fine stoneware factory, reaching 98% accuracy in separating defective from non-defective ceramic pieces; an operator performs the second validation and the discard decision.

sources.title: Sacmi supplies automated glazing system to Daelim Bath Korea | Ceramic World Web
sources.claim: In Sacmi's automated sanitaryware glazing island at Daelim Bath Korea, a FANUC R2000iB robot handles large one-piece WCs as they exit the inspection booths and a Gaiotto GA2000 robot glazes them; the inspection of the pieces itself is carried out in manual booths, not by a machine.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic handling of large ceramic sanitaryware. Cited to show that although robots handle such heavy, complex ware, the inspection step in these deployed lines remains in manual booths, i.e. no cited system completes large-ware examination.

tasks.label: Maintain supplies of tools, equipment, and materials, and order additional supplies as needed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Periodic stock check in a ceramics plant's material storeroom: walking racked pallets and shelves of boxed clay bodies, glaze chemicals, plaster, packaging and kiln furniture, counting/verifying quantities against par levels and records, then entering a reorder with suppliers.

Receiving an incoming supply delivery: pallets of 50-lb clay boxes, drums/sacks of glaze chemicals and cartons of consumables arrive by truck; unload from the trailer or van, check items against the packing slip, and put away into storeroom racking with pallet jack or cart.

Mid-shift replenishment of the production floor: fetching clay boxes, water, glaze buckets, bats, sponges, kiln shelves and posts from the storeroom and setting them out at jigger machines, wheels, wedging tables and the glaze bench, moving among working potters and ware in progress.

Keeping the small-tool and consumable supply in order: unpacking supplier cartons, sorting ribs, wires, needles, brushes, sandpaper, gloves and bats into labeled bins/cabinets at par levels, gathering strays from benches, culling worn or broken items, and noting what to reorder.

One-person or small artisan production studio kept as the potter likes it: cluttered benches and shelves, partially used clay bags, half-full glaze buckets and mixed jars of tools; stock is judged by eye and by lifting, and supplies are ordered online or by phone from a ceramics supplier.

sources.claim: Verity's fully autonomous inventory drones perform stock checks in over 80 client warehouses, including a manufacturer's plant, scanning racked stock daily and feeding inventory records used to prevent stockouts.

It is the same act as the potter's stock check - surveying stored, palletized/boxed materials in racking and reporting quantities against records so low items can be reordered - on comparable objects (cartons, sacks, palletized goods) in a comparable indoor storeroom.

tasks.label: Operate pug mills to blend and extrude clay.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Ceramics/pottery manufacturing plant: run the plant's de-airing pug mill/extruder that supplies plastic clay to forming stations — start up, keep the hopper charged from the clay prep area, set vacuum and speed, watch the extruded column for consistency and air pockets, cut pugs/slugs to length and move them to the jigger or press.

Clay body blending run: charge the pug mill/mixer with weighed body ingredients (dry clays, grog, additives) and water per a recipe, run the blend cycle, extrude test pugs, check moisture/plasticity and correct the water addition until the body is on spec.

Reclaim run: gather scrap, trimmings and slurry from the shop, bring it to workable moisture (slaking/plaster drying), feed it into the pug mill hopper, blend with virgin clay, extrude de-aired pugs and bag or store them for reuse.

Small production pottery or studio-scale pugging: hand-loading a studio de-airing pugmill (Peter Pugger/Bluebird class) with bagged clay and reclaim, extruding pugs, cutting to weight and bagging them for the potters, judging plasticity by hand as the pugs come out.

Mid-run troubleshooting: column laminating, hard/soft streaks, screen clogged with grog or debris, auger jam or blowback; stop the machine, clear or purge the obstruction, change or realign the die/nozzle, restart and requalify the extrusion.

Changeover and cleanout between clay bodies or at shift end: purge and open the barrel, scrape clay off the auger and chamber walls, swap dies/nozzles and vacuum seals, wash down, grease and reassemble the pug mill.

tasks.label: Perform test-fires of pottery to determine how to achieve specific colors and textures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Glaze-recipe test tiles in a small production pottery: weigh out several variations of dry glaze materials (feldspar, silica, clay, colorants), mix and sieve small batches, dip or brush bisque test tiles, stack them in a small electric test kiln with shelves and posts, run a cone 6/cone 10 schedule, unload after cooling, and judge fired color, gloss and surface texture to decide the next round of variations.

Test pieces fired inside the production kiln: candidate glazed tiles/pots plus cone packs are set at several positions in a loaded gas or electric kiln, the firing (including reduction/oxidation and cooling schedule) is run with the production load, then the pieces are unloaded and compared position by position to work out what firing and glaze changes give the wanted color and texture.

Test-firing a candidate glaze on an actual production form (mug, bowl, vase, tile): the form is dipped or sprayed with the trial glaze, wiped, dried, fired, then evaluated for color break over the body and form, crazing, pinholing, matte/gloss texture; recipe or application thickness is revised and refired.

Specialty atmospheric firing trials (raku, wood, salt/soda, saggar, pit): loading a fuel-burning kiln in the kiln yard, side-stoking wood or introducing salt/soda, judging flame, ash and reduction by eye, pulling red-hot ware with tongs into combustibles for post-fire reduction, then reading the highly variable surfaces produced.

Clay body / slip / texture trials: blending clay with grog, sand, stains or oxides, forming test bars and textured tiles, drying, bisque and glaze firing, then measuring shrinkage/absorption and judging fired body color and surface texture.

tasks.label: Start machine units and conveyors and observe lights and gauges on panel board to verify operational efficiency.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Shift-start of the clay/body-preparation line in a mid-to-large ceramics plant (tile, sanitaryware, tableware): the operator starts blungers/mixers, pug mill, filter press and the feed conveyors in the correct sequence from a panel board or HMI, then watches run lights, motor-amp and pressure gauges to confirm every unit came up and the line is running at rate.

During-run monitoring on the production floor: the operator repeatedly checks panel lights and gauges (press hydraulic pressure, extruder vacuum and amps, dryer and kiln temperatures, conveyor running/fault lamps) through the shift, compares readings to normal ranges, and flags or reports anything off so line efficiency is verified.

Starting one forming machine and its feed/take-off conveyor (jigger, ram press, extruder/pug mill) at the start of a ... or after a changeover, then verifying that machine's own gauges (vacuum, hydraulic pressure, speed) and ready/fault lights before production is released.

Small craft-scale pottery or stoneware manufacturer: the operator throws local disconnects and start switches scattered on individual older machines (pug mill, clay mixer, small belt or dryer), with no central panel board, judging correct running from a pilot lamp, an ammeter or pressure dial and the sound of the machine, in a cluttered, non-standard shop.

Kiln/dryer area: starting the kiln car pusher, kiln/dryer conveyors and burner systems and verifying burner and interlock indicator lights plus temperature and pressure gauges on the kiln control panel, then continuing to verify readings over the firing cycle.

tasks.label: Operate drying chambers to dry or finish molded ceramic ware.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Large ceramics plant (sanitaryware / high-volume tableware): worker moves racks or cars of freshly molded, standardized greenware into a chamber or tunnel dryer, selects the drying program (temperature/humidity/time) on the control panel, monitors the cycle, and withdraws the hardened ware for finishing.

Mid-size production pottery or tableware factory: worker loads jiggered plates/cups or slip-cast ware, still on moulds or on trays, into a batch or leatherhard dryer, sets heat and airflow, checks pieces for dryness, and unloads to the fettling/finishing bench.

Small production pottery (5-20 person shop): worker places varied hand-thrown, jiggered, or cast greenware of assorted shapes on shelves in a heated drying room or cabinet dryer, adjusts heat/fan/damper by feel, turns pieces, and pulls each piece when leather-hard or bone-dry.

Drying large, heavy, or awkward fragile ware (large basins, WC bowls, big vases, handled or sculptural pieces) that must be supported and dried slowly and evenly; careful lifting into the chamber and controlled, longer cycles to avoid cracking or warping.

Establishing or correcting a drying cycle for a new clay body, mould, or product: running trial loads, diagnosing cracking/warping/uneven shrinkage, changing the curve and re-running, and recording the settings that work.

Routine dryer tending during a shift: watching chamber temperature and humidity gauges, logging readings, making small adjustments to hold the curve, checking airflow and burner operation, cleaning debris from the chamber, and reporting faults.

tasks.label: Adjust pressures, temperatures, and trimming tool settings as required.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Forming station in a ceramics/tableware plant: operator checks formed ware (wall thickness, profile, density) coming off a jigger/roller-head machine or ram/isostatic press and adjusts forming pressure, roller-head depth, spindle speed and mold clearance until pieces are within tolerance. Factory floor, standard machines, institution controls premises.

Trimming/fettling/sponging station: operator resets a trimming or turning tool's height, angle and depth of cut (and sponge/contact pressure) on a semi-automatic trimming machine or lathe after inspecting rims, feet and edges of leather-hard or dry ware; re-sets after tool wear or a product changeover. Factory floor.

Clay preparation/extrusion: operator adjusts pug mill / vacuum extruder settings — vacuum level, extrusion pressure, auger speed, die clearance, water addition — in response to slugs that are too stiff, too wet, or laminated. Plant clay-prep area.

Drying and firing: operator sets and revises dryer and kiln temperature settings — ramp rates, soak/hold times, zone setpoints, damper/atmosphere and pressure settings — in response to cracking, warping, under/over-firing seen in the ware. Kiln room of a plant or production pottery.

Small craft/production pottery studio: potter adjusts wheel speed and the angle, depth and pressure of hand-held trimming tools while trimming hand-thrown leather-hard ware by feel, and adjusts the studio kiln controller's program between firings. Cluttered small studio, one-off and short-run ware.

tasks.label: Design clay forms and molds, and decorations for forms.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production pottery/ceramics shop: designing a new ware form (mug, bowl, vase) — deciding the profile, proportions, wall thickness, foot and handle, and dimensions adjusted for clay shrinkage; output is a sketch, drawn profile/template layout, or CAD model with specifications handed to the model shop or the thrower.

Designing the tooling for an existing or new form: choosing between press mold, slip-cast mold, or jigger/jolley operation; specifying parting lines, number of mold pieces, draft, spare/reservoir, and the profile-template geometry; output is drawings, dimensioned specs, or a CAD/3D file for the model maker.

Designing surface decoration for a form: motifs, banding, relief/sprig patterns, glaze and color schemes, and decal or screen-print artwork placement on the ware's curved surface; output is artwork, a painted or drawn sample, and a decoration specification for approval.

Adapting an existing design to a customer or seasonal requirement: adding a logo or lettering, resizing a shape to a new capacity, or recoloring a pattern line; output is revised drawings, artwork files, and specs.

Revising a design after trial pieces or a production run: correcting warping-prone profiles, mold release problems, or decoration that fired off-register or off-color; output is an updated form/mold/decoration specification.

tasks.label: Teach pottery classes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Beginner wheel-throwing class at a community art center or recreation-department studio: 8-12 students at wheels, instructor wedges and demonstrates centering/opening/pulling on a demo wheel, then circulates to correct hand pressure, re-centers or rescues collapsing pots for individual students, distributes and reclaims clay, and manages tools, wheels and kiln loading for the class's work.

In-plant instruction at a pottery/ceramics manufacturer: the potter teaches new hires or apprentices in a class/training session on production equipment (pug mill, jigger/jolley machine, slip casting, wheel), demonstrating machine setup and technique, watching trainees run the equipment, correcting their handling of clay and molds, and enforcing safety rules.

Intermediate/advanced or specialty workshop in a studio: handbuilding, glaze mixing and application, trimming/handles, or a raku/pit firing session; instructor demonstrates on the material, critiques and physically adjusts student pieces, mixes and tests glazes with the group, and supervises kiln firing.

Private or small-group lessons in the potter's own home or private studio, or in a student's space: layout and equipment vary, teacher shares one or two wheels, works elbow-to-elbow with one to four students, adapts the lesson on the fly, and handles clay, tools and the studio kiln personally.

Outreach/pop-up teaching: portable wheels or handbuilding kits taken to a school classroom, library, festival booth, senior center, or corporate team-building event; unfamiliar room, mixed ages and abilities, instructor sets up, demonstrates, guides many hands quickly, and packs out the wet work for later firing.

tasks.label: Examine completed work to detect defects and verify conformance to work orders, and adjust machinery as necessary to correct production problems.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Corrugated box plant, flexo folder-gluer / rotary die-cutter: operator pulls finished boxes off the counter-ejector every few minutes, checks print registration and ink coverage, slot depth, score lines, glue-lap alignment (fishtail), squareness and bundle count against the work order and customer sample, then corrects print register, glue application, feed skew or slotting/scoring settings from the console and scraps bad bundles.

Corrugator (single-facer/double-backer/dry end): operator checks running board for warp, blister/bond failure, caliper, crush, cut length and score position against the order spec, and adjusts steam pressure, wrap arms, glue gap, moisture spray and slitter-scorer positions to bring board back into spec.

Folding carton plant, flatbed die-cutter and folder-gluer: operator inspects blanks and finished cartons for cut-to-print register, nicks, cracked creases, print blemishes, glue-seam quality, braille and barcode, comparing to the approved sample/work order; adjusts register, die pressure, glue nozzles and folding rails.

Tissue/towel/napkin converting line: operator checks log-saw cut quality, roll diameter and firmness, perforation, embossing, tail seal, sheet count and wrapper seal against the order; adjusts rewinder tension, saw blade position/sharpening and wrapper timing.

Paper bag, envelope, cup or specialty converting machine: operator pulls samples, measures dimensions and gusset/seam placement, checks glue seams, window patch and print, and adjusts folding plates, glue pots, timing and guides to correct running defects.

Small shop or older/specialty equipment (stitcher, sheeter, small gluer, bundler/bander): inspection is done by hand and eye at the delivery table — count, stitch or wrap integrity, damage — and corrections require manual mechanical adjustment (hand cranks, wrenches, repositioning guides, changing a worn part) rather than console settings.
