tasks.label: Measure amounts of products, lengths of extruded articles, or weights of filled containers to ensure conformance to specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Packaging/food/pharma plant: helper pulls filled containers (tubes, jars, bags, cases) off the filling or packing line at set intervals, sets each on a bench or platform scale, reads and records the weight on a check sheet, and tells the operator to adjust the filler when weights drift over/under the target.

Plastics/rubber/metal extrusion plant: helper checks extruded articles (pipe, hose, profile, tubing) as they leave the cut-off saw — tape-measures cut lengths, calipers outside diameter/wall — compares to the spec sheet, marks or sets aside off-spec pieces, and logs the readings.

Machining/assembly plant: helper does bench dimensional checks on batches of small parts using digital calipers, micrometers and go/no-go gauges at a station beside the line, records measurements for SPC, and sorts pass/fail into bins.

Food/chemical batch production: helper measures out amounts of product or ingredients — scoops, pours or pumps into totes, pails or hoppers — weighs to a target on a platform scale, tops off or removes material to hit spec, and labels/records the batch weight.

Mixed ad-hoc checks around the plant at the supervisor's request: verifying fill levels/quantities in filled bottles or cases, weighing partially filled drums or totes on a floor scale, and measuring odd items staged in aisles or storage areas.

tasks.label: Signal coworkers to direct them to move products during the production process.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: On a noisy plant floor, the helper faces a forklift or powered pallet-jack operator and uses hand signals (come ahead, slow, stop, lower) to guide the operator in picking up and repositioning a pallet of finished goods or raw stock; purpose is served entirely by the operator receiving and acting on the direction.

Working a production line, the helper signals a coworker stationed at the other end of a conveyor, press, or packing station — a wave, thumbs-up, or pressing a call buzzer/light — to start, hold, or advance the flow of product between stations.

The helper acts as spotter for an overhead crane or hoist operator, giving standard rigging hand signals to direct lifting, travel, and setting down of heavy coils, dies, or bulk containers into a machine or staging area.
At a shipping dock, the helper signals a truck driver backing a trailer into the dock and then signals loading crew on where to place and how to move palletized product into the trailer.

In a large or multi-bay facility, the helper coordinates movement of work-in-process between departments using a two-way radio, headset, or shouted call-and-response with coworkers out of line-of-sight.

tasks.label: Position spouts or chutes of storage bins so that containers can be filled.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-plant dry-bulk packaging station (plastics compounding, food ingredient, mineral plant): helper swings the chute/spout of an overhead surge bin or hopper over a gaylord/octabin, tote, or fiber drum staged on a pallet or roller table, adjusts the fill head height, seats the dust skirt, starts flow, watches level, then indexes the container out. Container types change with the run.

Bagging line: helper positions the inflatable fill spout/chute of the weigh hopper for FIBC bulk bags or valve/open-mouth bags — slides the bag neck over the spout, hooks the four loops, inflates the seal, fills, releases. Repetitive, standard bags, indoor bagging room.

Bulk loadout bay at an elevator, feed mill, or cement/aggregate terminal: helper positions the telescopic loading spout/chute from the silo over the hatch of a pneumatic tanker, hopper railcar, or open trailer parked roughly on the scale, lowers and seats it, monitors fill and dust, then retracts. Outdoor/covered drive-through bay, driver present, weather varies.

Liquid/paste filling in a chemical, coatings, or food plant: helper positions the fill lance/spout from a supply tank or bin over the bunghole of a drum or the opening of an IBC placed by forklift, fills to weight, closes. Openings not pre-aligned; containers dirty or labeled.

Ad-hoc/small-batch work: helper swings or holds a portable chute, flexible sock, or bin spout to fill assorted odd containers — buckets, carts, mixer hoppers, drums, a wheelbarrow or a pickup bed in the plant yard — placement improvised each time, sometimes steadying the chute by hand while material flows.

Nonroutine or maintenance rigging inside the plant: helping riggers/millwrights sling an odd-shaped machine subassembly, a hose or pipe run being removed, or a one-off shipment item in a tight space or overhead, deciding sling type, wrap points, and protection for each unique object.

tasks.label: Break up defective products for reprocessing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Plastics/rubber molding or extrusion plant: helper collects short shots, flashed or off-color moldings, sprues, runners and purge from press-side bins and gaylords, breaks up oversize pieces and feeds them into a beside-the-press or central granulator so the regrind returns to the material stream. Foundry, die-cast shop or metal fabrication plant: helper knocks gates, sprues and biscuits off scrapped castings, breaks defective castings or weldments apart with hammer, press or torch, and charges the pieces into the remelt scrap bin. Hot, noisy shop floor, heavy pieces.

Glass, ceramic, brick or concrete-products plant: helper smashes defective ware  regreenware, tiles, bottles, blocks  re with a mallet or by tipping it into a crusher so it returns as cullet, grog or recycled aggregate to the batch or pug mill. Dusty indoor plant, brittle heavy items.

General/mixed manufacturing scrap station: helper breaks up heterogeneous defective finished goods  re assembled housings, packaged units, multi-material products, electronics  re at a bench or scrap area with hammer, press or by feeding a shredder, separating metals, plastics and other materials for reprocessing. The product mix changes with whatever the plant rejects that day.

tasks.label: Perform minor repairs to machines, such as replacing damaged or worn parts.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: At a production machine on the plant floor: swap a worn consumable/wear part — cutting blade or insert, punch or die insert, welding electrode tip, abrasive belt/pad, spray nozzle, wear plate. Lock out the machine, pull a guard or clamp, remove and fit the part, torque it, restart and verify the first piece.

At a machine or conveyor on the plant floor: replace a broken or worn drive belt, chain, sprocket, conveyor roller or bearing block. Remove the guard, release the tensioner, route the new belt/chain over pulleys in tight clearance, re-tension and align it, refit the guard, run and check tracking.

At a machine on the plant floor: replace worn seals, gaskets, O-rings or a clogged filter element on a hydraulic, pneumatic, coolant or lubrication system — isolate and drain, break the joint, scrape off the old gasket, fit the new one, reassemble and check for leaks under pressure.

In-situ replacement of small damaged hardware in awkward access: stripped or sheared fasteners, a worn bushing, a bent guard or chute panel, a knocked-off limit switch or photo-eye with its wiring, a burnt lamp. Involves improvisation, working overhead or inside the machine frame, and re-terminating wires.

In the plant's maintenance area/tool crib: a worn subassembly (small pump, gearbox, tool head, mold insert, roller assembly, fixture) has been pulled and brought to a bench. Disassemble it, press out and replace a worn bearing, bushing or insert, reassemble, lubricate and bench-test before it goes back on the machine.

Repairs to non-production shop equipment wherever it sits: replacing casters or a handle on a cart or hand truck, swapping a damaged power cord or chuck on a portable tool, replacing a torn strap, a cracked bin, or an air hose and fitting.

instances.label: Classroom or briefing-room instruction for a new-hire ramp/cargo agent cohort at an airline or ground-handling station: company SOPs, ramp safety rules, jet-blast and danger-zone awareness, hazmat/dangerous-goods awareness, weight-and-balance and load-planning basics, delivered with slides, manuals, and Q&A, followed by a written quiz.

Guided ramp walk-through orientation on the airfield: the supervisor takes one or two new employees around a gate area and explains marked safety zones, FOD control, aircraft servicing points, chocking and coning rules, hearing protection, and radio/hand-signal conventions, conveying the information verbally while pointing things out.

Hands-on equipment familiarization for one new employee on ground support equipment (belt loader, baggage tug, container loader, tow tractor): the supervisor explains and demonstrates pre-use inspection and controls, then talks the trainee through operating it in a quiet ramp area, correcting technique and stopping unsafe actions.

On-the-job supervised training during live aircraft turns: the supervisor shadows a new loader through bag-room sorting, bulk loading, container/pallet handling, net and strap securing, and load-sheet paperwork, coaching in real time under time pressure, noise, and weather.

Competency check-off and recurrent/refresher briefing: the supervisor observes the trainee perform required procedures, evaluates against a checklist, gives corrective feedback, and completes training records, sign-offs, and certification paperwork.

tasks.label: Distribute cargo to maximize use of space.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bulk-loading a narrowbody aircraft (737/A320) belly hold on the ramp: loose suitcases and loose freight arrive by belt loader and must be stacked wall-to-wall and floor-to-ceiling inside the cramped hold, distributed between forward and aft compartments per the load plan so that everything fits and stays put. Airline/airport-controlled ramp, all weather, tight turnaround.

Building up ULD pallets and containers in an air cargo terminal from mixed general freight: cartons, crates and irregular pieces of varying size and weight are stacked to fill the ULD contour and cube, then netted/strapped. Warehouse floor with forklifts, scales, and build-up stations.

Loading departing passenger bags into ULD containers or baggage carts at a make-up position in the airport baggage hall: bags arrive on a conveyor/chute in random sequence and must be packed tightly so the container is filled before it is dispatched to the aircraft.

Placing and locking ULDs and contoured pallets into widebody lower-deck and main-deck positions using a high loader and the aircraft's roller floor, sequencing units so every usable position is filled per the load plan and locks engage.

Loadmaster distributing pallets, rolling stock, and loose cargo aboard a military or charter freighter (C-17/C-130/747F) at an austere, remote, or disaster-relief field: mixed unpalletized loads, improvised restraint, no standard terminal equipment.

Fitting outsize/special cargo into the hold or main deck: aircraft engines, vehicles, livestock stalls, AOG shipments and odd-shaped crates that must be maneuvered, shored and positioned around existing load with minimal clearance.

sources.system: ABLE / ABLE Mk2 (Automated Baggage Loading Equipment), AAT Automation, with SICK Visionary-T Mini 3D camera
sources.title: 3D cameras take automated baggage loading to the next level at Schiphol airport | SICK
sources.claim: AAT Automation's ABLE system uses an industrial robot fed by the baggage conveyor to pick each bag and place it into a waiting ULD container, using 3D camera data on bag shape and the free space remaining in the container to find a custom fit; in operation at Amsterdam Schiphol.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: packing bags into a ULD container rather than into an aircraft belly hold. Transfer holds for the E1 counterfactual because the objects (suitcases, loose bags), the required precision (custom-fit placement computed from remaining free space in a confined box), and the goal (fill the container's cube) are the same as bulk hold stacking; widebody belly loading is in fact performed by filling these same containers in the terminal.

sources.system: Schiphol baggage-hall loading robot (BOOST programme trials)
sources.developer: Royal Schiphol Group with suppliers and handlers (Aviapartner, dnata, KLM, Menzies, Swissport, Viggo)
sources.title: Schiphol introduces lifting aids at every workstation in its baggage halls as it adopts advanced tech
sources.claim: A robot has been independently (autonomously) loading departing baggage into baggage carts and containers in Schiphol's baggage halls for more than six months as of July 2025, alongside a separate automated container-unloading system running since June 2025.
sources.transferJustification: Same objects and purpose as the baggage make-up instance (filling containers/carts bound for the aircraft); the article also notes fully machine-based suitcase loading is still immature worldwide, which is why the judgment stops at a fixed, conveyor-fed station.

sources.claim: Speedcargo with Güdel launched a robotic air-cargo system in which AI-optimised ULD build-up plans are executed automatically by precision gantry robots fed cargo in an optimised sequence; the underlying capability was demonstrated in 2018 by automatically building and breaking down a full freighter ULD of high-mix, high-payload cargo.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: warehouse mixed-case pallet building rather than air-cargo ULD build-up. The objects (mixed cartons up to ~30 kg), the placement precision, the space-maximising objective and the fenced, conveyor/AGV-fed cell are the same as a terminal build-up station; ULD pallets are built by the same stacking logic plus a contour limit.

sources.claim: Lödige's Elevating Transfer Vehicle is a fully automated rail-guided ... machine that moves and precisely positions ULDs (up to 15–20 ft, 6,800–13,600 kg) vertically and horizontally into dense storage positions in air cargo terminals, with powered roller decks handling automated ULD transfer at hubs such as Istanbul and dnata Amsterdam.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: indexing ULDs into dense rack positions rather than into aircraft deck positions. Same objects (ULDs of identical size/weight), same precision class (handover onto roller decks with interlocks preventing transfer errors), and the same 'fill every position' objective; it substantiates only the E1 form, where ULDs arrive on powered decks.

sources.system: DexR
sources.title: Dexterity partners with FedEx to debut trailer loading robots - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Dexterity's DexR mobile two-armed robot autonomously drives to the back of a trailer, connects to a powered conveyor and packs boxes into the trailer, planning arm trajectories to work inside the confined trailer without collisions; tested with FedEx for Ground trailer loading.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: packing a road trailer instead of an aircraft hold. It corroborates that conveyor-fed robots can build tight stacks inside a confined, low-clearance container; it remains a pilot, so it supports only the structured, conveyor-fed (E1) form of hold loading.

tasks.label: Accompany aircraft as a member of the flight crew to monitor and handle cargo in flight.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Military/contract airlift loadmaster aboard a C-17/C-130-class freighter: rides in the cargo compartment for the whole sortie, walks the load in flight to check 463L pallet locks, chains and straps, watches for shifting, hazmat leaks, temperature and smoke, communicates load status to the flight deck, and re-secures items that work loose in turbulence.

Civil freighter/heavy-lift charter loadmaster (747F, An-124, L-100, DC-8) accompanying outsized or heavy machinery: in-flight inspection of lashings and shoring, monitoring for load movement during climb/turbulence, main-deck fire/smoke watch, and hands-on retensioning or re-chocking of a shifted piece en route.

Live-animal charter (horses, cattle, zoo animals) with a loadmaster/flying groom aboard: monitoring animals in flight, feeding and watering, checking stall partitions and restraints, calming or restraining a distressed animal, and adjusting ventilation/positioning as needed.

Airdrop or special-mission sortie: in-flight rigging checks of platforms/CDS bundles and static lines, opening the ramp and door at altitude, releasing restraints on the pilot's signal, retrieving static lines and deployment bags after the drop, and re-securing the compartment.

Part 135 feeder/small freighter (Caravan, Metroliner, Beech 1900) where the cargo handler rides along with loose-loaded freight: monitoring nets and straps in flight, restowing boxes that shift, and handling/unloading freight at remote or unattended stops.

Cargo flight carrying supernumeraries/couriers: briefing riders on seat belts, oxygen, escape hatches and emergency procedures, performing periodic in-flight walk-throughs of the cargo compartment, and reporting cabin/cargo condition to the crew.

sources.system: Stratom eXpeditionary Cargo Loader (XCL)
sources.title: Stratom, AFRL demonstrate new C-130 cargo handling system
sources.claim: Stratom's eXpeditionary Cargo Loader, demonstrated with AFRL for C-130 operations, is a remote-controlled (teleoperated) ground loading device; it moves pallets into the aircraft on the ground and does not ride along or work the load in flight.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: on-aircraft cargo loading. It does not transfer to in-flight monitoring and handling — the work is done on the ground, under remote control, and the machine is not aboard during flight.

sources.claim: Elroy Air's Chaparral autonomously located and grasped a cargo pod in a hangar and attached it to the aircraft, but cargo handling occurs on the ground and no system monitors or manipulates the load during flight.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous pickup/release of a sealed cargo pod. It does not transfer: the pod is handled on the ground and carried externally, with no in-flight inspection, restraint adjustment, animal care, or airdrop release.

sources.system: Reliable Robotics automated Cessna 208B Super Cargomaster

roles.description: Directly supervise and coordinate the activities of helpers, laborers, or material movers, hand.

tasks.label: Maintain a safe working environment by monitoring safety procedures and equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Active-shift floor supervision in a warehouse or distribution center / freight dock: the supervisor moves among 10-25 laborers loading and unloading trailers and moving freight with pallet jacks and forklifts, watching for unsafe acts (missing hi-vis vest or safety shoes, improper lifting, unstable stacking, riding on equipment, pedestrian-forklift conflicts, unchocked trailers), stopping unsafe work, coaching the crew on the spot, and clearing hazards (spilled product, banding, pallet debris, blocked aisles) as they appear during a busy shift.

Scheduled documented safety walkthrough of a warehouse, plant, or terminal (weekly/monthly or start-of-shift housekeeping round): verify emergency exits and electrical panels are clear, fire extinguishers present, charged and unobstructed, machine guarding and pallet-rack condition, eyewash/first-aid stations, lighting, spills and leaks, and log each deficiency into the safety checklist with work orders for corrections.

Pre-use and periodic equipment safety checks: verifying operators completed forklift/pallet-jack daily checklists, physically testing horn, brakes, lights, seatbelt, forks and hydraulics, checking dock levelers, hoists, slings, ladders and fall-arrest harnesses for wear or damage, and tagging out and removing defective equipment from service.

Supervising a laborer crew on an outdoor jobsite (construction/demolition helper crew, utility or landscaping supply yard, disaster or debris cleanup): monitoring changing hazards such as excavation edges, overhead loads, fall exposure, moving vehicles, weather and heat stress, enforcing PPE and work procedures, halting work when conditions change, and correcting or barricading hazards on ground that differs day to day.

Supervising a moving/delivery or hand-unloading crew working at customer homes and small businesses: monitoring safe lifting and team-carry technique, stair, ramp and dolly use, floor and doorway protection, load securement in the truck, and site-specific hazards (ice, pets, narrow stairs, street traffic) at a different, uncontrolled site each stop.

sources.system: Spot quadruped + Orbit fleet management (AI Visual Inspection)
sources.title: Boston Dynamics releases software updates to Orbit fleet management platform, Spot robots - Robotics 24/7
sources.claim: Boston Dynamics' Spot autonomously patrols industrial facilities capturing images at inspection points, and its Orbit software flags safety issues such as spills, missing fire extinguishers and equipment wear — i.e. an automated version of a documented facility safety walkthrough.
sources.transferJustification: Direct: this is a scheduled facility safety/condition inspection round producing flagged deficiencies, the same output as a supervisor's documented safety walkthrough of a warehouse or plant.

sources.system: Spot with thermal camera and acoustic imager
sources.title: Digital Transformation at Nestlé Purina | Boston Dynamics
sources.claim: Spot is deployed in a working food-manufacturing plant running recurring autonomous inspection missions (thermal, acoustic leak detection) on production equipment, with findings feeding maintenance work orders.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (equipment condition inspection rounds) in the same class of facility as a warehouse/plant safety walkthrough: same navigation problem, same recurring checkpoint list, same deficiency-reporting output.

sources.system: ANYmal quadruped inspection robot
sources.title: Quadruped robot boosts safety and maintenance at aging cement plant
sources.claim: ANYbotics' ANYmal has been in service since early 2025 at a cement plant, autonomously walking nightly routes over six levels to inspect 450+ checkpoints for defects, overheating and gas leaks ..., completing 33,000 inspections.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (autonomous plant inspection rounds detecting hazards such as leaks and overheating) transfers to a supervisor's safety/condition walkthrough: comparable route-following through a cluttered industrial facility and comparable checkpoint-by-checkpoint hazard reporting.

sources.system: Spot + Orbit AIVI-Learning with Gemini Robotics-ER 1.6
sources.developer: Boston Dynamics with Google DeepMind/Google Cloud
sources.title: Boston Dynamics integrates Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics model into Spot inspection platform
sources.claim: With Gemini Robotics-ER integrated into Orbit's AI visual inspection, Spot can reason about site conditions during inspections — reading gauges and identifying hazards such as spills, debris, or a door left open — without constant human oversight.
sources.transferJustification: Direct support for the hazard-spotting content of a safety walkthrough (spills, debris, egress/door state) rather than only fixed asset gauges.

sources.system: Spot fleet (1,000+ robots, 35 countries)
sources.title: A Retrospective on Uses of Boston Dynamics' Spot Robot
sources.claim: Across the installed Spot fleet, customers ran thousands of autonomous data-collection missions inspecting over 130,000 industrial assets in ... plants and construction sites during 2025; manipulation work (picking objects, opening doors) was done by manually driving the robot.
sources.transferJustification: Establishes the scale and the boundary of autonomy: routine inspection rounds are autonomous, while physical intervention (grasping objects, opening doors) is done under manual driving — relevant to whether hazard correction and equipment testing can be done autonomously.

tasks.label: Review work throughout the work process and at completion to ensure that it has been performed properly.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Warehouse/DC supervisor walks the floor mid-shift observing pickers, loaders, stockers and forklift crews: watching technique and pace, spotting mis-picks, damaged goods, sloppy stacking, blocked aisles or unsafe handling, and correcting the crew in the moment.

End-of-shift or periodic accuracy audit in the same DC: verifying that putaway and replenishment work was done properly - pallets in assigned slots, labels/LPNs correct, pick-face quantities matching the WMS - and reporting discrepancies for correction.

Outbound dock check at completion: supervisor inspects a trailer or container the crew loaded - count and SKU mix against the BOL, load pattern and weight distribution, straps/load bars/dunnage securement, shrink wrap, no crushed or leaking freight - before releasing and sealing it.

Plant/packaging operation: supervisor checks completed units of manual work presented on a line or staging lane - cases packed to spec, correct labels and counts, pallets built and wrapped to standard, kits complete - and accepts or rejects them.

Outdoor crews (construction helpers, yard, landscaping, refuse, rail laborers): in-process and final walk-throughs of the site - materials staged and stored correctly, excavation/backfill and cleanup to standard, debris removed, barricades and PPE in place - in weather and changing site conditions.

Customer-site crews (household/office moving, delivery and install): final walk-through of a home or office - items placed as directed, nothing missing, no damage to goods, floors, walls or doorways, packing debris removed - and sign-off with the customer.

sources.system: Corvus One (Corvus Robotics)
sources.title: LAPP USA Transforms Inventory Operations with Corvus Robotics' Autonomous Drone System
sources.claim: Fully autonomous inventory drones fly nightly missions inside an active 134,000 sq ft US distribution center, validating pallets and locations and flagging discrepancies, replacing manual cycle-count crews.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous inventory audit. It is the machine equivalent of the supervisor's completion check on putaway/replenishment work - same objects (pallets, labels, pick faces), same facility, same discrepancy/accept output.

sources.system: Verity autonomous inventory drones

sources.claim: Verity's warehouse drones scan pallet and picking locations without human intervention and use computer vision to count items and identify discrepancies.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: verifying stored inventory against the WMS record, i.e., checking whether material handlers' putaway and pick-face replenishment was performed properly.

sources.system: Verity autonomous inventory drones at DSV

sources.claim: Verity's autonomous drone system is deployed at scale in third-party logistics warehouses, starting with a 24,500 sqm site with 57,000+ pallet locations and expanding across DSV's network.
sources.transferJustification: Same as above: an audit of completed material-handling work (location and inventory accuracy) inside a working warehouse.

sources.claim: Pre-configured robotic inspection cells with a robot-guided 3D scanner perform repeatable dimensional and visual inspection of finished workpieces on the factory floor, checking them against spec.

Transfers to a supervisor's completion check on packed/palletized output - rigid goods, far looser tolerances than metrology, same accept/reject output - when work is presented in a purpose-built cell.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated verification that a completed pallet matches the required build (stack pattern, case placement, barcodes) - the machine analogue of a supervisor checking a finished pallet, inside a fenced palletizing cell.

sources.system: Spot quadruped with FieldAI autonomy
sources.title: Case Study: Practical Autonomy on Construction Sites | Boston Dynamics
sources.claim: Spot with FieldAI autonomy walks active construction sites daily without prior maps, capturing data that feeds BIM/digital-twin progress tracking, quality verification and ..., plus safety observations such as PPE compliance and hazards.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous site reality-capture and deviation analysis. Cited because it is the closest existing system to a supervisor's site walk-through, but it verifies installed structure against a model rather than judging a laborer crew's manual work.

sources.system: Spot + Orbit AI visual inspection at Cargill Multiseed
sources.title: Boston Dynamics Robot Dog Spot Inspects for Safety Hazards
sources.claim: Spot with the Orbit AI visual-inspection feature performs autonomous rounds in a food-processing plant, flagging facility conditions such as product spills and blocked emergency exits.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous facility-condition inspection rounds. Cited to show the scope of mobile inspection robots in a structured plant - housekeeping and equipment conditions, not review and acceptance of a crew's handling work.

tasks.label: Inspect equipment for wear and for conformance to specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Warehouse/DC supervisor's condition-and-wear check of powered material handling equipment (sit-down forklifts, reach trucks, electric pallet jacks, order pickers): walking the fleet looking at tire/wheel wear, fork blade wear, bends and cracks, mast chain condition, hydraulic leaks, body and overhead-guard damage, and whether capacity plate, decals and guards conform to spec; tagging units out of service.

Functional side of the powered-truck inspection in the same warehouse: operating the truck to verify brakes, steering, horn, lights, backup alarm, seat belt/operator-presence switch, and lift/tilt hydraulics for drift; checking fluid levels, LP tank or battery connections, before a shift or after an incident.

Fixed facility equipment in a DC or plant: walking conveyor lines, sortation, stretch wrappers, balers, dock levelers and doors and their drive motors/gearboxes, looking and listening for belt wear, misalignment, hot bearings, worn rollers, missing guards, and logging items for maintenance.

Hands-on inspection of small, heterogeneous, often flexible gear: web and chain slings, hooks and shackles, ratchet straps and load bars, hand trucks, dollies, four-wheel carts, manual pallet jacks and pallets - flexing webbing, feeling for frays, cracked welds, bent hooks, seized wheels, checking capacity tags.

Outdoor yard, intermodal or freight terminal: checking trailers, containers, chassis, yard tractors and lift gear arriving or staged - panel/roof/floor damage, tire and brake wear, coupling and lifting-point condition - before loading or dispatch.

Off-site unstructured work: moving-and-storage crews, temp-labor gangs or construction-support laborers at customer premises and job sites; inspecting truck ramps and lift gates, dollies, pads and straps, ladders, hand tools and fall-protection harnesses in whatever space is available.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: daily condition/wear inspection of a fleet vehicle. Transfers to inspecting powered material handling equipment - same class of wheeled, hydraulic, tired vehicle, same wear/damage findings (tires, leaks, structural damage) judged against fleet standards.

Construction jobsite or contractor materials yard: supervisor checks a delivery of lumber, pipe, rebar, drywall or fixtures against the order/packing list — dimensions, grades, quantities, damage — outdoors, with site-specific layout, weather, and only partial labeling.

Manufacturing plant receiving/shipping area: supervisor verifies raw materials and components (coils, drums, cartons, totes) against production work orders — part numbers, heat/lot numbers, quantities, and accompanying certificates.

Moving/relocation crew or field delivery at a customer's premises: supervisor checks household goods, furniture or job equipment against a written inventory sheet/work order, recording item descriptions and pre-existing damage on unlabeled, one-off items.

Port, intermodal, or bulk terminal: supervisor verifies container/trailer numbers, seal numbers, container size/type, commodity and weights against terminal work orders and manifests during loading and discharge.

Output is a build/loading sequence for the handling crew.

Marine terminal, rail intermodal yard, or breakbulk/project-cargo operation: supervisor inspects containers, machinery or breakbulk cargo for weight, dimensions, condition and discharge port, and determines stowage/loading sequence with the stowage plan. Output is a sequenced stow/load instruction for lashing gangs and equipment operators.

instances.label: Routine walkthrough of an indoor recycling processing facility (MRF or transfer station) owned/contracted by the program: coordinator walks the tipping floor, sort lines, baler and conveyor areas checking housekeeping, blocked aisles and exits, spills/leaks, guarding and equipment condition, accumulated fluff and hot-spot fire risk, lighting, signage, extinguishers and eyewash placement; findings photographed and logged on a checklist.

Condition check of an outdoor municipal drop-off recycling center / transfer-station yard with public access: roll-off and bin condition and fill level, overflow and windblown litter, contamination and illegally dumped hazardous items, ground spills or stains, signage, gate/fence and pavement condition, safe traffic flow; noted for service and repair follow-up.

Inspection of a household hazardous waste (HHW) collection facility or hazardous-waste accumulation area: drums, totes and lab-packs checked for leaks, corrosion, bulging and closed lids, labels and accumulation dates, aisle spacing and incompatible-material segregation, secondary containment and berm integrity, spill kits, PPE, ventilation and vapor/gas conditions.

Scheduled compliance audit of a contracted third-party site the coordinator does not run day to day (e-waste processor, contracted MRF, composting or scrap yard): one-off visit to an unfamiliar layout, walking the site against a service-contract and safety checklist, photographing deficiencies and discussing them with the operator on the spot.

Non-routine inspection after an incident or complaint: fire in a tipping pile, chemical spill, storm or equipment damage. Coordinator assesses disturbed and atypical areas (charred material, damaged roof or wall, flooded containment, drainage, bunkers), judges what is unsafe and what must be repaired before restart.

instances.label: Running the processing line at a municipal or private MRF: starting up conveyors, screens and optical sorters, setting/adjusting sorter recipes and belt speeds for the incoming stream, monitoring throughput and purity, stopping the line and clearing jams, wrapped film/tanglers on disc screens and chute blockages, then shutting down. Dusty, noisy indoor plant with staff on catwalks and platforms.

Working a sort/QC station on a moving conveyor: picking target commodities (OCC, PET, HDPE, aluminum) or pulling contaminants (film, textiles, non-recyclables) out of a single-stream flow at a picking platform inside a MRF, at typical line speeds and mixed, variable material.

Operating a horizontal baler at a MRF or transfer station: feeding loose fiber/plastic from a storage bunker or infeed conveyor (sometimes by loader or by hand), cycling the ram, tying/wiring the bale, ejecting it, and moving finished bales with a forklift to the loadout/storage area; clearing wire jams and misfeeds.

Operating crushing/size-reduction equipment: glass crusher, aluminum can densifier, plastic granulator or e-waste shredder at a processing facility — feeding the hopper, monitoring for oversize/unshreddable items, adjusting screens, and clearing plugged feed throats.

Operating small-scale equipment at a drop-off center, transfer site, school or municipal collection yard: hand-loading a vertical baler or can crusher with mixed, unpredictable public-dropped material, hand-tying and wrestling out the bale, staging bales; partly outdoors, layout varies by site.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Inside a materials recovery facility (MRF) or recycling warehouse: running a counterbalance forklift to carry finished bales (OCC, mixed paper, PET, aluminum) from the baler discharge to storage rows, stacking them two to three high, and later loading them onto flatbeds/van trailers at the dock. Floor is industrial, with debris, dust, other lift trucks and workers moving nearby.

Operating a skid steer or front-end loader on the tipping floor / in the yard of a MRF, transfer station or drop-off depot: pushing and scooping loose commingled recyclables, glass, or residue into the infeed hopper or into storage piles, and keeping the floor clear while collection trucks tip loads nearby.

Driving a local truck (box truck, flatbed, or roll-off) on public streets between drop-off sites, schools and municipal buildings and the processing facility: backing into tight sites, dropping and retrieving containers or carts, dumping the load at the facility, and spotting the vehicle at the dock.
Driving a loaded tractor-trailer of baled recyclables over the road from the facility to a mill, broker or end market and returning empty; mostly highway miles with terminal/dock stops at each end.

Operating a forklift or small loader at an outdoor municipal drop-off center, transfer station, or a one-day e-waste/HHW collection event: staging and swapping gaylords, carts, pallets and roll-off boxes while members of the public drive through and unload, with variable weather and no fixed load positions.

Moving palletized or containerized recyclables inside the facility's storage warehouse or dock area: putaway and retrieval of pallets of baled cans, gaylords of plastic, pallets of e-waste or office paper, staging them for shipment in a fixed rack/floor layout.

tasks.label: Investigate violations of solid waste or recycling ordinances.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Residential curbside route review: coordinator (or inspector) walks/drives a collection route on set-out day, lifts recycling or organics cart lids at individual addresses, judges whether prohibited materials are present, photographs and records the address, and leaves an 'oops' tag or triggers a warning letter for the household. Public street/parkway, all weather, dogs, parked cars, carts placed variably.

Waste evaluation at a facility: samples of material collected from a suspect route or generator are tipped and hand-sorted on a tipping floor or sort table at a transfer station/MRF, prohibited contaminants are identified, weighed and photographed, and a documented contamination finding is produced for enforcement or hauler follow-up.

Commercial/multifamily container inspection: visit a business or apartment complex, open the enclosure gate and dumpster/compactor lids, look inside trash, recycling and organics containers for prohibited contaminants or diverted recyclables landfilled, photograph the contents, and document a contamination violation for the account.

Commercial compliance investigation beyond container contents: verify that the generator subscribes to required recycling/organics service, check container labeling and signage, review hauler service records and waiver claims, interview the property manager or janitorial staff, and issue a notice of violation with a corrective-action deadline.

Illegal dumping investigation: respond to a report of waste dumped in an alley, roadside, vacant lot, or at an unstaffed drop-off recycling site; photograph and measure the pile, open bags and sift debris for mail, receipts or other identifying evidence, check any camera footage or witness statements, and build a case naming a responsible party.

Complaint-driven residential field visit: respond to reports of set-out time violations, uncontained or overflowing waste, scavenging of recyclables, unpermitted haulers, or trash placed at a neighbor's cart; observe conditions at the address, photograph, talk to the resident if present, leave a door notice, and re-inspect on follow-up.

tasks.label: Examine, measure, or weigh cargo or materials to determine specific handling requirements.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Distribution-center inbound dock: as trailers are unloaded, the supervisor inspects arriving pallets and cartons for crush damage, leaks, wet or shifted/overhanging loads, verifies pallet dimensions and weight against the BOL using a floor or forklift scale or pallet dimensioner, and sets handling (forks vs. clamp, restack/break down, quarantine as damaged, segregate hazmat).

Parcel hub or LTL freight terminal: supervisor measures and weighs individual shipments (dimensioner, in-motion DWS, floor/forklift scale) to catch oversize/overweight pieces, checks packaging integrity and hazmat labeling, and assigns handling — do-not-stack, fragile, special equipment, placement in the trailer.

Marine/intermodal container terminal or rail yard: supervisor examines containers, chassis and trailers for structural damage, seals, placards and door direction, confirms verified gross mass / overweight status, and identifies out-of-gauge, reefer or damaged boxes needing special equipment or removal from the flow.

Manufacturing plant, steel service center or heavy-equipment yard: supervisor examines large unit loads (coils, castings, crated machinery, bundled stock), determines weight and approximate center of gravity, checks lift points, slings and clearances, and specifies crane/rigging or forklift attachment requirements.

Aggregate yard, quarry or construction site: supervisor measures bulk material stockpiles and delivered bulk loads (volume/tonnage), checks material condition (moisture, contamination, size), and determines loading, hauling and equipment requirements for the day's moves.

At a customer's premises or a field site (household-goods move survey, oversize/awkward item pickup, scrap or bulk waste collection): supervisor examines and measures items and access routes (doorways, stairs, driveway), estimates weights, and determines crew size, equipment, packing and protective handling.

tasks.label: Explain and demonstrate work tasks to new workers or assign training tasks to experienced workers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Warehouse/distribution-center floor: supervisor onboards a new forklift, reach-truck or electric pallet-jack operator - walks them through the pre-shift inspection, then operates alongside to show pick, putaway, stacking, wrapping and RF-scanner steps in live aisles with other traffic, watches the trainee try it, corrects fork position and travel speed, and signs off competency.

Loading dock / truck yard: supervisor demonstrates trailer loading patterns, load securing (straps, dunnage, load bars), dock-plate and trailer-restraint use, chock procedures, and yard-hostler/spotting technique and hand signals to a new hire, then observes and corrects the trainee's first attempts.

Outdoor variable site (construction, quarry, ready-mix, refuse route, rail-side yard): supervisor shows an operator how to run a loader, excavator, dump truck or packer at that day's site - where to set up, how to grade/dump/spot, ground-guide signals - with terrain, layout and hazards different at each site.

Port/intermodal terminal or plant material-handling area: supervisor demonstrates container handler, yard crane or specialized lift operation, twist-lock and interchange procedures, and terminal traffic rules to a new operator inside an institution-controlled terminal, then evaluates the trainee's runs.

Break room / office / training room: supervisor explains new SOPs, safety rules, WMS or telematics procedures in a toolbox talk or one-on-one, answers questions, and assigns training tasks - pairing a new hire with an experienced operator as mentor, assigning refresher modules or certification tasks - and tracks completion.

sources.system: TeachBot (Sawyer-based robotic instructor)
sources.title: TeachBot: Towards teaching robotics fundamentals for human-robot collaboration at work - ScienceDirect
sources.claim: TeachBot is an autonomous robotic ... delivers interactive lectures to workers using graphics and physical arm-motion demonstrations; it is a research prototype teaching a fixed robotics-fundamentals curriculum at a single workstation, not a system that trains operators on material-handling machines or assesses their hands-on performance.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered workforce instruction. Cited to mark the ceiling of demonstrated capability, not to support a positive judgment: TeachBot teaches a scripted curriculum about its own arm at a bench, and cannot demonstrate forklift, dock or yard work tasks, field a trainee's questions, watch a trainee operate a machine, or certify competency.

Shows a robot can execute the machine work a supervisor would demonstrate, but the instance requires teaching a person - narrating, answering questions, observing and correcting the trainee - which this system does not do.

instances.label: Distribution center / warehouse floor and dock: the DC or dock supervisor gets on a sit-down forklift, reach truck, or electric pallet jack to unload or load a trailer, put away or retrieve pallets, and clear a dock backlog when the shift is short-staffed or behind. Indoor facility, standard pallets and racking, associates working nearby.

Trailer yard, freight terminal, intermodal or marine terminal owned by the employer: the supervisor drives a yard hostler/spotter to hook, move and spot trailers between doors and parking rows, or runs a container handler/terminal tractor, to keep the gate and doors flowing. Paved, signed, controlled-access property with mixed traffic of trucks and people.

Point-to-point movement on public roads: the supervisor covers a driver gap by bobtailing a tractor, shuttling a loaded trailer between a DC and a store or cross-dock, or running a short line-haul leg; freight is loaded and unloaded by facility staff at each end. Highways and surface streets, public traffic.

Street-level route work with stops and handling: the supervisor covers a refuse/recycling collection route, a multi-stop local delivery run, or a transit street run — driving between stops plus curbside servicing of carts/containers, hand-offs at customer doors, and customer interaction on public streets.

Company-controlled outdoor bulk-material site (quarry, sand and gravel yard, landfill working face, mine, bulk terminal): the supervisor takes over a haul truck, wheel loader or dozer for a stretch of the shift to keep material cycling from the face/stockpile to the crusher, scale or dump point. Maintained haul roads, geofenced site, controlled access.

Site taken as found — a customer's yard, a construction or utility job site, or curbside: the supervisor operates a truck-mounted crane/boom, a rough-terrain forklift, or a loader to set down or pick up material, free a stuck vehicle, or lift material to the crew, amid changing ground conditions, other trades and bystanders.

tasks.label: Inspect or test materials, stock, vehicles, equipment, or facilities to ensure that they are safe, free of defects, and consistent with specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Warehouse/distribution center: supervisor performs or verifies pre-shift and periodic inspections of powered industrial trucks and material-handling equipment (forklifts, reach trucks, pallet jacks, conveyors) — walk-around for fork/chain/mast wear, cracked welds, tire condition, hydraulic leaks, fluid levels, plus functional tests of brakes, steering, horn, and lift; tags out defective units and signs off checklists.

Truck terminal or distribution yard (paved, outdoors, all weather): supervisor performs or spot-checks pre-trip/post-trip DOT-style inspections of tractors, trailers, and yard hostlers — tires, wheels, lights, air lines, brakes, fifth wheel/coupling, doors, leaks — and verifies drivers' DVIRs before release.

Loading dock / staging area: inspecting incoming and outgoing stock and loads — cartons and palletized freight checked for damage, crushed or wet packaging, correct item/quantity against the bill of lading or spec, pallet condition, load securement/blocking-and-bracing, and trailer or container interior condition and seals.

Facility safety walkthrough of the warehouse, terminal building, and yard: checking racking uprights and beams for damage, blocked aisles and exits, floor and dock-plate condition, spills and debris, guardrails, lighting, battery-charging area, fire extinguishers, and dock levelers, logging findings and issuing corrective work orders.

Construction, aggregate/quarry, or similar site taken as found: inspecting heavy material-moving equipment and rigging — haul trucks and loaders, crane hooks and wire rope, slings and chains, conveyors and stockpile equipment — on uneven ground in dust, mud, and weather, often at a site the employer does not fully control.

sources.transferJustification: Directly the task: inspecting vehicles for defects and safety. The scan is done in a purpose-built drive-through lane the vehicle is brought to, i.e., work presented to the machine.

sources.transferJustification: Same task class (safety testing of a vehicle to a regulatory specification), covering the functional brake test that a camera-only scanner cannot do; the vehicle is driven onto a fixed purpose-built test machine.

Cross-dock or DC dock, floor-loaded (fluid-loaded) freight: the supervisor gets in the trailer or container with the crew and hand-stacks or breaks down cases of mixed cartons onto a boom conveyor or pallet, in hot/tight trailer conditions.

Parcel/LTL sort hub: the supervisor steps onto a load line to help a loader wall-stack mixed-size parcels into a trailer or package car fed by an extendable conveyor, keeping the load tight and the door clear before dispatch cutoff.

Yard and dock support at a freight terminal or DC: the supervisor helps operators by spotting and repositioning trailers at dock doors with a yard tractor, hitching/unhitching, connecting air lines, chocking and staging equipment so loading can proceed.

Customer premises (household move, appliance/furniture delivery, or field delivery): the supervisor works with the crew carrying furniture, appliances and mixed goods down stairs and ramps, protecting doorways, and strapping the load inside a straight truck at a residence or small business.

Outdoor bulk/aggregate or construction jobsite: the supervisor runs a wheel loader or excavator to help load dump trucks with aggregate, spoil or debris and positions trucks under the loadout during a rush.

Rail car attendant supervisor ('on-car supervisor') or ferry attendant supervisor walks a passenger car / vessel passenger cabin at a station, yard or berth before service: seats, tables, windows, doors, lighting, HVAC, restrooms, emergency exits and equipment, damage, graffiti and cleanliness; defects reported to mechanical.

In-flight/cabin service supervisor checks an aircraft cabin (or vessel cabin) at the gate or base: emergency equipment presence and seals, extinguisher and oxygen bottle gauges, PBE and medical kit expiry dates, life vests, placards, seat/belt/tray condition, galley security.

Depot condition/damage inspection of a motorcoach or transit bus body and running gear only (post-route damage documentation, roadworthiness verification): body panels, glass, tires, undercarriage, leaks and lights, with the vehicle driven to the inspection point.

instances.label: Airline inflight supervisor/purser inspects an aircraft cabin at the gate during turnaround before boarding: checks galleys, lavatories, seat rows and seat pockets for cleanliness after the cleaning crew, verifies emergency equipment is present, stowed, sealed and in date (life vests under seats, extinguishers, oxygen bottles, first-aid/medical kits), and confirms galley and cabin equipment (ovens, boilers, lighting, PA, exit signs) are serviceable; deficiencies are logged and corrections directed before departure.

Supervisor conducts an in-service walk-through while the trip is underway (aircraft in flight, train or coach en route): checks lavatory cleanliness and stock, galley and service-cart condition, aisle and cabin tidiness and that service equipment is functioning to standard, in a moving vehicle occupied by passengers and working attendants.

Rail/transit passenger-services supervisor inspects passenger cars at a station platform or servicing yard after cleaning and commissary servicing: interior cleanliness (floors, seats, tables, windows), restrooms cleaned and stocked, trash removed, seat/table damage, and readiness of car equipment (doors, HVAC, lighting, PA, water/waste, wheelchair spaces) before the consist is released for service.

Motorcoach, transit or paratransit supervisor inspects vehicles at the depot before assignment: interior cleanliness and damage, presence and condition of safety equipment (fire extinguisher, first-aid kit, reflective triangles), stocked supplies, and functional test of accessibility equipment such as the wheelchair lift/ramp and securement straps.

Cruise-ship or ferry hotel/passenger-services supervisor makes an inspection round: spot-checks staterooms after housekeeping (bathroom, linens, amenities, surfaces), inspects public lounges, stairwells and pantries for cleanliness, and checks passenger-service equipment condition, recording deficiencies for the housekeeping and maintenance teams.

Supervisor inspects fixed passenger work areas at the terminal, station or gate: waiting areas and lounges, restrooms, boarding-area housekeeping performed by contract cleaners, plus condition and availability of passenger-service equipment (wheelchairs, boarding ramps, jet-bridge interior, carts, stocked supplies), and issues correction notices to cleaning or maintenance staff.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: routine equipment-condition inspection rounds in a facility. It shows autonomous navigation and documented anomaly/gauge reporting, but the checkpoints are fixed industrial assets, not the heterogeneous cleanliness, stock and safety-equipment criteria of a passenger cabin or lounge inspection.

tasks.label: Use instrumentation to guide flights when visibility is poor.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: En route/climb/descent segment of a scheduled airline flight conducted in IMC (in or above cloud, night, or haze): the crew navigates the filed route by reference to instruments — FMS/LNAV-VNAV, ILS/GNSS/IRS position, altimetry — accepts ATC clearances for level and heading changes, and monitors flight instruments with no outside visual reference. Standard transport aircraft, controlled airspace, published airways/arrivals.

Precision ILS approach and landing in instrument conditions to roughly CAT I minima (ceiling ~200–600 ft, visibility 1/2–2 SM) at a normal air-carrier airport: crew configures and arms the approach, tracks localizer and glideslope on the autopilot/flight director, monitors raw data and altitude callouts, acquires the runway at DH and lands (or autolands), then rolls out and vacates.

Category II/IIIa/IIIb low-visibility approach and landing in fog at an equipped runway with low-visibility procedures in force (RVR roughly 75–350 m, decision height 50 ft or none): fail-operational autoland flies approach, flare, touchdown and rollout guidance with the crew monitoring annunciations and prepared to go around; aircraft is then brought to taxi speed on the runway.

Low-visibility departure: taxiing to the runway in fog on an airport surface using charts/moving map and surface guidance, lining up, and conducting a takeoff at RVR of roughly 150–500 m using runway centerline tracking and HUD/takeoff guidance, followed by an instrument departure procedure into cloud.

Non-ILS instrument approach in IMC at a regional or terrain-constrained airport — RNAV(GNSS) LNAV/VNAV or LPV, RNP AR, VOR or localizer approach — including step-downs, possible circling or missed approach and hold, in cloud with no ground-based precision guidance.

Instrument flying in degraded or abnormal conditions in IMC: unreliable airspeed or attitude/ADIRU failure requiring standby instruments and pitch-power flying, icing, or convective weather requiring on-board radar interpretation, deviations negotiated with ATC and a diversion decision to an alternate.

tasks.label: Start engines, operate controls, and pilot airplanes to transport passengers, mail, or freight, adhering to flight plans, regulations, and procedures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scheduled mainline narrowbody passenger flight (A320/737-family), 1-3 hours, two-pilot crew: preflight/checklists, engine start and pushback, taxi at a busy hub under ATC, takeoff, climb/cruise with FMS and ATC reroutes, approach, landing, taxi to gate, shutdown, with 120-180 passengers aboard.
Regional airline leg (CRJ/E175/ATR-class), 45-90 minutes, several legs per day into smaller or terrain-constrained airports, quick turns, mixed towered/non-towered fields, 50-90 passengers.

Long-haul widebody international flight (777/787/A350), 8-14 hours, oceanic/track procedures, augmented crew rest rotations, ETOPS and fuel/alternate management, international ATC and customs procedures, 200-350 passengers.

Any of the above flown under degraded or abnormal conditions: convective weather deviation, icing, wind shear/gusty crosswinds, CAT II/III low-visibility approach, holding and diversion to an alternate, contaminated runway, or an aircraft system malfunction/passenger medical event requiring QRH work and coordinated decisions.

Scheduled all-cargo flight on a large jet freighter (767F/A300F/747F/MD-11F), typically night-time hub-and-spoke operations, heavy weights, dangerous-goods paperwork, ramp coordination with loaders, two-pilot crew.

Small feeder/regional freight flight on a single-engine turboprop or light twin (Caravan-class) carrying mail and parcels between a hub airport and outlying towered or non-towered airfields, single pilot, IFR in the national airspace system.

tasks.label: Work as part of a flight team with other crew members, especially during takeoffs and landings.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine takeoff and departure on a scheduled flight in benign conditions at a standard airport: pilot flying handles thrust, rotation and initial climb while pilot monitoring makes standard callouts (80 kt, V1, rotate), retracts gear and flaps on command, monitors engine and flight-path parameters, and works the after-takeoff flow with ATC.

Routine approach and landing in benign conditions at a controlled airport: approach briefing, configuration on command, stabilized-approach and altitude callouts, cross-checks, landing checklist, flare/touchdown, reverse and autobrake management, runway exit and taxi-in coordination between the two pilots.

Low-visibility CAT II/III straight-in approach at a properly equipped airport with surface winds within autoland limits: crew sets up and arms the automatic landing system, divides monitoring duties, calls deviations and minima, and the aircraft is landed and rolled out on the centerline.

Takeoff or landing in demanding conditions: gusty crosswind near aircraft limits, wet/contaminated or short runway, night with convective weather or turbulence, terrain-constrained or congested airport, requiring active cross-monitoring, dynamic reconfiguration, and joint go-around/reject decisions.

Nonnormal or emergency event around takeoff or landing (engine failure near V1 and rejected takeoff, windshear escape, TCAS RA, gear/flap or hydraulic malfunction, unstable approach) requiring explicit PF/PM role division, QRH work, ATC declaration and cabin-crew coordination.

Crew coordination surrounding takeoff and landing in other phases: pre-departure and approach briefings with the other pilot, challenge-response checklists and switch/flow verification, pushback and taxi coordination, sterile-cockpit discipline, and coordination with cabin crew, ground and dispatch.

sources.system: Airbus UpNext ATTOL (Autonomous Taxi, Take-Off and Landing) on A350-1000
sources.title: Airbus concludes ATTOL with fully autonomous flight tests
sources.claim: Airbus's ATTOL demonstrator flew an A350-1000 airliner performing fully automatic vision-based taxi, takeoff and landing at a real airport, with test pilots aboard only monitoring - i.e. the machine performing the pilot-flying role during takeoff and landing in an airliner cockpit.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: the pilot-flying half of a crewed takeoff/landing. Same aircraft class (transport airliner), same runway environment, same control actuation and rotation/flare precision; the humans on the flight deck acted only as monitors.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: conducting the takeoff and landing flying duties of a commercial flight. Same airport environment and phases (taxi, takeoff, landing, rollout) as the airline instance, with the human role reduced to supervision rather than control.

tasks.label: Respond to and report in-flight emergencies and malfunctions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Single-system fault in climb or cruise on a scheduled flight (ECAM/EICAS caution: pack or bleed fail, generator fail, hydraulic low, anti-ice fault, fuel imbalance). Crew identifies it, runs ECAM/QRH actions and switch selections, assesses altitude/speed/landing-distance consequences, advises ATC of restrictions, coordinates with dispatch and maintenance by radio or ACARS, and writes it up in the logbook; flight normally continues to destination.

Acute hazard alert requiring an immediate flown escape: TCAS resolution advisory or GPWS/terrain warning at altitude or on approach. Crew (or autopilot) flies the escape maneuver within seconds, reports the deviation to ATC, and returns to clearance.

Pressurization emergency or crew incapacitation: cabin altitude warning, masks on, emergency descent to a safe altitude while avoiding terrain, emergency declared and squawk set, diversion to a suitable airport, approach and landing, then reports.

Engine failure, engine or cargo fire, or major hydraulic/electrical loss: memory items, fire handle and bottle discharge, securing the affected systems, Mayday to ATC, cabin crew and dispatch coordination, abnormal-configuration approach and landing at a diversion field, evacuation decision, and post-event reports.

Medical emergency, unruly passenger, or cabin odor/smell reported by flight attendants: gather information from the cabin, consult ground medical advisory or company, decide whether to continue or divert, arrange medical or security response on arrival, and file the required reports.

Encounter or non-checklist event: severe turbulence, bird strike, lightning strike, smoke or fumes of unknown origin, or cascading/multiple failures needing improvisation beyond published procedures — assess airframe damage and cabin injuries, improvise a plan, possibly an off-airport landing or ditching on terrain taken as found, and report.

tasks.label: Inspect aircraft for defects and malfunctions, according to pre-flight checklists.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine exterior walk-around of a narrowbody at a jet-bridge gate in daylight and dry weather, done by the first officer inside a 20-40 minute turn: skin/panels/doors closed and flush, probes and static ports clear with covers off, antennas, drain masts, no fluid leaks, tires and brake wear indicators, oleo extension, gear pins removed, engine inlet and fan blades, chocks and ground equipment clear, ending in a go decision.

Exterior walk-around in darkness, rain, snow or high wind on a congested ramp with catering, fuel and baggage vehicles operating; includes the cold-weather critical-surface contamination check (visual and, after de-icing, tactile) of wings and control surfaces shortly before departure.

Flight-deck preflight inspection per checklist on an originating or through flight: circuit-breaker and panel scan, systems self-tests and warning/fire-loop tests, flight control free-and-correct check, oxygen mask pull-and-test, fire extinguishers, crash axe, escape rope/life vests and other emergency equipment, and review of the aircraft technical log/MEL for open defects.

First-flight-of-the-day or post-overnight thorough exterior inspection of a widebody or freighter with several hours of ground time: full airframe survey including high tail surfaces, upper wing, gear bays, engine inlets and cargo doors, at a maintenance-base stand or remote parking spot.

Focused follow-up inspection of a suspect item found on the walk-around or reported by the inbound crew or ground staff - bird-strike residue, a dent or scuff, a tire cut, a hydraulic drip, a lightning-strike burn mark - to judge whether it is within limits or maintenance must be called.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated general visual inspection of the aircraft exterior for damage. Same object (the parked airframe) and finer precision (dents to 0.1 mm) than a pilot's walk-around scan, so surface-defect detection carries over; it does not cover tires, brakes, fluid levels or gear pins.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: drone-collected pre-flight/general visual inspection of an airliner exterior. Same aircraft and same inspection intent as the pilot walk-around, but the imagery is interpreted by remote human experts rather than by the machine.

tasks.label: Monitor gauges, warning devices, and control panels to verify aircraft performance and to regulate engine speed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cruise/en-route: pilot monitoring scans engine indications (N1/EPR, EGT, fuel flow, oil pressure/temp, vibration), fuel burn vs. flight plan and systems synoptics on EICAS/ECAM, cross-checks performance against the FMS, and trims cruise thrust/speed with autothrottle and autopilot engaged in a standard air-carrier flight deck.

Takeoff and initial climb: set and verify computed takeoff thrust (N1/EPR, flex/derate), hand on thrust levers, monitor engine indications and warning annunciations through the high-power phase, call out thrust set/exceedances, then set climb thrust and verify climb performance.

Descent, approach, landing and go-around: manage thrust to speed/path targets, monitor engine spool-up and idle indications, verify autothrottle retard at flare, apply go-around thrust if required, and confirm engine parameters during reverse thrust and rollout.

Non-normal event: a master caution/warning or engine gauge deviation (oil pressure loss, high EGT/vibration, engine surge, fire loop) appears; crew verifies indications across gauges, diagnoses the malfunction, adjusts or retards the affected thrust lever, and runs the ECAM/QRH engine actions including shutdown if required.

Preflight/engine start, panel checks and taxi: verify overhead/control-panel switch configuration, monitor start sequence parameters (N2, EGT, oil pressure, ITT limits), check APU and bleed indications, and manage idle/breakaway thrust while taxiing.

Aircraft without autothrottle (older regional jets and turboprops, e.g., CRJ200, Dash 8, Saab 340): pilot sets and continually adjusts power by hand against torque/N1/ITT gauges for each phase, guarding limits manually.

tasks.label: Steer aircraft along planned routes, using autopilot and flight management computers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cruise on a domestic scheduled airline flight: autopilot coupled to the FMS holds the programmed lateral/vertical route and speed at FL300-400; crew monitors and executes occasional ATC amendments (direct-to a downstream fix, step climb, speed assignment) via FMS/MCP in radar-controlled airspace.

Departure and arrival phases: flying a published SID/STAR with altitude and speed constraints, then accepting radar vectors, crossing restrictions and runway changes in busy terminal airspace, switching between LNAV/VNAV and selected heading/altitude modes on the mode control panel.

Final approach through touchdown and rollout: coupled ILS/RNP approach flown by the autopilot/autothrottle, including CAT II/III autoland in low visibility at an equipped runway, or autopilot-flown approach to minimums before manual landing.

Weather work en route: interpreting onboard radar and datalink weather, requesting and flying deviations around convective cells, turbulence-driven altitude/offset changes, and rejoining the cleared route or accepting a full reroute from ATC.

Long-haul oceanic/remote flying: navigating an organized track or random route with RNP-4/10 accuracy, CPDLC/ADS-C clearances, strategic lateral offsets and step climbs, with no radar coverage and long periods of automation monitoring.

Non-normal steering: continuing along a revised route with degraded automation or aircraft systems (autopilot inoperative or downgraded, engine failure driftdown along an escape route, unreliable airspeed), including hand-flying to hold the route to a diversion airport.

tasks.label: Instruct other pilots and student pilots in aircraft operations and the principles of flight.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Full-flight simulator training/checking session at an airline or contract training center: instructor briefs the crew, runs the session from the instructor operating station (setting weather, failures, malfunctions), watches the two pilots fly, coaches through maneuvers such as engine-out V1 cuts and CAT III approaches, and debriefs against ATP/AQP standards.

Ground instruction at an airline training center or academy: classroom/CBT lessons on aircraft systems, performance, principles of flight, and SOPs, including answering trainee questions, whiteboard/mockup demonstrations, and assessing written knowledge.

Line instruction on revenue flights (IOE / line check airman): instructing a newly qualified first officer or captain from the other seat during real operations — busy ATC environment, weather, turbulence, passengers aboard — monitoring, coaching in real time, and taking or guarding the controls when the trainee's handling requires it.

Dual flight instruction of a student pilot in a light training aircraft (CFI role at a flight school): pattern work, stalls, steep turns, crosswind landings and emergency procedures, demonstrating maneuvers, correcting unpredictable student control inputs, at non-towered fields in variable weather.
One-on-one preflight briefings, post-flight debriefings, cockpit-procedures/flat-panel trainer walkthroughs, and jumpseat standardization mentoring of another qualified pilot.

instances.label: Post-maintenance functional check flight of a transport-category airliner out of an airline maintenance base: the crew flies a prescribed profile to specified altitudes to verify pressurization, hydraulics, flight controls, autopilot/autoland, engine parameters and warning systems, judges anomalies (noises, drifts, spurious alerts), and signs the aircraft off as serviceable.

In-flight operational verification checks flown on line or ferry flights of specific airliner equipment: autoland/CAT III performance and currency checks, HF/SATCOM/datalink and nav-receiver reception checks at cruise altitude, and ops checks of repaired or deferred items, evaluated and logged by the crew in whatever weather the route presents.

Verification/characterization flight of newly installed avionics or communications equipment (antennas, transponders, C-band datalinks, transponder/collision-avoidance or detect-and-avoid units) on a testbed aircraft: flying prescribed altitudes, ranges, headings and encounter geometries in a terminal area to determine reception quality, interference and alerting behavior.

Periodic flight inspection of ground navigation aids and instrument procedures: flying published approach, orbit and coverage profiles with a calibrated receiver to measure ILS/VOR/NDB/GBAS signal strength, alignment and receptivity at specified heights, and producing an ICAO Doc 8071-compliant inspection result.

Development or certification flight test of a new system or payload on an instrumented test aircraft at a flight test center: flying test points at specified altitudes and configurations while equipment performance (refueling store, radar, datalink, flight control laws) is recorded and evaluated against test cards.

Test evaluation that must be conducted in specific adverse weather taken as found: natural icing runs, heavy precipitation, turbulence, gusty crosswinds and low-visibility approaches, to characterize how equipment and systems behave in those conditions.

tasks.label: Perform minor maintenance work, or arrange for major maintenance.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Part 121 line flight, flight deck at the gate: an EICAS/ECAM fault, inoperative cabin or flight-deck item, or crew-reported anomaly must be handled. The pilot diagnoses per checklist, makes the maintenance-logbook write-up on the EFB or paper form, phones/ACARS maintenance control, coordinates the mechanic meeting the aircraft, and accepts the MEL/CDL deferral and sign-off before release. Physical content is limited to documentation and showing the mechanic the item.

Exterior defect found on the apron during walkaround or after an event (lightning or bird strike, hail dents, tire cut/wear, hydraulic or fuel seepage, cracked lens, damaged fairing). The pilot examines and assesses the damage, photographs and documents it, and arranges the required inspection or repair before departure. Outdoors on an airline ramp or maintenance base, day or night, weather and ground equipment present.

Minor corrective action performed in situ inside the aircraft during a turnaround: identify and reset a tripped circuit breaker, cycle or reset a system per QRH/checklist, reset IFE or galley equipment, replace a chart/dome lamp, re-seat or secure a loose panel, seat or sunshade, then verify function is restored and note the action. Flight deck and cabin, standard layout, hand tools only.

Commuter, corporate or trainer aircraft the pilot may legally service (14 CFR 43.3(g)/App. A(c)): check and add engine oil, top up hydraulic fluid, service main and nose tires to pressure, drain fuel sumps and check for water, at an FBO ramp or company hangar with a step ladder, oil cans and an air/nitrogen cart.

Same class of aircraft, small-component preventive maintenance in a hangar or FBO: replace a landing/nav/beacon light bulb, replace or charge the battery, replace a safety belt, remove and refit cowl or inspection panels with fasteners, clean and lubricate hinges and windshield, then confirm the item works and log it.

Outstation or remote strip with no maintenance support, aircraft parked outside in weather: brush snow and frost off wings and tail, fit or remove covers, chocks and tie-downs, connect external power or a battery cart for a start, secure the aircraft, and arrange by phone for a mechanic and parts to be flown in or for a ferry permit/aircraft swap.
