tasks.label: Wrap and secure goods using pads, packing paper, containers, or straps.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dry-van / reefer / LTL driver secures mixed palletized and loose freight inside a van trailer at a shipper's or consignee's warehouse dock: throwing and ratcheting cargo straps to E-track, setting load bars/decking beams, sliding dunnage pads or blankets between stacked freight so it will not shift in transit.

Flatbed / step-deck driver secures steel coils, plate, pipe, lumber bundles, or machinery at a mill yard, lumberyard, or job site: throwing chains and ratchet straps over the load, setting edge protectors and corner boards, tightening binders, and rolling or throwing tarps, outdoors in wind, rain, or heat.

Driver at a distribution-center or food-service dock stretch-wraps and straps palletized freight before loading (re-wrapping shifted pallets, banding stacked cases to the pallet) so the unit load rides safely.

Household-goods / office mover wraps bulky, regular items in a residence or office — sofas, mattresses, appliances, box springs — in blankets and shrink film, and packs standard cartons of books, linens, and kitchen goods with packing paper.

Household-goods mover pad-wraps and tapes irregular or fragile items in a customer's home — antique dressers, mirrors, framed art, marble tops, disassembled table parts — and individually paper-wraps china and glassware into dish packs.

Tow / recovery or car-haul operator secures a vehicle (often damaged, low-clearance, or non-rolling) to a flatbed deck or wheel-lift with ratchet straps, wheel nets, or chains at the roadside, in a parking lot, or in a wreck yard.

tasks.label: Operate idle reduction systems or auxiliary power systems to generate power from alternative sources, such as fuel cells, to reduce idling time, to heat or cool truck cabins, or to provide power for other equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Ten-hour off-duty rest in the sleeper berth: driver parks at a truck stop, rest area, or roadside shoulder, shuts down the main engine, and runs a diesel APU (e.g., Thermo King TriPac, Carrier ComfortPro) or a factory/aftermarket engine auto start-stop system to hold cab/bunk temperature and keep batteries charged through the night, then shuts it down in the morning. Conditions range from summer heat to sub-freezing nights; parking surfaces range from lit paved lots to gravel shoulders.

Short stationary periods of 30 minutes to 3 hours: waiting at a shipper/receiver dock, in a staging lane, or at a scale/roadside break. Driver engages idle-reduction (bunk heater, battery-based HVAC, or automatic engine start-stop) rather than idling the main engine, watches battery state of charge and cab temperature, and returns the truck to service on demand.

Hooking to an external power source instead of running any engine: at a carrier terminal, port/intermodal facility, cold-storage yard, or an electrified truck-stop bay, the driver parks in the designated space, retrieves and plugs in the shore-power cord or charging connector (extension cord to a pedestal, window adapter, or CCS/charging plug for a battery APU or electric tractor), verifies power, then disconnects and stows the cable before departure.

Running auxiliary power for onboard equipment during stops without idling the tractor: setting a trailer refrigeration unit to automatic cycling (CYCLE-SENTRY / auto start-stop) to hold setpoint on fuel-saving mode, and powering inverters, telematics, liftgate batteries, and cab electronics from the APU/battery bank at customer sites and en-route stops.

Exception handling and upkeep of the idle-reduction hardware: the APU won't start or shuts down (low fuel, plugged filter, dead battery, frozen lines, DPF regeneration required), a breaker or fuse trips, or the unit must be refueled/oil-checked. Driver climbs down, opens the frame-rail enclosure or hood in weather, diagnoses, resets/restarts, or falls back to main-engine idling and reports the fault.

roles.title: Light Truck Drivers
roles.description: Drive a light vehicle, such as a truck or van, with a capacity of less than 26,001 pounds Gross Vehicle Weight (GVW), primarily to pick up merchandise or packages from a distribution center and deliver. May load and unload vehicle.

tasks.label: Obey traffic laws and follow established traffic and transportation procedures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Suburban/residential leg of a parcel or food route: driving a van or step van on neighborhood and collector streets in daylight, fair weather — stop signs, uncontrolled intersections, parked cars, driveways, school zones, frequent curbside stops and pull-aways, all done lawfully.

Dense urban core leg: congested downtown streets with cyclists, pedestrians, buses, one-way grids, double-parked vehicles, loading-zone and no-stopping restrictions, signal-controlled intersections; driver must keep clear of crosswalks/bike lanes and avoid citations.

Line-haul/arterial leg: running a box truck or cargo van from a distribution center out to the delivery zone (or DC-to-store shuttle) on highways and multi-lane arterials — merging, lane discipline, posted speeds, following distance, toll/weigh/route restrictions.

Driving inside institution-controlled premises: distribution-center yard and dock apron, gated apartment/industrial-park or campus roads — following facility traffic rules, posted yard speeds, one-way aisles, spotter and pedestrian-lane procedures while positioning the vehicle.
Degraded-visibility conditions on public roads: night, rain, wet pavement and glare, fog, plus routine surface-street work zones, cone tapers, temporary lane closures and detour signage.
Winter/snowbelt conditions and irregular control: snow-covered or icy streets, obscured lane markings, snowbanks narrowing lanes, and flagger- or police-directed movement through closures.

sources.claim: Gatik operates freight-only (no driver, no safety observer) medium-duty box trucks in daily commercial middle-mile delivery on public highways and surface streets in Texas, Arizona and Arkansas, day and night.

sources.system: Gatik Driver

sources.claim: Gatik's driverless box trucks run scheduled routes up to 400 miles linking distribution centers, warehouses and retail ..., i.e. the same DC-to-store legs light truck drivers run.

tasks.label: Verify the contents of inventory loads against shipping papers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Parcel/package delivery driver (Amazon DSP, FedEx Ground, UPS package car) at a delivery station or hub before departure: pulls the route's bags/carts, scans each package label, matches the count and stop list to the route manifest, pulls missorts and reports missing packages. 150-300 mixed cartons and polybags, indoors on a staging floor.

Direct-store-delivery / route driver (beverage, snack, bakery, vending, foodservice) at the distribution warehouse dock: checks the staged pallets and loose cases loaded on the box truck against the load sheet/invoice, counts cases by SKU, notes shortages, damaged cases and expiry issues before signing for the load.

Delivery at a customer's receiving point (grocery/convenience store back room, restaurant kitchen door, repair shop, office): driver rolls cases/cartons in on a hand truck and checks them off line by line against the invoice or packing slip with the receiver, records shortages, damages and refusals, and obtains a signature.

Courier / parts / pharmacy / clinical-lab driver at a branch, pharmacy, or lab hub: verifies small sealed containers (totes, specimen bags, coolers, parts boxes) against a manifest — counting containers, matching IDs/part numbers, checking seals and sometimes temperature — before and after each run.

Home/curbside delivery of furniture, appliances, building materials or bulk goods: driver checks model/serial numbers and item condition against the delivery ticket at the residence or driveway with the customer, notes damage and missing pieces, and captures the customer's acceptance.

sources.system: Pickle Robot Unload System + Ambi Robotics AmbiStack
sources.title: Ambi Robotics and Pickle Robot Deliver Integrated Physical AI Solution to Fully Automate Inbound Logistics
sources.claim: Commercially integrated system in which mobile robots drive into floor-loaded trailers at ordinary warehouse dock doors, unload cases onto conveyor, and a robotic stacking cell identifies and scans every case for receiving — i.e., machine-generated identification of an entire truck load, in existing warehouses without redesign.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated inbound receiving. Verifying a load against shipping papers is exactly the receiving reconciliation this system produces — each case in the load is handled, identified and scanned against the inbound record; same objects (mixed cartons), same output (a per-item record of what the load contains), same environment (dock in a working warehouse).

sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous cycle counting/inventory audit. sources.transferJustification: Related task: inventory verification against records. The perception and reconciliation work (read pallet/case labels, count units present, compare to a document/record, report mismatches) is the same as checking a staged load against a load sheet, on the same pallet-and-case objects.

tasks.label: Inspect and maintain vehicle supplies and equipment, such as gas, oil, water, tires, lights, or brakes, to ensure that vehicles are in proper working condition.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Start/end-of-shift exterior condition check of a parcel or courier van at a delivery station or fleet depot yard: walk the vehicle, check all four tires (tread, cuts, nails, soft tire), all lamps, look under the vehicle for leaks and hanging/damaged parts, check body damage and brake condition, then log/report defects to the fleet manager. Standard van models, paved lot, institution-controlled premises.

Keeping the vehicle fueled or charged: checking the gauge/state-of-charge and refueling at the depot fuel island or a retail forecourt during or after the route (diesel/gasoline nozzle, occasionally DEF), or plugging an electric delivery van into a depot charger at end of shift.

Under-hood and in-cab checks and top-offs at the depot: open hood, check engine oil dipstick/level, coolant and washer-fluid reservoirs, add fluid as needed; check wipers, horn, mirrors, warning lights; put air in a soft tire with the yard hose before dispatch.

En-route check away from the depot: after a dash warning light, an odd noise, a curb strike, or a tire that feels low, the driver pulls over on a street, at a customer's lot or a truck stop, walks around the van, checks the tire, looks underneath for leaks, and decides whether to continue, add fluid/air, or call maintenance.

Small-operator variant (trades van, local courier, food/beverage or florist delivery, owner-operator): driver inspects and maintains their own light truck at home in a driveway, at a small business lot, or at a public gas station — checks oil and tops it up, checks tire pressure with a gauge and adds air, fills washer fluid, checks lights, fuels the vehicle.

tasks.label: Load and unload trucks, vans, or automobiles.

instances.label: Depot load-out, loose/tote loading: at a delivery station, cross-dock, or wholesale warehouse the driver loads the day's mixed cartons, totes, bags and case goods (1-50 lb) into a cargo van or box truck from carts, pallets, or a dock conveyor, stacking them to fill the cargo bay. Indoor, institution-controlled, standard dock equipment.

Depot load-out, route-sequenced step-van loading: parcel courier loads 150-300 packages of mixed size and shape into a step van's shelf racks in stop sequence, scanning and placing each parcel in a known shelf position so it can be found at the stop.

Residential/curbside stop unload: at each of 80-200 stops the driver locates that stop's 1-5 parcels among the load, removes them from the van, and carries them to a porch, apartment door, or gate. Street or driveway parking, weather, curbs, steps, gates, pets; no dock, no fixed layout.

Commercial stop unload/load: cases, cartons, roll cages or pallets delivered to a store, restaurant, clinic, office or warehouse using a dock, liftgate, hand truck or pallet jack, and returns/empties loaded back on. Premises controlled by the receiving institution, standard receiving equipment.

Heavy/bulky item handling: appliances, furniture, mattresses, tires, kegs, water coolers, lumber or equipment (75-300 lb) strapped in the truck; driver unstraps, operates the liftgate, and dollies items across driveways, thresholds and stairs into a home, office or job site, often with a helper.
End-of-shift return unload at the facility: undelivered parcels, customer returns, empty totes, bags, pallets and carts are removed from the vehicle and staged in the depot's returns/receiving area.

tasks.label: Drive vehicles with capacities under three tons to transport materials to and from specified destinations, such as railroad stations, plants, residences, offices, or within industrial yards.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Residential/consumer delivery in a metro area: driving a van or step van from a distribution center or store through suburban and urban residential streets, making a sequence of stops at homes and apartment complexes, pulling to the curb or driveway at each address, in ordinary weather. Task unit is the vehicle transport leg (loading/unloading is a separate O*NET task).

Business-to-business route delivery in a metro area: transporting parts, food service goods, pharmacy totes, linens or similar from a depot to stores, restaurants, offices and small plants over surface streets, entering retail and industrial parking lots and approaching loading docks or rear entrances, several dozen stops per shift.

Facility-to-facility shuttle/middle mile: driving a loaded box truck or cargo van between a distribution center, plant, railroad station or store, on a mix of freeway and arterial roads, one or a few fixed destinations per run, repeated multiple times per day.

On-premises material movement within an industrial yard or plant campus: moving materials, totes or trailers between buildings, docks and staging areas on private roads controlled by the employer, with pedestrian and forklift traffic present.

Rural or jobsite delivery: hauling building materials, appliances, feed or equipment over rural two-lane roads and then onto unpaved drives, farm lanes or active construction sites with no lane markings, mud/gravel, and shifting obstacles.
Degraded conditions on public roads: running the normal route during snow or ice storms, unplowed or slush-covered streets, heavy rain, fog, or flooded intersections, often before dawn or at night.

tasks.label: Turn in receipts and money received from deliveries.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Direct-store-delivery route driver (beverage/snack/food distributor) returns to the depot at end of route with a route bag holding cash, customer checks, signed invoices, credit memos and returns paperwork; counts the money, reconciles it against the day's invoices at the settlement window with a clerk, hands over cash, checks and paperwork, resolves shorts/overs and signs off.

Driver performs an unattended cash drop at the depot cash room: counts bills, coins and checks, writes a deposit slip, seals a tamper-evident bag, drops it into a floor/wall drop safe or smart safe, and files the day's signed delivery receipts and manifests in the labeled tray for accounting.

Courier / parcel / pharmacy / auto-parts branch driver checks in at the counter at end of shift, turning in a few COD cash envelopes and customer checks plus signed delivery receipts, undeliverable paperwork and the handheld scanner to a dispatcher or office clerk.

Small-business delivery driver (pizzeria, florist, small parts store, laundry route) returns to the storefront and hands the day's cash and delivery tickets across the counter or at a cluttered back-office desk to the owner/manager, counting down the cash bank together.

Driver is routed to a bank branch on the way back to deposit the day's receipts: carries a locked deposit bag with cash and checks inside, and either uses the night-depository chute or completes the deposit at a teller window/deposit ATM, returning with the validated deposit slip.

tasks.label: Use and maintain the tools or equipment found on commercial vehicles, such as weighing or measuring devices.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Parcel/courier route driver uses a handheld scanner or mobile delivery computer for every pickup and delivery: scanning package barcodes at load-out in the station, scanning at each stop, capturing signature/photo, then docking, charging, wiping down and battery-swapping the device at shift end and flagging faults. Work spans the station, business docks and residential doorsteps.

Box-truck or van driver at commercial stops (retail back rooms, warehouses, dock-equipped businesses) operates the truck's liftgate, ramp, hand truck or manual pallet jack to move pallets and case goods from the cargo box to the customer's floor, then stows the gear.

Residential/curbside delivery of bulky goods (appliances, furniture, kegs, bottled water, mattresses): driver runs the liftgate down, transfers the item to a hand truck or appliance dolly and works it over driveways, curbs, steps, lawns and apartment corridors, then re-stows gate and dolly.

Load-securement equipment in the cargo box: driver applies and releases ratchet straps, load bars, E-track fittings, cargo nets and shelf dividers as the load is worked down through the route, and inspects webbing, hooks and ratchets, pulling damaged pieces out of service.

Weighing and measuring at pickups: driver uses a portable or floor scale and a tape/dimensioner to weigh and dimension freight or parcels at a customer's shipping room or at the terminal, records the figures on the handheld, and zeroes/checks and cleans the scale.

Start/end-of-shift equipment check and upkeep in the fleet yard or delivery station: verify onboard tools are present and serviceable (dolly, straps, scale, safety kit, extinguisher, triangles), inflate dolly tires, top up liftgate hydraulic fluid, sweep out the cargo area, fuel or charge the van, and write up defects for the shop.

sources.claim: Boston Dynamics' Stretch autonomously unloads floor-loaded cases from trailers and containers in DHL supply-chain facilities, in commercial multi-country deployment at high throughput.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: unloading a truck's cargo. Transfers to the driver's use of on-vehicle material-handling equipment because the objects (cases/pallets), the confined cargo-box geometry and the accuracy required are the same; only the powered aid differs.

tasks.label: Perform emergency repairs, such as changing tires or installing light bulbs, fuses, tire chains, or spark plugs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Flat/blown tire on route: driver pulls the delivery van or light truck onto a street shoulder, curb lane or highway breakdown lane, sets triangles, chocks, retrieves the spare from an underbody carrier or cargo area, jacks the vehicle, breaks loose and removes lug nuts, swaps the wheel, torques nuts, stows the flat, and resumes deliveries - in live traffic, on uneven pavement, in whatever weather.

Tire found flat or damaged while the truck is on institution-controlled premises: distribution center yard, terminal parking area, or a customer's loading dock lot. Driver changes the wheel to the spare on flat paved ground with yard lighting and access to shop air/tools before continuing the route.

Burned-out exterior lamp (headlight, brake/tail, turn signal, clearance or cargo lamp) found at pre-trip inspection or flagged during the route. Driver opens the hood or lens/access panel, unclips the connector or bulb retainer, pulls the failed bulb from a cramped housing, seats a replacement, and verifies it lights - typically at the depot/DC yard.

Blown fuse kills a circuit mid-route (liftgate, dome/dock lights, wipers, refrigeration, power outlet). At a delivery stop or roadside, the driver locates the cab or under-hood fuse panel, reads the legend, pulls the blade fuse with a puller or fingers, checks the element, and inserts a correct-amperage spare.

Winter chain-control conditions: at a chain-up pullout or snowy roadside, driver lays out cable/link chains, drapes them over the drive tires, drives forward a few feet, hooks and tensions them (and removes them later) - kneeling in snow/slush, gloved, in cold and poor light.

Other minor emergency mechanical fixes to keep the truck moving: swapping a fouled spark plug or coil pack, cleaning/tightening a corroded battery terminal or jump-starting, replacing a wiper blade, re-seating a hose clamp or topping fluids - done at a stop, in the yard, or roadside with the hand tools carried in the truck.

sources.system: RoboTire (4th-generation robotic tire-changing system)

sources.claim: RoboTire's robotic tire-changing cell, installed and operating at Discount Tire retail stores, removes, lifts and installs tire-and-wheel assemblies on customer vehicles positioned on its platform, including unscrewing and torquing lug nuts.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: shop tire replacement. The operative physical acts of a roadside tire change - locating and removing lug nuts, pulling the wheel off the hub, hanging a replacement wheel and torquing nuts to spec on the same class of light vehicle - are exactly the acts RoboTire performs.

sources.system: RoboTire

sources.claim: RoboTire operation was machine-vision driven rather than scripted: after a VIN scan the robot arms locate the tire and lug nuts with on-board cameras and remove them, with force feedback preventing cross-threading; store technicians supervise and handle balancing.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as above; this item establishes the autonomy (vision-guided, not step-by-step teleoperation) of the wheel removal that a spare-tire swap requires.

sources.system: Radix Controls vision-guided lug-nut fastening cell
sources.title: Vision-guided robot fastens lug nuts
sources.claim: A vision-guided robot cell with Cognex In-Sight vision deployed at an automotive assembly plant locates each wheel in five axes on a roughly positioned vehicle and runs down and torques the lug nuts to spec within the line cycle time, replacing two human operators.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: wheel fastening on the vehicle assembly line. Same objects (light-vehicle wheels, lug nuts on a hub) and the same torque/precision requirement as installing a spare wheel, performed in a fixtured line cell.

sources.system: SmartBay
sources.title: Automated Tire decloaks with new autonomous tire-changing SmartBay
sources.claim: The current-generation robotic tire service bay on the market, Automated Tire's SmartBay, is only semi-automated: it changes tires with the wheels left on the vehicle and still needs a human operator ... load tires, connect the air line and place balance weights.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: shop tire service in 2026. Cited to bound present-day capability - it does not remove wheels and is not unattended, so it cannot substantiate any judgment above a fixtured cell.

sources.transferJustification: Context item on the commercial status of the decisive system; not used to support a positive judgment.

roles.description: Drive a school bus to transport students. Ensure adherence to safety rules. May assist students in boarding or exiting.

tasks.label: Comply with traffic regulations to operate vehicles in a safe and courteous manner.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Line-haul driving of the daily route between stops on residential and suburban streets in clear daylight/dawn conditions: obeying posted limits, stop signs and signals, yielding and right-of-way, tracking a 35-40 ft bus through narrow streets lined with parked cars, cyclists and turning traffic.

Route segments on arterials, multi-lane urban roads and freeways: merging, lane changes, speed-limit compliance at 45-65 mph, heavy congestion, plus occasional field/activity trips to unfamiliar destinations.
Pre-dawn darkness and wet weather: rain, spray, glare and patchy fog on the same suburban and arterial roads during the early AM run and after-dark activity runs.
Winter operation in northern districts: snow-covered or icy pavement, slush, reduced traction and visibility, sub-freezing starts, plowed but slippery streets.
Rural routes: narrow two-lane county roads, gravel/dirt sections without lane markings or shoulders, one-lane bridges, farm equipment, livestock and wildlife, dust and mud.

School arrival and dismissal: approaching and queuing in school-zone streets and the campus bus loop amid parent cars, obeying crossing guards' and police hand signals and reduced school-zone limits, and making curbside stops with children crossing in front of the bus.

tasks.label: Follow safety rules as students board and exit buses or cross streets near bus stops.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine curbside stop on a residential street in daylight: driver activates amber then red flashing lights, extends the stop arm to halt traffic both ways, opens the door, watches 2-6 elementary/middle students step from the curb and board (or exit) on the bus side, scans mirrors and the danger zone around the wheels for a dropped backpack or a child too close, closes the door, retracts the arm and pulls away only when all students are clear and seated.

The same curbside street stop but in darkness (winter morning run, evening activity run) or in rain, snow, fog or on an icy shoulder: reduced visibility of small children in dark clothing, slippery footing at the door, and motorists more likely to run the stop arm; driver must judge when it is safe to open the door and to move off.

Stop where students must cross the roadway in front of the bus: driver holds traffic with red lights and stop arm on a two-lane or multi-lane road, watches whether approaching motorists actually stop, gives the hand signal telling students when to cross, counts them across the front danger zone, and does not move until every crosser is on the sidewalk and accounted for.

School campus loading zone at morning arrival or afternoon dismissal: buses queue nose-to-tail in a bus loop on school property, school staff supervise the crowd, students load in sequence from the sidewalk side with no street crossing; driver watches for children darting between buses, keeps the door and mirrors under observation, holds position until the lane ahead and the danger zone are clear, and sweeps the bus for remaining riders.

Pre-K or special-education route: driver leaves the seat to operate the wheelchair lift or steps, escorts or steadies a small child up the steps, fastens a harness/child restraint and secures the wheelchair with straps, and at the stop releases the child hand-to-hand to an approved guardian at the curb, refusing release if no guardian is present.

Field trip or athletic/activity trip loading at an off-site location: unfamiliar parking lot or curb at a museum, stadium or park, mixed with pedestrian and vehicle traffic the driver does not control; driver positions the bus, supervises a large group boarding through one door, counts heads, and moves off only when the lot is clear of students.

sources.system: WeRide Robobus

sources.claim: WeRide's Robobus operates fully driverless with no safety officer on board at Resorts World Sentosa, carrying public passengers who board and alight at fixed stops inside an institution-controlled resort campus; it had already carried tens of thousands of passengers before removing the attendant.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: managing safe passenger boarding and alighting of a bus at designated stops (door control, waiting for riders, not moving until people are clear of the vehicle) in a pedestrian-filled, institution-controlled venue. Same vehicle class, same stop-side hazards and precision as students boarding and exiting a bus at a stop.

sources.system: May Mobility Toyota Sienna Autono-MaaS microtransit

sources.claim: May Mobility runs a commercial driver-out autonomous shuttle service with no one behind the wheel, picking up and dropping off passengers at eight pre-determined stops along a mapped corridor.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: fixed-stop passenger pick-up and drop-off without an onboard operator, i.e. stopping at the designated point and letting riders board/exit safely — the vehicle-side portion of school-bus loading and unloading. Requires pre-mapped fixed routes, so it does not transfer to unmapped or ad-hoc stops.

sources.system: Skyline (Hitachi Rail driverless metro, HART)
sources.developer: Hitachi Rail / Honolulu Authority for Rapid Transportation
sources.title: 'It's about time': Honolulu's long-awaited rail system has grand opening
sources.claim: Honolulu's Skyline is a fully automated driverless metro whose platform screen doors open only when a train is stopped, handling boarding and alighting of the riding public, including unaccompanied schoolchildren, without any onboard operator, in a purpose-built grade-separated guideway environment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: enforcing boarding/alighting safety rules for passengers at a stop — doors held closed until the vehicle is berthed, obstruction detection, departure only when the doorway is clear. Equivalent in objects (people, including children) and precision, in a purpose-built (E1) setting.

sources.system: Waymo Driver / Waymo One
sources.title: Waymo offers teen accounts for driverless rides
sources.claim: Waymo operates fully driverless ride-hailing on public streets and now allows unaccompanied minors aged 14-17 to be picked up and dropped off at the curb, showing autonomous curbside passenger boarding and exiting in unstructured settings, day and night.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: safe curbside pick-up and drop-off of minor passengers on public roads at all hours and in varied weather. Covers the door-side boarding/exiting element, but not stop-arm traffic control or supervising children crossing a roadway.

sources.system: Waymo driverless taxis (observed by BusPatrol stop-arm cameras)

sources.transferJustification: Direct negative evidence for the public-street (E3) form of this task: the school-bus stop-arm/red-light regime and the child danger zone around a loading bus are not handled reliably even by the most mature driverless fleet.

sources.system: WeRide Robobus

sources.claim: The WeRide Robobus used in these driverless deployments is described as having 360-degree sensing with no blind spots, 200 m obstacle detection and the ability to operate in all weather conditions.

tasks.label: Check the condition of a vehicle's tires, brakes, windshield wipers, lights, oil, fuel, water, and safety equipment to ensure that everything is in working order.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Morning pre-trip inspection at the district bus yard before the AM route: full state/FMCSA pre-trip on a Type C/D bus — walk-around checking tire tread, sidewalls and inflation, wheel lugs and rims, leaks under the bus; open the hood/engine access to check engine oil level on the dipstick, coolant/water level, belts and hoses, power-steering and washer fluid; in-cab checks of fuel gauge, gauges/warning lamps, horn, mirrors, wipers/washers and defroster; air-brake tests (leak-down, low-air warning, spring brake pop-out, applied-pressure/service-brake check); operate and verify all lamps including 8-way amber/red warning lights, stop arm and crossing gate; verify emergency equipment (fire extinguisher charge and seal, first-aid and body-fluid kits, reflective triangles), emergency exits, and child-check alarm; sign off the DVIR.

Between-runs / post-trip check at the yard or a school parking lot (midday kindergarten run, athletic trip, or end of PM route): shorter walk-around for new damage, tire condition, fluid drips, mirror alignment, lamp and stop-arm operation, wiper and washer function, fuel level, and presence/condition of emergency equipment; defects written up before the bus is parked or re-dispatched.

Pre-trip in adverse conditions at the yard: dark winter morning or hot/wet afternoon, snow, ice, road salt, mud or rain on the bus; frozen or crusted lamp lenses and mirrors, ice on wipers, low tire pressure from cold, cold-start air-brake build-up test, checking coolant/washer antifreeze levels, clearing snow from the roof, hood and stop arm before the systems check.

Pre-trip at an off-site location — bus parked overnight at a satellite lot, church/community lot, or the driver's home/street parking — same full inspection performed on uneven pavement or gravel with no lighting, no shop support, and passing traffic or parked cars nearby.

En-route or on-arrival condition check prompted by an event: dash warning light, unusual noise or smell, a curb strike or hitting a pothole, a reported soft brake pedal, or a wiper/light failure in rain; driver stops in a school driveway, at a stop, or on the shoulder and checks tires, lamps, fluids and brakes to decide whether the bus can continue with students aboard.

sources.system: UVeye heavy-duty inspection system (Helios/Artemis/Atlas)
sources.title: UVeye Expands AI-Powered Vehicle Inspections to Trucks, Buses, and Commercial Fleets
sources.claim: UVeye's drive-through AI scanners were extended to Class 6-8 trucks and buses with an automated 17-point inspection; vehicles drive through and are scanned without an operator.
sources.transferJustification: Same task family (vehicle condition inspection) on the same vehicle class (buses), but the scan covers only exterior, underbody and tires — it does not check oil or coolant level, wiper or lamp operation, brake application, or in-cab emergency equipment.

sources.system: UVeye heavy-duty inspection system
sources.title: UVeye expands AI vehicle inspections to heavy-duty fleets - FreightWaves

instances.label: Suburban/residential elementary (K-5) route: full-size yellow bus, ~20-30 curbside stops on neighborhood streets, red lights and stop arm deployed, driver checks the danger zone, escorts crossers, verifies kindergartners are released to a waiting guardian, holds a tight bell schedule.

Suburban/residential middle- and high-school route: 40-60 teenagers who board and exit unassisted at ~15 neighborhood stops on public streets; driver's duties are stop-arm procedure, mirror checks and on-time arrival.

Urban route, mixed ages: congested arterials and narrow residential streets, double-parked cars, cyclists and dense pedestrian traffic, frequent stops, crowded bus, schedule pressure from traffic signals and layover times at the school loading zone.

Rural route, mixed ages: 60-90 minutes over gravel/unpaved and unlit roads, farm driveways, stops on 55 mph highway shoulders where children cross the road, long gaps between stops, livestock/wildlife and washboard surfaces.

Any route run under adverse conditions: pre-dawn darkness, snow/ice, heavy rain or fog, poor traction on hills, construction detours and blocked streets, with the same fixed pickup times and stop locations.

Special-needs route: door-to-door pickup at the home, operating the wheelchair lift, rolling the chair aboard and securing it with four-point tiedowns and occupant belt, buckling harnesses/car seats, and hand-to-hand release of each student to a parent or aide at drop-off.

tasks.label: Escort small children across roads and highways.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Neighborhood/rural two-lane road stop: driver halts the bus, sets red flashers and stop arm, dismounts, checks both directions, then walks one to three kindergarten–2nd-grade students from the bus door across the roadway in front of the bus to the far shoulder or driveway, keeping them within arm's reach and watching for motorists who run the stop arm; repeated at several stops per run.

Crossing a higher-speed rural highway or multi-lane arterial: 45–55 mph traffic, hills/curves limiting sightlines, no sidewalk or shoulder; driver holds children back at the curb, judges gaps and stopped-vehicle compliance, uses a hand signal to release them, aborts and pulls children back if a vehicle fails to stop.

Adverse conditions crossing: dark winter mornings or dusk, rain, fog, blowing snow, icy or muddy shoulder; children in dark clothing, hoods up, dropping backpacks or papers; driver steadies or carries a small child, retrieves dropped items, and keeps the group visible to traffic.

Escorting a very young child or a student with a disability or behavioral needs who may bolt into the road, refuse to move, or need hand-holding; includes verifying a parent/guardian is present on the far side and releasing the child only to that adult, or returning the child to the bus if no one is waiting.

On school grounds: leading a line of small children across the bus loop, internal drive or parking lot between the parked bus and the building entrance/crosswalk, in coordination with school staff, other buses and parent traffic.

tasks.label: Drive gasoline, diesel, or electrically powered multi-passenger vehicles to transport students between neighborhoods, schools, and school activities.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Regular home-to-school route in a suburban/residential neighborhood in fair weather: full-size 65-77 passenger yellow bus, 25-50 designated stops, K-12 riders boarding and alighting, activating amber/red flashing lights and stop arm, monitoring children crossing in front of the bus, parked cars, driveways, mixed traffic, arrival at a school loading zone on a tight bell schedule.

Dense urban route: full-size bus on congested arterials and narrow one-way streets, double-parked vehicles, cyclists, jaywalking pedestrians, curbside stops with children crossing, queuing into a crowded school loading zone with dozens of other buses and parent cars.

Rural route: 45-55 mph two-lane and gravel/dirt roads, long distances between widely spaced stops, unlit predawn pickups, uncontrolled railroad crossings requiring the stop-look-listen procedure, livestock/deer, narrow shoulders and turnarounds in farm driveways.

Field trip / athletic or activity trip: drive a loaded bus to an unfamiliar destination (museum, stadium, another district) over highways and unfamiliar arterials, maneuver and park in an unfamiliar lot or curbside staging area, wait, then return, often after dark.

Special-needs / small-bus door-to-door route: lift-equipped bus, curbside pickups at individual homes, operating the wheelchair lift and securing chairs/occupants, handing students to a parent or aide at each end, tight driveway maneuvering and backing.

Regular route run under adverse conditions: snow, ice, heavy rain, fog or darkness; reduced traction and visibility, hill starts on unplowed neighborhood streets, chain-up requirements, judgment calls about which stops are safe to serve.

tasks.label: Keep bus interiors clean for students.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Between-runs / end-of-route walk-through of the parked bus at a school loop or the district lot: driver walks the ~30 cm aisle, picks wrappers, papers, juice boxes, bottles and food debris off seats, out of seat cracks and off the floor, bags it, and retrieves items students left behind.

Daily floor sweep-out of the parked bus at the district bus lot after loose trash has been bagged: broom-and-dustpan or depot vacuum over the aisle, stepwell and under-seat floor to remove sand, grit, crumbs, leaves and dried mud.

Periodic wipe-down/disinfection of high-touch interior surfaces (handrails, stanchions, seat tops and backs, driver area) and cleaning of interior windows and mirrors, done at the lot with spray bottle and cloths, often on a weekly or illness-season schedule.

Immediate cleanup of a spill or biohazard: a student vomits or spills a drink mid-route or at the school; driver pulls over or handles it at the loading zone, uses the absorbent/disinfectant kit, isolates the seat, and cleans it enough to finish the run, sometimes with students still aboard.

Periodic deep clean at the district bus garage (monthly / seasonal / summer prep): mop and scrub the rubber floor and stepwell, wash vinyl seat surfaces and seat backs, clean all interior glass, dust the dash and cage areas.
Removing chewing gum, sticky dried-soda residue, and pen/marker marks or small graffiti from seat cushions, seat backs and floor, using scraper, solvent and elbow grease.

tasks.label: Regulate heating, lighting, and ventilation systems for student comfort.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cold-weather morning route: driver starts the bus at the yard (or plugged-in electric bus), runs heater/defroster to warm the cabin before students board, then adjusts front and rear heater switches, fan speeds and defrost over the route as outside temperature and passenger load change.

Hot-weather route on a bus WITHOUT air conditioning (still roughly half of US school buses): driver hand-cranks/latches the roof escape hatches to the vent position, opens the driver window and entry door at stops, runs roof exhaust fans, and manages student window use (down for airflow, up in rain or for safety).

Hot-weather route on an air-conditioned bus (common in the South and standard on special-education buses): driver pre-cools the cabin before pickup, sets AC/blower and vent distribution, and adjusts through the route as the bus fills and empties.

Interior lighting: driver switches dome and stepwell lights on for pre-dawn and after-dark loading/unloading and for activity/athletic trips, and turns them down or off while driving so cabin glare does not impair night vision.

Mid-route balancing on a mixed day: students at the back call out that it is cold while the front is too warm; driver trims heat/AC zones, redirects vents, cracks a window for stale air or carsickness, and keeps windshield and entry-door glass defogged, all while driving the route on schedule.

Special-needs route with wheelchair-secured, medically fragile or nonverbal students: driver watches individual students for signs of overheating or chill and adjusts rear heaters, individual vents and window position per each student's care plan.

tasks.label: Make minor repairs to vehicles.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Pre-/post-trip fluid service in the district bus yard: driver releases the hood latch, checks dipstick and reservoirs, and tops off windshield washer fluid, engine oil or coolant from jugs kept in the garage, recaps and closes hood. Standard fleet buses, outdoor paved yard, all weather.

Replace a burned-out exterior lamp bulb, cracked lens, or blown fuse at the depot: unscrew a marker/stop-arm/clearance lamp lens or open the fuse panel, pull the failed bulb or fuse, seat a new one, check that the circuit works, reseal.

Tighten or adjust loose hardware with hand tools in the yard or garage bay: mirror bracket and crossing-gate bolts, handrail, entry-door hardware, corroded/loose battery terminal clamp; swap a worn windshield wiper blade and re-aim mirrors.

On-route roadside minor fix with students aboard: bus stalls, a door or stop arm sticks, a wiper comes off, snow/ice covers lamps and mirrors, or a battery cable works loose. Driver diagnoses on the shoulder, makes the quick fix or secures the item, and decides whether to call the shop.

Interior minor repair at the depot: reattach a loose seat cushion or seat back, retorque seat/floor bolts, secure a rattling interior panel, window latch or emergency-exit hardware, working inside the bus's narrow aisle between fixed seat rows.
Tire and wheel attention in the yard: check pressures and add air from the yard hose, replace a valve cap, pull a nail-flagged wheel or mount a spare, torque lug nuts before the shop signs it off.

roles.title: Bus Drivers, Transit and Intercity
aliases: CDL Bus Driver (Commercial Driver's License Bus Driver)
roles.description: Drive bus or motor coach, including regular route operations, charters, and private carriage. May assist passengers with baggage. May collect fares or tickets.

tasks.label: Drive vehicles over specified routes or to specified destinations according to time schedules, complying with traffic regulations to ensure that passengers have a smooth and safe ride.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dense urban fixed-route service: a 40-ft low-floor transit bus worked through city traffic on a mapped route with 30-60 stops, curb docking close enough for ramp deployment, jaywalkers, cyclists, double-parked cars, work zones, headway/schedule adherence, day and night, all weather.
Suburban/small-city fixed route: 35-40 ft bus on signalized arterials, residential collector streets and park-and-ride lots, moderate traffic, timed transfers at a transit center, occasional detours.

Low-density community circulator or small-vehicle shuttle route on public streets (cutaway/8-15 seat bus, senior or neighborhood loop, station connector), light traffic, few passengers, modest speeds.

Intercity/express coach: 45-ft motorcoach line-haul on interstate highways between city terminals, several hours, night driving, rain/wind/mountain grades, terminal approach and gate docking on schedule.

Charter and private-carriage trip: motorcoach taken to varied, often unfamiliar destinations (school groups, casinos, event venues), unmapped local streets, hotel driveways, event parking lots and curbside loading zones, itinerary set by the client.

Institutional shuttle circulator on institution-controlled premises: airport employee/terminal shuttle roads, university campus loops, resort or medical-center grounds, fixed short loop, controlled access, pedestrians present.

tasks.label: Park vehicles at loading areas so that passengers can board.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Low-speed, mapped local route (campus circulator, suburban feeder, small-city downtown loop): driver eases a small/mid-size bus to a marked curbside stop on a public street, light-to-moderate traffic, stops at fixed sign posts, doors open for boarding.

Standard urban fixed-route service with a 40-60 ft transit bus: pulling out of dense mixed traffic into a curbside stop, docking parallel within inches of the curb for kneeling/ramp deployment, dozens of stops per trip, stops often blocked by delivery trucks, parked cars, snow banks or waiting crowds, all weather, day and night.
Transit center / park-and-ride: bus pulled into a numbered sawtooth berth at an agency-controlled hub, aligned with the shelter door zone, layover, then loading of a queued crowd before departure.

Intercity motorcoach at a bus station gate: 45-ft coach maneuvered into a numbered loading bay on a station platform (often nose-in with a later reverse-out), positioned so baggage bays and the door face the platform queue.

Charter / private carriage pickup: coach positioned at a hotel porte-cochere, school driveway, church, casino, wedding venue or event parking lot; loading spot improvised on arrival amid cones, crowds, parked cars, sometimes double-parked on a street.

Airport terminal curb and airport shuttle stops (rental-car center, employee lot, hotel shuttle): bus stopped in a designated, marshalled bus zone on airport-controlled roadway, congested with other buses and shuttles.

tasks.label: Inspect vehicles and check gas, oil, and water levels prior to departure.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Transit bus pull-out from a division garage/yard: driver locates the assigned 40-ft bus in the yard, reviews the prior DVIR, walks around checking tires, wheels, lights, mirrors, body damage and leaks under the bus, opens the rear engine hatch to check engine oil and coolant levels, checks the fuel/gauge readings in the cab, performs the air-brake tests (build-up, applied leakage, low-air warning, spring-brake set), cycles the wheelchair ramp, doors and destination sign, checks fire extinguisher/triangles and interior, then signs the pre-trip report. Outdoors, all weather, other buses moving in the yard.

Intercity/commuter motorcoach pre-trip at the carrier's terminal or maintenance facility before a scheduled run: driver inspects a 45-ft coach including baggage bay doors and latches, tires and duals, air suspension, engine compartment oil/coolant levels and belts, lavatory/HVAC, emergency exits and hatches, lighting, and full air-brake checks, then completes the DVIR before departing on a several-hundred-mile run.

Charter/tour coach pre-trip at a remote overnight location — hotel, casino or school parking lot, or on-street parking — where the coach has been sitting overnight with no facility support: driver walks around in whatever lighting and weather exists, checks tires/lights/leaks and engine-bay fluid levels, runs the brake checks and boards to check the interior before picking up the group.

Relief/mid-shift takeover at an on-street relief point or curbside layover: incoming driver takes over a bus already in service, does a quick walkaround for tire condition, body damage and leaks, boards to check mirrors, gauges (fuel/air pressure), brake feel, wheelchair ramp and interior condition, and notes any defects before continuing the run, all within a few minutes at the curb in traffic.

Pre-departure re-check in the depot service lane/indoor bay right after servicers have fueled, washed and topped off fluids: driver verifies fuel and fluid levels and gauge readings, confirms the items on the last work order, walks the bus for damage from the wash/fuel island, checks lights and brakes, and signs off before pulling out.

tasks.label: Announce stops to passengers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Assist passengers, such as elderly or individuals with disabilities, on and off bus, ensure they are seated properly, help carry baggage, and answer questions about bus schedules or routes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Fixed-route city transit, curbside stop: a power wheelchair or scooter user boards. Driver kneels the bus, deploys the ramp, clears/folds the securement-area seats, waits while the rider positions the device rear-facing, secures it (or confirms self-securement), then releases and re-deploys the ramp at the alighting stop.

Fixed-route transit: an ambulatory passenger who is elderly, frail, blind, or uses a cane/walker needs a steadying arm up the steps, help lifting a walker or grocery cart aboard, guidance to a priority seat, and the driver holding the bus until they are seated; conditions vary (rain, snow, high curb, crowded aisle).

Intercity motorcoach at a bus terminal loading bay: driver stands at the open underfloor bays taking 30-50 lb suitcases from a queue of passengers, tagging and stacking them in the bay, then unloading and handing them back at destination, under a departure-time clock.

Purely verbal assistance: a passenger at the door, on the curb, or from a front seat asks whether this bus goes to a given destination, when the next one runs, where to transfer, or what the fare is; driver answers, sometimes points out the stop and calls it out later.

Intercity coach, charter or private carriage at a varied pickup point (hotel entrance, event venue, roadside, senior center): driver operates the high-floor wheelchair lift, physically maneuvers a passenger who cannot self-position onto the platform, transfers/straps them, and stows the mobility aid in the bay.

tasks.label: Regulate heating, lighting, and ventilating systems for passenger comfort.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Regular urban/suburban fixed-route revenue service on a modern low-floor transit bus: at pull-out and throughout the shift the operator switches the HVAC master on, verifies/sets the cabin temperature setpoint, runs the driver's-area fan and defroster, and turns saloon interior lights on/off (and dims them to cut windshield glare) as daylight, weather and passenger loads change over a 6-10 hour shift.

Intercity motorcoach or long charter run: driver sets front/rear zone temperatures and fan levels at departure, dims or extinguishes cabin lighting at night or during on-board video while leaving reading-light circuits and passenger air vents live, and re-adjusts setpoints as the coach crosses climate zones or as groups of passengers say they are too warm/too cold.

Extreme-weather pre-trip at the garage/yard: operator starts the bus, runs the heater/defroster (or pre-cools in summer) to bring the saloon to a comfortable temperature and clear/de-ice windshield and windows before pull-out, and checks that interior and step-well lighting works, all inside an agency-controlled depot.

Hands-on adjustment beyond the console: older or non-thermostatic buses with manual heater/fan levers and separate light switches, or situations where the operator must physically open/close roof hatches or sliding vent windows, close a stuck vent, or reposition a passenger seated in a draft, in response to an individual rider's complaint mid-route.

Comfort-system malfunction in service: A/C blows hot in summer, heater fails in winter, or interior lights go out; operator diagnoses, resets breakers/switches, mitigates by opening hatches and windows, informs passengers, radios dispatch and writes a defect report or waits for a bus swap.

tasks.label: Maintain cleanliness of bus or motor coach.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Transit route bus at an end-of-line layover or on pull-in at the garage: the operator walks the aisle and picks up newspapers, coffee cups, bottles, food wrappers and bags from seats, seat wells and the floor, bags the trash, and gives the aisle and stepwells a quick sweep. Litter is varied and unpredictable; some items are sticky or wedged between cushions.

Operator-area upkeep during a shift: wiping the dash, farebox surround, steering wheel, grab rails and inside of the windshield, cleaning smudges and fingerprints from mirrors and the operator barrier, and wiping high-touch surfaces with disinfectant between runs; done in a few minutes at a terminal or layover.

Mid-route incident cleanup on a bus in revenue service: a passenger spills a drink or is sick, or glass/food is smashed in the aisle. The driver uses the onboard spill kit (absorbent, scraper, gloves, disinfectant, bags), cleans and disinfects the area or removes the bus from service, with passengers aboard and a schedule running.

Motorcoach charter/intercity turn between trips, at a depot, terminal or parking lot: empty the seat-back and door trash receptacles, vacuum the aisle, seats and parcel racks, wipe tray tables, armrests, handrails and interior windows, straighten seat belts and curtains, and restock supplies before the next group boards.

Servicing the onboard lavatory of an intercity/charter coach: wipe the bowl, sink and walls in a very confined compartment, empty the waste bin, deodorize, restock tissue and hand sanitizer, and (at the service yard) dump and recharge the holding tank.

Exterior cleaning at the depot service lane or fuel island: run the bus/coach through the wash, and clean the windshield, mirrors, headlights, entrance door glass and road grime by hand with squeegee, brush and hose before pull-out.

It is the closest demonstrated capability to bus interior cleaning, but it is a proof-of-concept that does not pick up and bag loose litter.

sources.transferJustification: Same environment (transit bus interior) but a narrower task: surface disinfection only. It does not sweep, collect litter, or wipe operator-area surfaces, so it cannot substantiate completion of the driver's cleanliness instances.

sources.claim: Tesla has shown a fixed robotic arm that cleans a Cybercab cabin — vacuuming debris, picking up trash and wiping surfaces — and a Texas permit lists a 'Cleaning Robot' installed at its Austin robotaxi hub; the public evidence is a promotional video and a building permit, with no independent verification of autonomous, worker-quality operation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: cleaning a passenger vehicle cabin between rides. Transfer to a 40-ft bus is weak (two-seat pod vs. 40 seats, aisle, stepwells), and autonomy is unverified, so it is recorded but not relied on for a positive judgment.

Exterior robotic washing is commercial (supports E1 exterior washing); interior arm cleaning is limited to passenger-car cabins at one beta site, so it does not substantiate a bus interior turn.

tasks.label: Load and unload baggage in baggage compartments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Intercity line-run departure at a bus terminal platform: driver stands at the open underfloor bay, takes tagged suitcases from queuing passengers or a baggage cart, lifts them (typically 20-50 lb) and stacks them to fill the bay, keeping bags for different drop-off stops sorted by bay; must finish within the scheduled dwell of a few minutes.

Charter/tour coach at a hotel porte-cochere or airport curb: a bulk pile of 30-50 group suitcases on the pavement must be lifted and packed tightly into two or three side bays so everything fits; passengers, bellstaff and traffic are moving around the coach.

Arrival unloading at a terminal platform or hotel curb: driver opens the bays, pulls bags out (often from the back of a packed bay), sets them on the curb, and hands them to the correct passengers or checks claim tags, under time pressure with passengers crowding the bay door.

Team, school or church group charter loading in a school/stadium parking lot: mixed irregular items - duffels, hockey/band equipment bags, coolers, instrument cases, boxes of supplies - handed over in no particular order and wedged into the bays.

Intermediate roadside or street-corner stop: a few bags loaded or retrieved at a curb, gas-station lot or rural flag stop with no platform, in whatever weather and lighting is present, with the bay opened at the roadside.

sources.system: Vanderlande BAGLOAD
sources.title: Our vision for automating the handler processes at airports - Vanderlande
sources.claim: Vanderlande's BAGLOAD is a commercial robotic system that fully automatically loads passenger bags from the baggage handling system into containers/carts in an airport make-up hall (a fenced, conveyor-fed robot cell).
sources.transferJustification: Related task: airport baggage make-up. The objects are the same (passenger suitcases and soft bags, ~20-50 lb, mixed shapes) and the act is the same (lift each bag and stack it to fill a wheeled compartment); only the surrounding environment differs, which is what the E1 counterfactual holds fixed.

sources.system: Vanderlande BAGLOAD with Mujin control and Zivid 3D cameras (Oslo Airport)

sources.transferJustification: Same as above: robotic lifting and stacking of real passenger luggage into transport containers, in live airport operation, differing from the bus task only in the environment and in who hands the bag over.

sources.claim: Grenzebach's fully automated robotic baggage loading system has been in operation at Frankfurt Airport since 2013, loading ramp carts and containers with passenger bags at industrial throughput while staff supervise rather than lift.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic loading of passenger suitcases into ramp carts and containers. Same objects and same stacking/space-filling requirement as packing a coach bay; the robot works from a conveyor in a purpose-built cell, i.e. the E1 counterfactual.

sources.system: Sarcos / Changi Airport Group outdoor baggage-handling robot
sources.developer: Sarcos Technology and Robotics (now Palladyne AI) with Changi Airport Group

sources.transferJustification: Directly analogous task (loading loose passenger bags into a vehicle hold in an institution-controlled outdoor setting); cited to show the E2 case is a prototype whose autonomy is not established, so it cannot support a positive E2 judgment.

roles.title: Shuttle Drivers and Chauffeurs
roles.description: Drive a motor vehicle to transport passengers on a planned or scheduled basis. May collect a fare. Includes nonemergency medical transporters and hearse drivers.

tasks.label: Test vehicle equipment, such as lights, brakes, horns, or windshield wipers, to ensure proper operation.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Pre-shift check of an airport/hotel/university shuttle bus or 15-passenger van in the operator's yard or garage: driver walks around while cycling headlights, tail/brake lights, turn signals and hazards, sounds the horn, runs wipers and washers, checks mirrors and tires, and does a pedal or air-brake application test, then signs the inspection sheet.

Chauffeur/black-car or limousine driver checking a sedan, SUV or stretch before a client run, in the company garage or fleet lot: headlights/high beams, marker and brake lamps, turn signals, horn, wipers and washer spray, brake feel, plus interior equipment; defects reported to dispatch/maintenance before the vehicle leaves.

Non-emergency medical transport driver's daily vehicle inspection at the provider's yard: lights, horn, wipers, brakes, plus cycling the wheelchair lift or ramp and checking securement hardware, recording results on a DVIR.

Driver checks a vehicle parked outdoors overnight in an unstructured spot (residential driveway, street parking, funeral-home apron, hotel forecourt): tests lights, wipers/washers, horn and brakes before the first trip, in whatever weather and lighting is present.

En-route/mid-shift check at the curb, a rest area or a passenger pickup: a warning lamp appears, a wiper streaks in rain, or a passenger reports a lamp out; driver tests the item on the spot and makes a go/no-go call.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: factory brake/ABS functional testing of complete vehicles; it verifies the same braking equipment a driver checks, with the vehicle brought to and fixtured on the machine.

tasks.label: Check the condition of a vehicle's tires, brakes, windshield wipers, lights, oil, fuel, water, and safety equipment to ensure that everything is in working order.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Start-of-shift pre-trip inspection of a 15-passenger shuttle van or 40-ft shuttle bus in the operator's yard/depot: walk-around for tire tread/pressure/lug nuts, lights and turn signals, mirrors and glass, wipers/washer, hood raised to check engine oil, coolant/water and belts, fuel level, service/air-brake test, horn, and in-cab emergency equipment (fire extinguisher, triangles, first-aid kit), then sign the DVIR.

Chauffeur/black-car or limo driver's pre-service check of a sedan, SUV or stretch limo at the company garage or lot before the first client pickup: tires and pressures, lamps, wipers and washer fluid, oil and coolant levels, fuel top-off, warning lights on the dash, emergency kit, plus glass and body condition.

Non-emergency medical transport / paratransit driver's daily check of a wheelchair van at the fleet yard: cycling and inspecting the lift or ramp, checking securement straps and belts, oxygen/first-aid kit and fire extinguisher, plus tires, lights, wipers, oil, coolant and fuel.

End-of-shift/post-trip condition check of a shuttle van or bus at the operating base, focused on the vehicle's exterior mechanical condition: tires (tread, cuts, embedded nails, pressure), wheels, body damage, cracked or broken lamps, and fluid leaks or undercarriage wear, producing a defect report for the maintenance shop.

Quick between-runs walk-around away from base (airport shuttle holding lot, hotel entrance, casino or hospital curb, client site): eyeballing tires, checking lamps and glass, looking for puddles/leaks under the vehicle, topping washer fluid, and confirming fuel level before the next passenger run.

instances.label: NEMT/paratransit pickup at a private residence: driver parks at the curb or driveway, goes to the door, escorts or pushes the rider in a manual or power wheelchair over uneven walkway, operates the powered lift or ramp, positions the chair in the vehicle, attaches four tie-down straps to the chair frame plus a lap/shoulder occupant belt, drives on public streets to a clinic, and reverses the process at the destination.

Round trip between institutional facilities (nursing home, dialysis center, hospital discharge, adult day program): staff hand off a frail or cognitively impaired wheelchair passenger, driver loads via lift, secures chair and occupant, signs paperwork, drives public roads, and hands the passenger off at the receiving facility door.

Fixed-route accessible shuttle on institutional premises (airport terminal-to-rental-car or parking lot bus, hotel/casino shuttle, senior community or hospital campus shuttle): a wheelchair rider boards via lift/ramp at a marked stop, driver secures the chair and belt, stows luggage or a walker, and drives the loop while other passengers board and alight.

Special-needs school or agency transport: driver (with or without an aide) picks up students with disabilities at home curbs, loads wheelchairs on a lift, applies tie-downs, fastens harnesses or child safety seats, monitors behavior and medical devices en route, and releases each student only to an authorized adult.

Semi-ambulatory rider with special needs in a lift-equipped van (walks with a cane, low vision, or mild cognitive impairment): boards unaided using the steps and handrail, sits in a regular seat and fastens the seat belt themselves; the driver confirms the belt and provides safe curb-to-curb transport on public streets.

instances.label: Between runs, the driver pulls the shuttle van or sedan into a public self-serve gas station, swipes a fleet card, selects grade, inserts the nozzle, fills the tank (often in rain, cold, or at night), replaces the cap, takes the receipt, and logs the gallons/odometer.

At the company lot or garage, the driver opens the hood, pulls and reads the engine oil dipstick, checks coolant reservoir and windshield washer level, and tops off oil, coolant, or washer fluid from jugs kept on site.

Away from base — hotel parking lot, airport hold lot, or roadside — the driver tops off windshield washer fluid or adds coolant/water from a jug carried in the vehicle after a warning light or empty washer during a trip.

instances.label: Hotel/airport shuttle run: at the hotel porte-cochere and the terminal curb the driver lifts guests' rolling suitcases, duffels and boxes off the sidewalk into the van's rear cargo bay or trailer, stacks them so nothing shifts, then unloads and hands each bag back to the right guest; passengers board the van's steps on their own.

Chauffeur/black-car pickup: driver meets the client at a residence, office lobby or airport arrivals, opens and holds the passenger door, offers a hand or umbrella as the client sits down and again on exit, and stows briefcases, garment bags and suitcases in the sedan/SUV trunk.

Non-emergency medical transport of a wheelchair user: driver goes to the door of a home or clinic, pushes the manual wheelchair over thresholds and curbs, deploys the lift or ramp, rolls the passenger aboard, positions and secures the chair with four tie-downs and a lap/shoulder belt, and reverses the process at the destination.

NEMT/senior-shuttle ambulatory passenger: driver steadies a frail, visually impaired or unsteady rider by the arm, places their hand on the grab bar, helps them step up into the van and settle in the seat, folds and stows the walker, cane or oxygen bottle, buckles the belt, and helps them out at the clinic.

Fixed-route employee/campus/hotel shuttle at a stop: driver kneels the bus and deploys the ramp for a wheelchair or stroller, lifts riders' backpacks, boxes and roller bags into the interior luggage rack, and steadies older riders up the steps, working in traffic, rain or snow within a short dwell time.

Funeral coach/limousine service: driver opens limousine doors at the funeral home, church and graveside, hands elderly mourners in and out on uneven ground, and carries flowers, coats and personal effects for the family.

instances.label: Hotel/airport courtesy shuttle van (8–15 passengers) looping between terminal curb, parking lot and hotel: driver sets dash climate at shift start, boosts A/C or heat as the door cycles open at every stop, aims/opens rear vents, switches interior dome lights on for night boarding, and answers occasional 'too hot/too cold' requests while driving public streets.

Chauffeur / black-car or stretch-limousine service: cabin pre-cooled or pre-heated before the client boards, rear-zone temperature and ambient/reading lights set to the client's stated preference, adjusted mid-ride on spoken request, ventilation balanced for a partitioned rear compartment.

Nonemergency medical transport van: driver keeps the cabin warm/cool for frail, elderly or wheelchair-seated passengers, runs heat while the lift door stands open during loading, redirects vents away from a patient, ventilates for odor or nausea, dims interior lighting for a sensitive rider.

Large employee/parking-lot/casino shuttle bus (25–40 passengers) with roof-mounted passenger-compartment HVAC: driver works the dash climate panel and interior lighting switches for the saloon, runs defrost/fresh-air modes, opens roof hatches or windows when cooling can't keep up on a hot day of frequent door openings.

Scheduled fixed-route shuttle circulating inside an institution-controlled campus (hospital, university, corporate site, retirement community, airport airside/landside roads): frequent stops, controlled premises and standard vehicles; driver keeps cabin temperature and lighting steady across a repeating loop.

Hearse or funeral-procession family car: subdued interior lighting, gentle, quiet climate setting for mourners in the limousine, ventilation managed for floral arrangements and slow-speed procession driving.

Occasional cash payment with change. Pickups at private residences, office curbs and public streets.

Tour, charter or event walk-up shuttle at a public curb or street stop: driver collects cash fares or discount coupons/vouchers from walk-up riders, makes change from a cash apron, and issues a paper ticket or receipt, outdoors in weather and crowds.

tasks.label: Collect fares or vouchers from passengers, and make change or issue receipts as necessary.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: App/e-hail prepaid trip (Uber/Lyft/Curb/Arro-type dispatch): at drop-off the fare is charged automatically to the rider's stored payment method; driver ends the trip and the rider gets a digital receipt; no cash or paper changes hands, though a cash tip may be offered.

Metered street-hail or radio-dispatch trip paid by credit/debit card on the in-cab terminal or the driver's reader: driver closes the meter, presents the terminal, rider taps or dips and selects a tip, driver confirms approval and hands over a printed receipt or sends an emailed one; done curbside, often with traffic behind and the rider in a hurry.

Cash fare at the curb: rider hands over bills (often a $20 or $50 for a small fare), driver counts them under poor light, makes change from his own bank of bills and coins, returns the change with a printed or hand-written receipt, and secures the cash.

Corporate/account or e-voucher trip: the ride is billed to a business account, hotel/airline arrangement, or dispatch-app voucher code; driver records the account/voucher reference and no money changes hands at drop-off.

Paper voucher or taxi scrip trip (medical/paratransit, senior scrip, corporate chit): driver inspects the voucher for validity and coverage, writes in trip details and fare, collects any co-pay, obtains the passenger's signature, and retains the voucher for reimbursement.

Problem transaction: card declines or the terminal is down, rider is short of cash or wants to split cash and card, disputes the metered fare or a toll/surcharge, demands a hand-written receipt for a different amount, or attempts to leave without paying; driver negotiates, calls dispatch, or documents the incident.

Assisted-mobility or non-emergency medical fare: wheelchair-accessible van requiring ramp deployment and wheelchair securement, or a frail/elderly or blind passenger needing door-through-door help into and out of the vehicle plus loading of walkers, groceries or bags.

tasks.label: Follow relevant safety regulations and state laws governing vehicle operation, and ensure that passengers follow safety regulations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine fare on city and suburban public streets and arterials in fair, dry conditions (day or night): obeying posted speed limits, signals, stop signs, lane and turn restrictions, yielding to pedestrians and cyclists, and making a lawful curbside pickup and drop-off without blocking a hydrant, crosswalk or driveway.

Fare through dense congested downtown or mixed-use corridors where compliance is contested: double-parked delivery trucks, bus-only and bike lanes, no-stopping zones, school zones and stopped school buses with stop arms out, work zones with flaggers, approaching emergency vehicles, and occasional direction by a police officer or a pull-over.

Fare driven in routine adverse conditions - night rain, wet glare, fog, wind, dust - requiring lawful speed reduction, greater following distance, headlight/wiper use and cautious stopping distances on public roads.

Fare driven in severe conditions - heavy thunderstorm with ponded or flooded roadway, snow, sleet or ice - requiring the driver to judge whether a road is passable, avoid flooded crossings, and either proceed lawfully at greatly reduced speed or refuse/abort the trip.

Routine in-cabin safety-rule enforcement during a fare: confirming all occupants are belted before moving, holding the passenger count to the vehicle's legal capacity, keeping doors shut and limbs and objects inside the vehicle, no smoking/vaping or open containers, and requiring a child restraint for a small child.

Fare with a non-compliant passenger - intoxicated late-night rider who refuses to buckle, tries to smoke, hangs out the window, opens a door in traffic or becomes belligerent - requiring the driver to gain compliance, stop safely, refuse or terminate service, or summon police.

Airport or major-venue trip governed by the property owner's rules: entering the designated taxi/TNC staging lot or holding area, following ground-transportation queue and posted routing rules, and loading or unloading only in the assigned curb zone on airport property.

tasks.label: Perform routine vehicle maintenance, such as regulating tire pressure and adding gasoline, oil, and water.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Mid-shift refueling: driver pulls the taxi into a public self-service gas station, pays at the pump, opens the fuel flap, fills the tank with gasoline, replaces the cap and returns to the road. Forecourt is operator-controlled, standard dispensers, mixed traffic and weather.

Charging an electric/plug-in taxi: driver pulls into a fleet depot bay or public DC fast-charge stall, plugs the connector into the vehicle inlet, authorizes the session, monitors it and unplugs when charged.

Tire pressure check and top-up: driver uses a gauge on all four tires at a station air pump or in the fleet yard, adds air to spec on the low ones (valve caps off/on), and confirms pressures before the shift.

Under-hood fluid check and top-up between shifts at home, curbside or in a parking lot: pop the hood, pull and read the oil dipstick, add a quart of oil if low, top up windshield washer fluid and radiator/coolant overflow with water/coolant. Ground may be uneven, lighting variable.

Pre-shift service check at the taxi company's garage/yard: attendant-style routine on a fleet vehicle — fill from the fleet fuel pump, check oil and coolant levels under the hood, top up washer fluid, and set tire pressures, all in one pass inside a controlled fleet facility.
